He found out which day the farmer would be plowing a certain field and buried two fake yuanbao ingots there ahead of time, weighing a hundred taels in total. While the farmer was hard at his plowing, the crook deliberately wandered the hillside nearby, pretending to search left and right. The farmer asked, “What are you looking for here?” The con man said, “I am looking for something. What is it to you?” The farmer had to keep quiet. The con man then examined one tree, then another, like a man who had lost something. The farmer spoke again: “You are a strange one—what do you mean by going all over the hill checking trees?” The con man said, “I will not hide it from you. Years ago my late father was captured by roving bandits and joined their gang. Later he came into so much silver that he could not carry it alone, so he buried it in various places and left an account book recording the spots, meaning to come back for it—but he died, poor man. Now I have come with the book to find the one under a tree here, and I cannot tell which tree it is. Lucky for me you are here. Come help me look; if we find it, I do not mind sharing some with you.” The farmer took his hoe and searched with him. Sure enough, under one tree they found two yuanbao. The con man feigned great delight and said, “If we have found this one, all the other spots can be found. I am truly willing to share it with you—only we have no hammer or chisel here.” He went on, “I have nowhere to keep this silver. Why not go to your house? Help me finish the search, and I will thank you with several ingots. What do you say?” The farmer said, “Fine with me. But you and I have never met. If you suddenly start coming and going at my house, will people not grow suspicious?” The con man said, “We should say I am some relative or old friend.” The farmer said, “I have it. I had a brother-in-law, my wife’s brother, who was sold at six or seven to a merchant from outside the province, and nothing has been heard of him since. We will pass you off as my wife’s brother, come back to see his sister and her husband. Why not?” And he told the con man, one by one, the names and appearance of his wife’s parents.

paragraphs.zh: 遂领至家下，叫妻子出来见舅。其妻相见，问：“弟弟面貌，如何与我不相类？”棍应云：“弟出外省，那边风水不同，以此不类。”其妻又问云：“我父何名，形状何如？母何名，形状何如？”其棍对言不差。又问：“我叔何名，形状何如？”棍应曰：“我小时出去，只记得父母，记不得叔了。”妻遂信之。杀鸡烹鲜，设为盛馔，以待其弟。乡农兄弟诸人，各设席相待甚厚。棍对姊夫曰：“我要些零碎银用，可在你家取过十五六两，与我杂用。”乡农遂取己真银十餘两，与棍用。
paragraphs.en: He led him home and called his wife out to meet her "brother." When she saw him, she asked, "Why does my brother’s face look nothing like mine?" The con man answered, "I went away to another province; the local fortune there is different, so I do not resemble you." She asked again, "What was my father’s name, and what did he look like? My mother’s name, and her looks?" The con man answered without a mistake. She asked, "And my uncle—his name and looks?" He answered, "I left home as a small child; I remember only my parents, not my uncle." The wife believed him. She killed a chicken and cooked fresh fish, laying out a fine feast for her "brother." The farmer’s brothers and the rest of the family each gave him a generous meal in turn. The con man said to his "brother-in-law," "I need some loose silver for spending. Let me take fifteen or sixteen taels from your house for my sundry expenses." The farmer then took out more than ten taels of his own genuine silver and gave it to the con man.

paragraphs.zh: 过数日，棍将帐与姊夫查，更有元宝十餘个，在某山某庵中。其庵无人居住，姊夫带饮食二盒，挑至庵中。时庵中棍已预令二贼在彼伺候，即将乡农背缚于柱中。其二贼抽出牛尾尖刀，再三要杀之。棍佯劝云：“我受姊夫厚款，吃得他兄弟鸡鱼多，勿杀我姊夫。”三贼将饮食吃了即去。其乡农叫天不应，入地无门。至次日午后，一牧童至，乡农叫救命，得解缚归家。妻子问曰：“何待今日方归？舅何不回？”乡农应曰：“勿说他，勿说他。”至今被人骗者，俗语曰“勿说他”。
paragraphs.en: A few days later, the con man checked the ledger with his brother-in-law: there were still over a dozen gold ingots hidden in a chapel on such-and-such a hill. The chapel was empty. The brother-in-law packed two boxes of food and drink and carried them there on a pole. Two accomplices the con man had posted in the chapel were already waiting; they bound the farmer backward against a pillar. The two drew ox-tail knives and repeatedly threatened to kill him. The con man pretended to plead for him: "My brother-in-law has treated me generously, and I have eaten plenty of his family's chicken and fish. Do not kill my sister's husband." The three crooks ate the food and left. The farmer cried out to heaven but got no answer; he had no door into the earth. Not until the afternoon of the next day did a herdboy pass by. The farmer shouted for help, was untied, and made his way home. His wife asked, "Why are you only back today? Why didn't your brother come back?" The farmer answered, "Don't speak of him. Don't speak of him." To this day, when someone has been swindled, the common saying is, "Don't speak of him."

paragraphs.zh: 近有江源地方一人，被一棍亦如此骗。其妻有智，即以其元宝凿来与他，知是锡。遂将此棍捆打，勒其供状，始释之。苟非其妻有识，亦蹈前乡农覆辙也。彼时悔之，宁不晚乎！
paragraphs.en: Not long ago, a man in Jiangyuan was swindled by a con man in exactly the same way. His wife was sharp: she had the silver ingot chiseled open at once and saw it was tin. They bound the crook, beat him, forced a written confession out of him, and only then let him go. Had his wife not been so clever, he would have met the same fate as the earlier farmer. To regret it only then—would that not have been too late?

paragraphs.zh: 按：此乡农心苦力勤，啬用薄奉以致富，幸矣！何乃为贪心所使，落贼牢笼，以致失财被辱，反不如江源之妇之智哉！然末世滋伪，奸宄百出，近有丢包贼骗人甚多。更江淮间，又有扯遂法，尤难防检。贼止问你一句，你若答应一句，即被他迷。此妖术也，害人尤多。世道人心，一变至此极乎！偶因前事，遂备述之，以为出途者警。
paragraphs.en: Note: This farmer worked himself hard, scrimped on food and clothing, and so grew rich—a fortunate man. Why did he let greed drive him into the crooks’ cage, to lose his money and be shamed, ending up less wise than the woman of Jiangyuan? But in these latter days deceit flourishes and villains appear in a hundred shapes. Lately “dropped-bundle” thieves have cheated a great many people, and in the country between the Yangzi and the Huai there is another trick, called “the tug-and-drop,” that is even harder to guard against: the thief only has to ask you one question—answer him once and you are spellbound. It is sorcery, and it has harmed even more people. Have the ways of the world and the hearts of men really sunk to this? Coming across these stories, I have set them down in full as a warning to all who travel.

stories.title_en: Setting Up Fake Ingots to Swindle Country Farmers

paragraphs.zh: 钱天广，福建安海人也。时买机布，往山东冒州药王会卖。会期四月十五日起，二十五日止。天下货物，咸在斯处交卸。无牙折中，贸易二家自处。
paragraphs.en: Qian Tianguang was a man of Anhai in Fujian. Once he bought loom-woven cloth and took it to sell at the Medicine King Fair in Maozhou, Shandong. The fair ran from the fifteenth of the fourth month to the twenty-fifth, and goods from all over the empire were unloaded and traded there. There were no brokers to set a middle price; buyer and seller dealt directly with each other.

paragraphs.zh: 一棍以漂白银来买布。每五两一锭，内以真银，如假银一般，色同一样。棍将丝银先对。广以铁槌凿打，并无异样。打至十餘锭，通是一色。广说：“不须再凿槌打。”棍遂以漂白出对，共银六百餘两，内只有细丝银一百餘两，餘者皆假也。银交完讫，布搬去了。广收其银，检束行李，与乡里即雇骡车，直到临清，去买回头货物。取出其银，皆假银也。那时虽悔不及，然广不甚动情，只说云“是我方承得此会，他人出外贸易，从此止矣。”人慨斯人量大，有此大跌，后必有大发也。棍虽脱骗得金数百，然天理昭昭，子孙必不昌隆。盖假银天下处处有之，故录此以为后人之提防，勿蹈天广之覆辙也。按：棍之用假银，此为商者最难提防，必得其梗概，方能辨认。余于壬子秋，在书坊检得一小本仔，辨说银之真假，甚是明白。故录之，以为江湖诸君览之，则假银若一入眼，灼然明白。略陈其一二于左：
paragraphs.en: A con man came to buy cloth, paying with washed silver. Each ingot weighed five taels; genuine silver was mixed in with the fake, identical in color. The con man first presented fine-thread silver for testing. Guang hammered and chiseled them and found nothing amiss. After testing over ten ingots, all uniform, Guang said, "No need to hammer and chisel any more." The con man then brought out the washed silver to settle the payment: over six hundred taels in total, of which only about a hundred were genuine fine-thread silver—the rest was all fake. The silver was handed over, and the cloth was carried away. Guang packed his bags, hired a mule cart with fellow townsfolk, and went straight to Linqing to buy goods for the return trip. When he took out the silver, it was all fake. Regret was useless by then, but Guang did not take it too hard. He only said, "I was the one who took this bait at this fair. Let it end with me; may no other traveling merchant suffer the same." People marveled at his magnanimity: after such a great fall, he was bound to rise high. The crook may have gotten away with several hundred taels, but Heaven’s principle is clear—his descendants will not prosper. Fake silver is found everywhere in the empire, so I record this as a precaution for those who come after: do not repeat Qian Tianguang’s mistake. Observation: Of all the traps a merchant faces, fake silver is the hardest to guard against; you must grasp the general method before you can spot it. In the autumn of the renzi year, I came across a little booklet in a bookshop that explained how to tell true silver from false, very clearly. I transcribe it here for traveling merchants to read, so that fake silver is plain the moment it meets the eye. I give a few of its points below:

paragraphs.zh: 夫元宝者，坑淘出而原宝。今之官解钱粮，亦倾煎如坑淘出厚色，而成元宝也。俗云“圆宝”是也。
paragraphs.en: A yuanbao is the "original treasure" as it comes directly from the mine pits. Today, the government's shipments of tax silver are likewise melted and refined to high purity, just like pit-washed silver, and cast into yuanbao. In common speech, this is called "round treasure."

paragraphs.zh: 松纹，与细丝一样，其皆足色也。
paragraphs.en: Pine-grain (songwen) is the same as fine-thread (xisi); both are silver of full fineness.

paragraphs.zh: 摇丝，色未甚足。银泻入，以手摇动而成丝也，曰摇丝。
paragraphs.en: Shaken-thread (yaosi): the purity is not yet high enough. The silver is poured in and shaken by hand until threads form—hence the name "shaken-thread."

paragraphs.zh: 水丝，又名曰干丝，自七成、八成、九成、九五止，通名曰水丝。
paragraphs.en: Water-thread (shuisi), also called dry-thread (gansi): all grades from seven-tenths to nine-and-a-half tenths fine are collectively known as water-thread.

paragraphs.zh: 画丝，即水丝。泻出而无丝，以铁锥画丝于其上，曰画丝。
paragraphs.en: Drawn-thread (huasi) is water-silk. It is poured out as a mass without distinct threads, so an iron awl is used to draw thread-like lines on its surface—hence the name "drawn-thread."

paragraphs.zh: 吹丝，即九程水丝。银一入，口含吹筒即吹之以成丝也，曰吹丝。
paragraphs.en: Blown-thread (chuisi) is water-thread of nine-tenth fineness. Once the silver is poured, the maker holds a blowpipe in his mouth and blows it into threads—hence the name "blown-thread."

paragraphs.zh: 吸丝，以湿纸盖其上，中取一孔，以银从孔泻下，吸以成其丝也，曰吸丝。今人以铁箔盖于上，亦中取一孔，银从孔泻下，亦吸以成丝也。盖吸丝自七成起，九五止。九五者，亦看得足色也。
paragraphs.en: Sucked-thread (xisi): wet paper is laid over the top with a hole in the middle; silver is poured through the hole and drawn into threads—hence the name. Nowadays, people use iron foil instead, again with a central hole, pouring silver through to draw it into threads. This technique covers fineness from seven-tenths up to nine-and-a-half; the latter can pass for pure silver.

paragraphs.zh: 茶花，以纹银九钱，入铅一钱，入炉中锅内不用一毫之硝，明倾取出，以把淡底填于脚。后泻银于内，铅方不露，而自成其粗丝也，曰茶花。
paragraphs.en: Tea-flower (chahua): take nine qian of fine silver and one qian of lead, put them in the furnace pan without a speck of niter, and pour it out openly. A pale base is packed into the feet, and the silver is then poured in so the lead does not show, while coarse threads form of themselves—hence “tea-flower.”

paragraphs.zh: 鼎银，即汞银也，又曰水银。以纹银五钱，以汞五钱半，入铁鼎中，倾其色通红于内，取出候冷，拿出其银，止有一两，拆汞五分，可打之而成，或造之以成饼。以银薄贴于外，以墨微洒之，以掩其太白。更能造酒器，及诸项首饰。能拔银丝，亦犹细丝者，只是色略青些。更有赤脚汞银，文银三钱，铜丝二钱，汞五钱半，如同前，倾煎取出，不能打造，亦如同水丝一般。若辨汞银，其色脚嫩，上面银薄贴，色不同赤脚者。然色赤而带嫩，终不如水丝色老。此上古所传。造此换人，亦发家数千。子孙继迹不肖，而家即萧条。害众成家，终不悠久。
paragraphs.en: Tripod silver (dingyin) is mercury silver, also called quicksilver. Take five qian of fine silver and five and a half qian of mercury in an iron tripod; heat until the inside glows red. Remove it, let it cool, then extract the silver: you get only one tael, with five fen of mercury recoverable. It can be hammered into shape or cast into cakes. Silver leaf is pasted on the outside, lightly sprinkled with ink to mask its overly white appearance. It can also be made into wine vessels and various ornaments, drawn into silver wire much like fine thread, though slightly greener in hue. There is also "barefoot" mercury silver: three qian of fine silver, two qian of copper wire, and five and a half qian of mercury, treated similarly—melted, poured, and extracted. It cannot be worked further and resembles water-silk. To identify mercury silver: the base color is soft, and the silver leaf pasted on top differs from the barefoot variety's hue; reddish yet soft, it never achieves the aged look of water-silk. This lore has been passed down since ancient times. Those who fabricated this silver to deceive others amassed fortunes of thousands, yet their descendants proved unworthy, and the family soon fell into decline. Harming the public to build a fortune never endures.

paragraphs.zh: 铜，以铜嵌四旁，而后以银泻下，藏其铜于中，曰铜。辨之虽看其丝，终不如细丝之明。其丝粗而带滞碍，即可疑而凿之，方露其铜。
paragraphs.en: Copper-core: copper is set around the four sides and silver is poured over it, hiding the copper inside—this is what they call "copper." You can examine the threads, but they will never shine as brightly as those of fine silver. If the threads are coarse and stiff, suspect it and chisel it open to reveal the copper.

paragraphs.zh: 铁碎，以铁碎先放于内，然后以银泻诸，适均入其银内，包藏铁于其中。至低者亦有九成，九五者有丝。
paragraphs.en: Iron-bits (tiesui): broken iron is placed inside first, and then molten silver is poured over it so that it takes the iron in evenly, encasing it in the middle. Even the lowest grade still comes out at nine-tenths purity, and at nine-and-a-half tenths it even shows fine silver threads.

paragraphs.zh: 或以铜碎如前，名曰包销银。至低者亦有九成；九五有丝，九成无丝。
paragraphs.en: Some use bits of copper as described earlier, calling it "baoxiao silver." The lowest grade is still ninety percent fine; at ninety-five percent there are silk threads, at ninety percent none.

paragraphs.zh: 钞仔铜，用铜一两，入银三分，入炉中。以白信石如硝抽入，泻入中。取出铗四旁者三四分重片，中心者又入炉中倾。再铗，如此者数次。然后用银末，以碗极细，用酸砒草捣汁，入硼砂三分，以罐仔同煮。后放前银末三分，入砒草汁内。以前铜入罐中，以筋炒之，取出，以白水洗去其砒草汁，其色甚白。有一人问曰：“铜中只用银三分，后又以银末三分，何能使银相交于外？”其人对曰：“世间宝物，惟金银为至宝。若先不以银三分入铜倾煎，则后用银末亦为煎煮，必不能入。先以银三分入内，则后用此银末煮之，自然相应也。”故造假银，俗曰“神仙”。然辨此铜，当认银色，乃死鱼白，无青白之色。再看其脚，有两样：或用胭脂点，或用石点。须在点脚及死鱼白处辨之处，则真、赝了然。
paragraphs.en: Chaozai copper: Put one tael of copper and three fen of silver into the furnace. Add white arsenic, drawing it in like niter, and pour it into the center. Remove the piece and trim off three or four fen from the four sides; return the center to the furnace to melt again. Repeat this clipping and melting several times. Then take silver powder ground extremely fine in a bowl, pound sour-arsenic herb to extract its juice, add three fen of borax, and boil them together in a small pot. Next, add the initial three fen of silver powder into the herb juice. Place the copper into the pot, stir with chopsticks, remove it, and wash away the herb juice with clean water until the color is very white. Someone asked, "You used only three fen of silver in the copper initially, then another three fen of silver powder—how does that make silver appear on the outside?" The answer was: "Of all the world's treasures, gold and silver are the most precious. If you do not first melt three fen of silver into the copper, boiling it later with silver powder will never work. With the first three fen of silver inside, the subsequent boiling with silver powder naturally bonds." That is why making fake silver is popularly called "the immortals' art." To spot this copper, examine the silver color: it is a dead-fish white, lacking any blue-white sheen. Then inspect the feet, which come in two varieties—some dotted with rouge, others with mineral pigment. Judge it by the dotted feet and the dead-fish white, and the true versus the false will be plain.

paragraphs.zh: 漂白，用银倾煎细丝一样，只是甚热而壁乃薄，而后以，去其下面者，只留上面其薄者，中以白铜倾一无壁，以前上面安于其上，下面用银箔合其下，用焊焊之。后用滓槌槌其脚，为风锅无二。虽以凿凿开，必不能辨。如辨此，则当时烧焊之际，以火烧去其青青自然之色，如死鱼之白，故曰漂白。以此辨之，灼然明白矣。
paragraphs.en: Bleached (piaobai): silver is melted and poured just like fine-thread, except that because it is poured while extremely hot, the walls come out thin. Next, the bottom is removed and only the thin top is kept. White copper is poured into the middle with no wall of its own; the saved top is fitted over it; silver foil is joined underneath; and the whole piece is soldered together. Its base is then beaten with a dross hammer until it is indistinguishable from a genuine wind-pot casting. Even chiseling it open cannot tell them apart. To recognize it: during soldering, the fire burns away the natural bluish sheen and leaves a dead-fish white—hence the name "bleached." Judge it by this, and the difference is crystal clear.

paragraphs.zh: 煎饼银法，每铅一钱，销铜一分。若九成银一两，可用铅一两；八成可用铅二两，七成可用铅三两，灰堤中用炭装炉，慢扇其火，煎至铅化。若过后，必急扇其火，待油珠大如豆者，即以盖盖之，煞出止九五色。如待金花灿烂，煞出即结布于上，曰布心饼，又曰焦心饼。下面蟹眼回珠，二面皆白，即松纹足色。
paragraphs.en: The method for refining cake silver: for every qian of lead used, melt in one fen of copper. For one tael of nine-tenths silver, use one tael of lead; for eight-tenths, two taels; for seven-tenths, three taels. Pack charcoal into the furnace within an ash-lined hearth and fan the fire gently until the lead melts. Afterward, fan vigorously; when oil beads grow as large as beans, cover the pot and remove it immediately—this yields ninety-five percent purity. If you wait until golden flowers blaze before removing it, a crust forms on top called "cloth-heart cake" or "scorched-heart cake." Below lie crab-eyes and returning pearls, with both faces white: this indicates pine-grain silver at full fineness.

paragraphs.zh: 九成饼，亦出炉白。上乃鸡爪面，下面脚亦白。
paragraphs.en: A nine-tenths purity ingot also appears white upon removal from the mold: its top surface bears a chicken-claw texture, while the base below is likewise white.

paragraphs.zh: 八成饼，出炉略黑，必用天砂擦之方白。上面蚤斑之痕，剪开略白。
paragraphs.en: Eight-tenths cake comes out of the furnace slightly black; it must be rubbed with fine polishing sand to turn white. There are flea-spot marks on top; snip it open and it is slightly white inside.

paragraphs.zh: 七成饼，出炉墨黑，亦用砂擦及用盐梅洗之方白，其剪口带赤。
paragraphs.en: Seven-tenths cake comes out of the furnace ink-black; it too must be rubbed with sand and washed with salted plums to turn white, and the snipped edge carries a reddish tinge.

paragraphs.zh: 六成比七成犹不同些。
paragraphs.en: Six-tenths purity is still not quite the same as seven-tenths.

paragraphs.zh: 五成即梅白饼。
paragraphs.en: Five-tenths purity is called a plum-white cake.

paragraphs.zh: 盐烧饼，二钱五分银出一两，取出以盐烂水，调上一重在其饼上，入火烧之，取出以锤打去一重铜皮；又用盐烧之，再锤打。如此者数次，则外面铜去而自然白，曰盐烧。
paragraphs.en: Salt-burned cake: two qian and five fen of silver are made into a one-tael piece. Take it out, mix a corrosive brine of rotted salt, spread a layer over the cake, and heat it in the fire; then take it out and hammer off a layer of copper skin. Coat it with the salt mixture and fire it again, then hammer it once more. After repeating this several times, the copper on the surface is gone and the piece turns naturally white—this is called "salt-burned."

paragraphs.zh: 白铜倾者即白盐烧。
paragraphs.en: What is poured from white copper is what they call "white salt-smelted" silver—a deceptive alloy used to mimic real silver.

paragraphs.zh: 三铗饼，底是足色饼，用如纸薄，中用白饼熔一饼于中。上面用银入炉中倾出细丝，入铅二三钱，取出，泻入炭锅，成一饼样，亦用甚薄，盖于其上。然后用焊焊成一饼，铗去其四旁者，中间的饼对面剪铗，尽可瞒人。辨之其饼厚，上下皆真银，中间色目异样。知者以银面于杉木擦之，即见三样色。
paragraphs.en: The Three-Soldered Cake: The bottom is a full-fineness cake, rolled paper-thin; a core of white metal (lead or tin) is melted inside. For the top, silver is melted in the furnace and poured into fine threads, mixed with two or three qian of lead, then taken out and poured into a charcoal pan to form another very thin cake, placed over the top. The whole is then soldered together, and the four sides are trimmed off. The center is cut through from both sides to hide the seam, making it passable to the untrained eye. To detect it: the cake appears thick; the top and bottom are genuine silver, but the middle shows a different color. Those who know will rub the silver surface on fir wood, revealing three distinct colors at once.

paragraphs.zh: 车壳即灌铅，以松纹细丝面，以落锥落一孔，然后以割仔入其内割之，尽取其囊中者，留其银壳。后用铅灌其内填满，再用银打一尖仔尖之，又以铁錾仔錾之，如风锅一般。然辨此银，要看其两面之痕处，即见明白。
paragraphs.en: The silver shell is made by turning a piece of silver, creating a hollow cavity. On its surface, which has a fine, pine-grain-like texture, a hole is punched with a pointed tool. Then, a small chisel is used to cut away the interior, removing all the contents and leaving only the silver shell. Lead is poured in to fill the cavity, and a silver point is hammered in to seal it. An iron graver is then used to smooth and finish the surface until it resembles a wind-pot ingot. To identify such counterfeit silver, examine the marks on both sides; they will reveal the truth.

paragraphs.zh: 倒茅饼，先以上号白信石，用熔成罐不洧水者，以盐泥固济，入信石于内。打二炷香升灯盏上，轻清者听用。以银七钱、铜三钱五分熔。将起炉时，以前信石七分入银内，将盖盖之。取出天砂擦之，其面上亦鸡爪面，如九成银一般。辨之九成出炉自白，不待砂擦；然此饼铗口带黄，九成饼铗口自白。以此辨之朗然。
paragraphs.en: Dao Mao Bing (Fake Silver Cake): First, take top-grade white arsenic and place it in a non-porous crucible sealed with salt mud. Heat it over two sticks of incense beneath a lamp dish; collect the light, clear sublimate for use. Melt seven qian of silver with three qian five fen of copper. Just before removing from the furnace, add seven fen of the arsenic to the silver and cover it. Remove the cast and rub it with arsenic powder: the surface will show chicken-claw marks identical to nine-tenths silver. To distinguish them: genuine nine-tenths silver emerges from the furnace naturally white without rubbing; however, this fake cake's pouring gate shows a yellowish tint, whereas a genuine nine-tenths cake's gate remains white. This distinction makes the deception obvious.

paragraphs.zh: 更有铁线饼、江山白、华光桥、神仙饼、糁铜饼、倒插铅，其餘奇巧假银数十样，非言语笔舌所能形容。知者引申触类，观此思过半矣。有等游惰好闲、不务生理、受磨丧心、用此假银苟计衣食，以度时光，此犹穷徒，故不足责；然今贪黜之辈，家颇殷足，尚换此银，用以毒众，自图富厚，以遗子孙。不知丧心悖理，岂有善报，子孙其能昌乎！凡四民交易，止可用七成以至细丝，更低者不可用也。如昧心欺人，不唯阴遣之罪难偿，而阳报之网亦不漏矣。
paragraphs.en: There are also iron-wire cakes, Jiangshan white, Huaguang Bridge, immortal's cake, sprinkled-copper cakes, inverted lead, and dozens of other ingenious fakes that words cannot fully describe. Those who know can reason from one case to the whole: study this and you have grasped more than half. There are idle loafers who will not ply a trade, suffering hardships until they lose their conscience, using this fake silver to scrape together clothes and food and pass their days—these are poor wretches and not worth blaming. But nowadays greedy men whose households are already well off still pass this silver to poison the public, scheming riches for themselves to leave to their sons and grandsons. They do not see that those who deaden their conscience and defy Heaven's principle can have no good reward—how could their descendants prosper? In all dealings among the four classes, only silver of seven-tenths fineness up to pure silk thread should be used; anything lower must not circulate. If you deaden your conscience to cheat others, not only will the debt of unseen punishment be hard to repay—the net of open retribution will not let you slip through.

stories.title_en: Accepting Bleached Counterfeit Silver at the Maozhou Fair

paragraphs.zh: 里有寡婦，富蓋鄉鄰。止生一子甘澍，年方弱冠，恪守祖業，不敢生放。鄉人路五两問之借銀谷，皆不肯，心恨之。歸與妻胡氏謀，要賴他强姦。妻許曰：“可。”又托心友支九为干证，即往分巡道处告。道亲提审，先問胡氏曰：“甘澍因何到你家？”胡氏曰：“他家豪富，终日无图，只是姦淫人婦女。知我男人未在家，无故来调戏我；不从便强抱亲嘴，骂他不去。支九来邀我夫贩货，甘澍方走去。”再問支九：“你往路五家何干？”支九曰：“小的與路五都挑贩为生，因邀他买货，听得（里）面婦人喊骂，甘澍走出。”又問甘澍曰：“你因何與婦人角口？”甘澍曰：“并无到他家，哪有角口？問路五左右鄰便知。”左右鄰都称：“甘澍寡婦之子，素不敢非为。外间并未聞姦情，此是装情捏他。”路五执曰：“他万金巨富，岂不能买两个干证？”左右鄰曰：“我鄰近不知，他支九隔越一街，岂不是买来作证？”道曰：“路五贫民，何能买人作证？”将左右鄰并甘澍各责二十，定要問做强姦。甘澍出而惧甚，思无解释。
paragraphs.en: In the district there was a widow, the richest of all her neighbors. She had only one son, Gan Shu, just come of age, who kept strictly to the family estate and dared not lend money out. A villager named Lu Wu repeatedly asked him for loans of silver and grain; both times Gan Shu refused, and Lu Wu bore him a grudge. Lu went home and plotted with his wife, née Hu, to falsely accuse Gan Shu of rape. His wife agreed: "All right." He also enlisted his close friend Zhi Jiu as a witness, and they went straight to the circuit inspector's office to lodge the charge. The inspector took up the case himself. First he asked Hu, "Why did Gan Shu come to your house?" Hu said, "His family is rich and he idles all day; he does nothing but debauch other men's wives. Knowing my husband was not at home, he came for no reason and made advances on me; when I refused, he seized me and forced kisses on me. I cursed him and still he would not leave. Only when Zhi Jiu came to invite my husband out to buy goods did Gan Shu finally go." Next he asked Zhi Jiu, "What business did you have at Lu Wu's house?" Zhi Jiu said, "Lu Wu and I both make our living carrying goods for sale. I went to invite him to buy stock, heard a woman inside shouting curses, and saw Gan Shu come out." Then he asked Gan Shu, "Why were you quarreling with the woman?" Gan Shu said, "I never set foot in their house—how could there be a quarrel? Ask Lu Wu's neighbors on either side and you will know." The neighbors all said, "Gan Shu is a widow's son and has never dared misbehave. None of us around here has heard of any affair; this is a story cooked up to frame him." Lu Wu shot back, "His family is worth ten thousand—why couldn't he buy a couple of witnesses?" The neighbors said, "We live right next door and know nothing; this Zhi Jiu lives a whole street away—isn't it plain he was bought to testify?" The inspector said, "Lu Wu is a poor man—how could he buy testimony?" He had the neighbors and Gan Shu each given twenty strokes, and was bent on convicting him of rape. Gan Shu left the court in terror, with no idea how to clear himself.

paragraphs.zh: 晚堂退后，道已封门，在后堂周旋闲行，沉默思想，忽自言曰：“错矣！错矣！”又周行数次，遂拂衣而入。适有防夫涂山，在外窥道举动，聞其言错，想必是审此姦情一事也。夤夜越墙而出，扣甘澍歇家门。歇家开门延入。甘澍正忧闷无计。涂山曰：“你今日事要关节否？”澍曰：“甚关节可解？正要求之。”涂山曰：“道爷适有妻舅到，三日内即要打发起身，唯此最灵。若投他，明日即复审，更大胜矣。”澍曰：“如此得可好。须銀几何？”涂山曰：“此翻自案事，不比别人情，须百金方可。”澍曰：“百金我出，只要明日复审。”涂山曰：“舅爷今酒席尚未散，吾当即入言之。”澍與歇家送出。道大门已封，涂山复从居旁民家越墙而入。
paragraphs.en: When the evening session ended, the inspector had the gates sealed. He strolled about the rear hall, thinking in silence, then suddenly said to himself, "A mistake! A mistake!" He paced around several more times, then snapped his sleeves and went in. Now a watchman named Tu Shan was outside, spying on the inspector's every move. Hearing him say "a mistake," Tu Shan guessed it must be about this illicit affair. In the dead of night he climbed out over the wall and knocked at the door of the inn where Gan Shu was lodging. The innkeeper opened up and let him in. Gan Shu was sitting in gloom, out of ideas. Tu Shan said, "About today's case—do you want to work an inside connection?" Gan Shu said, "What connection could clear me? That is exactly what I am desperate for." Tu Shan said, "His Honor happens to have his wife's brother visiting, and within three days the man must be seen off with his parting gifts. This channel works like a charm. If you go through him, there will be a rehearing tomorrow, and you will win bigger still." Gan Shu said, "If that can be done, good. How much silver will it take?" Tu Shan said, "This means reversing a case on his own docket—not like an ordinary favor. It will take a hundred taels." Gan Shu said, "A hundred taels I will pay, so long as the case is reheard tomorrow." Tu Shan said, "The uncle's banquet has not yet broken up; I will go in and speak to him at once." Gan Shu and the innkeeper saw him out. The yamen's main gate was already sealed, so Tu Shan climbed back in over the wall by way of a neighboring house.

paragraphs.zh: 次日，道出早堂，即出牌复审强姦事。甘澍大喜，以为果验也。下午再审甘澍曰：“路五曾問你措借否？”澍曰：“他两次問借銀谷，我皆不肯，因此仇恨，妆情诬我。”再审胡氏曰：“甘澍未到你家，哪有强姦事？将拶起！”路五边未用銀，一拶即紧。胡氏难忍，即吐实“未有强姦。只措借不肯，故妆情告他。”又将路五、支九各打三十，将甘澍全解无罪。涂山即跟出索銀。甘澍曰：“吾乐與之。”涂山自索谢，澍另以十两與之。涂山以銀入道卸起，再出索添谢，又得十两。当时以舅爷关节之力，岂知出道之自悔，而銀尽为涂山所风騙乎！
paragraphs.en: The next day, after opening morning court, the magistrate immediately ordered a rehearing of the rape case. Gan Shu was overjoyed, believing the connection had worked. In the afternoon, the magistrate questioned Gan Shu again: "Did Lu Wu ever ask you for a loan?" Gan Shu replied, "He twice asked to borrow silver and grain; I refused both times, so he holds a grudge and fabricated this charge." The magistrate then questioned Hu: "Gan Shu never entered your house—how could there be a rape? Seize her!" Since Lu Wu had spent no silver on bribes, the finger-squeezers were tightened mercilessly. Hu could not bear the pain and confessed: "There was no rape. He refused our loan request, so we made up the charge." Lu Wu and Zhi Jiu were each beaten thirty strokes, and Gan Shu was cleared and released. Tu Shan immediately followed him out to demand payment. Gan Shu said, "I will pay gladly." Tu Shan then asked for a personal thank-you gift, and Gan Shu gave him another ten taels. Tu Shan carried the silver into the office, deposited it into the official's account, came back out to beg for an additional token of gratitude, and received another ten taels. At the time, Gan Shu credited everything to the power of his uncle's influence—how could he know it stemmed from the magistrate's sudden change of heart, and that every tael had been swindled away by Tu Shan?

paragraphs.zh: 按：衙役皆以騙养身供家，丰衣足食，其騙何可枚举！蓋事事是騙，日日是騙，人人是騙。虽罄南山竹，何能悉之；虽包拯再生，何能察之？予素不入公庭，此中情弊，希所知聞。此其偶得于真见者，故述其弊窦如此。然衙中虽人人是姦徒，事事是騙薮，吾唯早完公课，百忍不讼，虽贪吏悍卒，其如我何！故曰：机虽巧，不蹈为高；鸩虽毒，不饮为高；衙役虽騙，不入为高。纵有无妄之灾，必有明官能昭雪之者。何也？官皆读书人，明者多而昏者少也。无奈在衙人役，各以阴云霾雾蔽之耳。故唯忍小忿，不入衙为高也。
paragraphs.en: Note: Yamen underlings all feed and clothe their households by swindling—how could their tricks ever be numbered? Every affair is a swindle, every day a swindle, every man a swindler. Use up every bamboo on the southern hills and you still could not write them all down; bring Bao Zheng back to life and even he could not see through them. I have never been one to enter a court of law, and of the abuses within I have heard little; this one I happened to witness with my own eyes, so I record these malpractices as they are. Yet though every man in the yamen is a knave and every business a nest of swindles, I need only pay my public dues early and endure a hundred wrongs rather than go to law—then what can greedy clerks and bullying runners do to me? Hence the saying: a snare may be cunning—the wise course is not to step in it; poison may be deadly—the wise course is not to drink it; yamen men may be cheats—the wise course is not to enter their gates. Even if some undeserved calamity should strike, there is bound to be a clear-sighted official to right the wrong. Why? Officials are all men who have read the books; the clear-headed are many and the muddled few. The pity is that the underlings around them screen them in dark cloud and fog. So swallow small angers and stay out of the yamen—that is the wise course.

stories.title_en: Overhearing the Official's Words, Then Going Out to Swindle

paragraphs.zh: 富民元植者，家温行谨，奕世良善，偶與鄉权贵有隙。鄉贵素善叶推官，乃吹毛求疵，砌元植之恶十餘件。叶推官为之送访，按院即批與叶审。叶提元植，谕之曰：“汝之恶迹，我已备晓，罪在有定。只汝家殷富，不許央关节。若有关节，罪有加无减。且收入监，候拘到被害，即听审定罪。”叶推官素廉正，从来不纳分上。今元植既承面诫，越不敢展转，只惶惧待罪耳。
paragraphs.en: There was a well-to-do commoner named Yuan Zhi, comfortably off and careful in his conduct, from a family decent for generations. By chance he fell out with a powerful man of the district. That man had long been friendly with Judge Ye, so he went hunting for flaws and manufactured more than a dozen charges of Yuan Zhi's "crimes." Judge Ye forwarded them for investigation, and the investigating censor approved the case and assigned it to Ye for trial. Ye had Yuan Zhi brought in and told him, "I already know your misdeeds in full; the punishment is fixed by statute. But your family is rich, so hear this: you are not to beg any inside connections. If there is any back-door pull, your punishment will be increased, not reduced. Take him to jail for now; once the alleged victims have been brought in, the case will be heard and sentence passed." Judge Ye had always been honest and upright and never accepted private intercession. Now that Yuan Zhi had been warned to his face, he dared even less to scheme or stir, and only waited in dread for his sentence.

paragraphs.zh: 适眷亲易鄉官，素與植相善，知其事属仇陷，默地代诉于太府，托转释于四尊。太府乘间缓颊及之。叶四尊大怒，歸取元植，责之曰：“我叫你不得投分上，反央太爷来讲。这样刁恶人，定要拟你谪戍！”元植茫不知来历，叩头曰：“老爷素不纳关节，一府通知；又蒙钧旨面谕，怎敢央太爷？实不知事从何来。”叶爷曰：“且入监去，定是军罪。”元植出查，方知事出易鄉官，自以己意代释，并不使植知也。植思无处可解，寻其用事凌书手，密商曰：“能为我减军入徒，当以厚礼谢。”凌书曰：“能出百金，为汝计之。”植許曰：“可。”以銀封讫。
paragraphs.en: Now it happened that a close relative, the retired official Yi, had long been on good terms with Yuan Zhi. Knowing the case was an enemy's frame-up, he quietly pleaded Yuan Zhi's cause to the prefect and asked him to put in a word with Judge Ye for a release. The prefect found an opening and spoke gently on his behalf. Judge Ye was enraged. He went back, had Yuan Zhi fetched, and berated him: "I told you not to send in any private word—and you went and got His Honor the prefect to speak for you! A vicious schemer like you—I will certainly sentence you to garrison exile!" Yuan Zhi had no idea where this had come from. He kowtowed: "Your Honor has never accepted back-door appeals—the whole prefecture knows it. And you instructed me to my face; how would I dare beg the prefect? I truly do not know how this arose." Judge Ye said, "Back to jail. It will be a military sentence for certain." Yuan Zhi came out and made inquiries; only then did he learn that the matter had come from the retired official Yi, who had spoken for his release on his own initiative, never letting Yuan Zhi know. Yuan Zhi could think of no way out. He sought out Ling, the scribe who had the judge's ear, and said in secret, "If you can get my military exile reduced to penal servitude, I will thank you with a rich gift." Scribe Ling said, "Put up a hundred taels and I will work it out for you." Yuan Zhi agreed, and sealed up the silver.

paragraphs.zh: 叶爷果唤凌书手作招曰：“须寻一军律拟来。”凌书故以绞罪拟上。叶爷命改招，只可拟军。凌书过一日再以绞罪拟曰：“访单中惟謀死亲弟一件最重，正合绞罪。餘某条某条，只是徒罪，并无合军律者。”叶爷寻思：“有对头之状，尚不轻入人绞，况是拿访，而可绞人？”曰：“造化了他，只拟徒罢。”后拟上三年徒。元植欣然纳赎，凌书遂安受百金之贿。在叶爷，宁知其外受金而内拟人重罪乎？故衙役之欺官，虽神君不及察也。
paragraphs.en: Judge Ye did in fact call in Scribe Ling to draft the sentence: "Find a law on military exile and propose it." Ling deliberately proposed strangulation. Judge Ye ordered the draft changed—only military exile would do. A day later Ling again proposed strangulation: "On the investigation list, the heaviest count is scheming to kill his own younger brother, which fits the strangulation statute exactly. The remaining counts, this one and that one, are only servitude offenses; none of them fits a military exile law." Judge Ye thought it over: "Even on a complaint with a named accuser I would not lightly send a man to the cord—still less on a warrantless investigation like this." He said, "Lucky for him. Just propose servitude." In the end the sentence proposed was three years' penal servitude. Yuan Zhi gladly paid the redemption money, and Scribe Ling pocketed the hundred-tael bribe at his ease. As for Judge Ye—how was he to know that outside his clerk had taken gold, while inside he was deliberately proposing too heavy a sentence? So it is when yamen underlings deceive their official: even a magistrate with the insight of a god would not catch it.

paragraphs.zh: 按：善有旌奖，恶有拿访，此朝廷激劝一大机权也。今旌者多由攒刺之巧，访者或由权贵之嗾，其虚实益相半耳。然犹幸有拿访一途，可以少惕刁顽，稍为良民吐气。特被访者出入于問官之心，高下于权书之手，其情得罪当者亦少矣。当官持权者，或遇大故重情，必虚心详审，明察沉断，庶可杜姦欺之一二耳。
paragraphs.en: Note: The good are commended and the wicked arrested for investigation—this is one of the court's great levers for encouraging virtue and warning vice. Nowadays those commended often owe it to clever toadying and string-pulling, and those investigated are sometimes set upon at the instigation of the powerful; the ratio of false to true cases is now roughly equal. Still, we should be glad this avenue of investigation exists: it can give the cunning and obstinate a scare and let honest folk breathe a little easier. The trouble is that the investigated man's fate rises or falls in the examining judge's mind, while his sentence is pitched high or low in the scheming clerk's hand—so few in the end receive the punishment their case truly merits. When those who hold office and wield power meet a grave case with heavy stakes, they must empty their minds, examine every detail, see clearly and decide with firm resolve; only then can they stop one or two of the cheats.

stories.title_en: Deceiving with a Heavy Sentence to Release the Prisoner

paragraphs.zh: 传包孝肃为官，清廉明察，用法无私，诈不得以巧辨售，罪不得以权贵免，又不纳分上。故人称之曰：“关节不到，有阎罗包老。”
paragraphs.en: It is told that when Bao Xiaosu held office he was clean-handed and clear-sighted, and applied the law without favor: no cheat could talk his way out with clever arguments, no guilty man could escape through powerful friends, and he accepted no private intercession. So people said of him, "Where no back-door appeal can reach, there stands old Bao, dread as King Yama of the underworld."

paragraphs.zh: 适有富豪子犯姦情真，知难逃洞察，预與一老胥謀曰：“包爷精明，察事如神。我所犯情真，干证又直证，罪实难逃。若重罚犹可输纳；唯痛责实是难堪。有何计可以减责，必不惜厚费图之。”老胥曰：“明日若当责时，你奔近案前，强辩求申。我从旁呵斥，为你分责，或可减你一半。此外，别无策可图也。”
paragraphs.en: It happened that a rich man's son was truly guilty of an illicit affair. Knowing he could not escape Lord Bao's piercing insight, he plotted in advance with a veteran clerk: "Lord Bao is sharp and sees through cases like a god. My offense is real, and direct witnesses confirm it—there is no escaping conviction. A heavy fine I could still pay; it is the painful beating I cannot bear. If there is any scheme to reduce the strokes, I will spare no expense to work it." The veteran clerk said, "Tomorrow, when the beating is about to begin, run up close to the bench and argue stubbornly, begging to be heard. I will bawl you out from the side and take half the strokes for you; perhaps we can cut your share by half. Beyond that, there is no scheme to be had."

paragraphs.zh: 次日，包公审得真情，发怒要打富子四十。富子奔近案（前），哓哓申辩不已。老胥从旁大声呵之曰：“速去受责，何须許多说话，罪岂赦你！”包公见之，大恨此吏揽权起威，恐后日窃势騙人，外必生事，即先责老胥二十板，偏减去富子二十，欲使威不自胥出，不知正落其謀中也。老胥遂得厚赂，而包公漠不知之。
paragraphs.en: The next day, Lord Bao uncovered the truth, flew into a rage, and ordered forty strokes for Fu Zi. Fu Zi rushed up to the bench, clamoring endlessly in self-defense. An old clerk shouted from the side: "Go take your punishment at once! Why all this talk? Do you think your crime will be pardoned?" Lord Bao saw this and bitterly resented the clerk for seizing authority and putting on a show of power. Fearing the man would one day usurp such power to swindle people and cause trouble elsewhere, he first gave the old clerk twenty strokes—and perversely reduced Fu Zi's penalty by twenty—wanting to show that awe did not stem from any clerk. He did not realize he had fallen squarely into their trap. The old clerk then collected a fat bribe, while Lord Bao remained completely unaware.

paragraphs.zh: 按：吏为姦，皆是知本官性情，而变幻用之。老胥知包公严明，岂容胥吏招权？故旁呵犯人，包公必责吏而故恕犯人，以见胥吏之无权，欲外人不畏慑之。岂知于难减责之中，故分责以取其贿，又孰从而察之？公且受胥騙，况后之为官者哉！
paragraphs.en: Note: When clerks work their frauds, it always begins with knowing their own official's temperament and turning it to their use. The veteran clerk knew Lord Bao was strict and clear-sighted and would never let underlings gather power. So he shouted at the prisoner from the side, certain that Lord Bao would beat the clerk and deliberately spare the prisoner—to prove that clerks hold no power and keep outsiders from standing in awe of them. Who would have guessed that, inside a beating that could hardly be reduced, he was splitting the strokes to collect a bribe? And who could possibly detect it? Even Lord Bao was swindled by a clerk—what hope is there for the officials who come after him?

stories.title_en: A Clerk Berates a Convict to Split the Beating

paragraphs.zh: 京城有房八者，为人痴蠢，以淘街为生，家止一老母。一日，房八淘街，往小河边洗。靠晚来有一妇人，身穿麻衣，旁立看淘洗讫，谓房八曰：“我将往娘家，今晚不能到，暂借你家一歇。”房八曰：“我家歇不得，何不往客店歇？”妇人曰：“客店人丛杂，（住）宿不便。你家有何人？”房八曰：“家有老母。”妇人曰：“有母便可同歇。”
paragraphs.en: In the capital lived a man named Fang Ba, dull-witted and earning his living by scavenging the streets. He had only an old mother at home. One day, while scavenging, he went to a small river to wash himself. Toward evening, a woman dressed in hemp mourning clothes stood nearby and waited until he finished washing. She then said to Fang Ba, 'I am heading to my maiden family's home, but I cannot arrive tonight. May I rest at your house for the night?' Fang Ba replied, "My home is no place to stay. Why not go to an inn?" The woman said, "Inns are crowded with all sorts of people; lodging there is inconvenient. Who else lives in your house?" Fang Ba answered, "Only my old mother." The woman replied, "If you have a mother, then we can stay together."

paragraphs.zh: 房八引至家，妇人把银与籴米买酒菜，夜间三人同食。妇人问：“曾娶媳否？”房母答：“家下仅能度日，哪得银娶媳？”妇人曰：“我前夫死已葬讫，家无亲人。今收拾家财，将回娘家，奈娘家又远。看你儿子孝善，偶然相遇，亦似天缘，意欲为你媳妇，以供奉朝夕，何如？”房母曰：“你虽好意，只恐儿不能供三口人。”妇曰：“我亦带有些少银本，谅勤治女工，亦足自给。”房八喜曰：“我算命今年当招好妻。一人自有一人禄，何患不能供？”是晚，遂成亲同宿。一夜之间，叙尽风流。男称前未娶，今如渴而得浆；女称久失偶，今如热而遇凉。二人交爱，真如鱼水。房母亦大喜天赐贤媳。
paragraphs.en: Fang Ba led her home. The woman gave silver to buy rice, wine, and dishes, and at night the three ate together. She asked, "Has he taken a wife?" The mother said, "We can barely get through the day. Where would we get silver for a daughter-in-law?" The woman said, "My former husband is dead and already buried. I have no kin at home. I have gathered my household goods to go back to my mother's, but her house is far. I see your son is filial and kind. Meeting by chance seems Heaven's match. I would like to be your daughter-in-law and serve you morning and night. How would that be?" The mother said, "You mean well, but I fear my son cannot feed three mouths." The woman said, "I have also brought a little silver to start with. If I work diligently at needlework, it should be enough." Fang Ba was pleased: "My fortune this year says I should get a good wife. Each person has their own allotted lot. Why worry we cannot feed ourselves?" That night they became husband and wife and slept together. In one night they gave themselves over to every pleasure of love. The man said he had never married, and now it was like thirst meeting drink; the woman said she had long been without a mate, and now it was like heat meeting cool. They loved each other truly like fish in water. The mother too was overjoyed at Heaven's gift of a worthy daughter-in-law.

paragraphs.zh: 次日，妇以银六钱与夫籴米买菜蔬。第三日，问婆母曰：“何不做身衣服穿？”婆称无银。妇又出银六钱，叫夫在汪客大布店买之。房八既得妻，又前后得银作家，心中扬扬喜色，往汪店买青布二端归。妇各将剪去三尺，故持尺量曰：“此是剪剩之布，未成全匹。何被人瞒也？可持去与换。有好银买布，他何得如此亏人？”房八听妻言去换。汪店言：“我家哪有零布？是你自剪起胡赖我。”二人各争一场。汪客令家人再以二端与之。及持归，妇背地以剪刀刺破几叶，后将展开，又曰：“如何又换两匹碾烂布？这布店好可恶！他欺你纯善，故敢诳你。今次不换，可放言骂他，怕他什么！”房八被妻激，忿忿往说：“你以破布诳我。”汪客说：“你买一匹布，来换许多次，店中哪有此功夫！”不换与他。房八便纵言秽骂。汪客怒，喝令家人扯打一顿，后以两匹布打开看明，掷与之。房八执布归，言被打之恨。妻怒，顿足曰：“有银买布，反招他打。他靠财势，可拼命与他作对。吾与婆能替你申冤。”又激夫到店凶泼。汪店家人又群起痛打，带重伤而归。妇哭曰：“必往告保辜状。”遂往御史处告准。归买好酒好菜，劝夫多饮，方可散血。夫被其劝，酩酊大醉。夜乘醉，紧绑其手足，以沙塞口鼻，至三更死已久，解其绑绳。妇故喊曰：“你儿身冷了，硬了，莫非是死？”吓得婆起看，儿已死。二人相对哭尽哀，复往御史处补状。差官检验收贮，遍体都有重伤。汪客惊惶无措。
paragraphs.en: The next day, the woman gave her husband six qian of silver to buy rice and vegetables. On the third day, she asked her mother-in-law, "Why not have some clothes made?" The old woman said she had no silver. The woman then produced another six qian and told her husband to buy cloth at Merchant Wang’s large shop. Fang Ba, having already secured a wife and accumulated silver over time, was flushed with triumph. He went to Wang’s shop, bought two bolts of blue cloth, and returned home. The woman cut three chi from each bolt, then deliberately took a ruler and said, "This is leftover cut cloth, not a full bolt. How were we cheated? Take it back and exchange it. We paid good silver for cloth; how can they short us like this?" Fang Ba listened to his wife and went to exchange it. Wang’s shop retorted, "When did we ever have remnant cloth? You cut it yourself to cheat us." The two argued. Wang ordered his men to give them two more bolts. When he brought them home, the woman, behind his back, stabbed several folds with scissors, then spread them out and said again, "How is it you exchanged two more bolts of crushed, ruined cloth? This shop is hateful! They see you are simple, so they dare lie to you. If they won't exchange this time, curse them out loud. What is there to fear?" Stirred up by his wife, Fang Ba went in a rage and said, "You tricked us with broken cloth." Wang replied, "You buy one bolt and come to exchange it many times. What shop has time for that?" He refused to exchange. Fang Ba then let fly with filthy abuse. Wang grew angry, ordered his men to drag him and beat him, then opened the two bolts, inspected them, and threw them at him. Fang Ba took the cloth home and recounted the beating with resentment. The wife stamped her foot in anger: "We paid silver for cloth and instead got a beating. He relies on money and power. Fight him tooth and nail. Your mother and I can plead your wrong." She stirred her husband up again to go to the shop and cause a violent scene. Wang’s household men rose together and beat him badly; he came home with heavy wounds. The woman wept: "We must file a complaint to hold them liable for the wounds." She went to the censor and had the complaint accepted. Coming home, she bought good wine and dishes, and urged her husband to drink heavily so the bruising would disperse. Urged by her, he got dead drunk. That night, while he was drunk, she bound his hands and feet tight, stuffed sand in his mouth and nose, and by the third watch he had long been dead. She untied the ropes. Then she deliberately cried, "Your son’s body is cold and stiff—can he be dead?" The frightened mother rose to look: her son was dead. The two wept together in full mourning, then went back to the censor to file an additional complaint. Officers examined and impounded the body: there were heavy wounds all over. Wang the merchant was terrified and at a loss.

paragraphs.zh: 过三日将审，妇与婆到汪客店曰：“我夫被你打死已的，只我婆年老，我一妇人难独供膳，把你偿命亦无益。你能出银三百两，与我供奉婆婆，叫婆具息免检罢。”汪客闻言心喜，令人担议，许出银二百两，与房母养赡。房母依妇言，自具息言：“身贫老，儿死妇寡，莫能存命。凭亲邻劝谕，着汪出银一百两，与氏养赡，免行检验。”官准息，将汪客打二十，又罚一大罪，令房八妻领银而归。过两日，妇窃银二百两，夜间逃去，不知所往。房母再欲告，汪客又重出二十两与之，以息其事。
paragraphs.en: Three days before the hearing, the woman and her mother-in-law went to Wang’s inn and said, "Your beating killed my husband—that is certain. My mother-in-law is old, and I alone cannot support us. Paying with your life helps no one. If you can hand over three hundred taels to support my mother-in-law, have her withdraw the complaint and skip the inquest." Wang was delighted, sent someone to bargain, and agreed to pay two hundred taels for Fang’s mother’s upkeep. Following the woman’s lead, she herself submitted a petition: "I am poor and old; my son is dead, and I am a widow. We cannot survive. At the urging of kin and neighbors, let Wang pay one hundred taels for my support and waive the inquest." The official approved the petition, ordered Wang beaten twenty strokes, imposed a heavy fine, and allowed Fang’s wife to take the silver home. Two days later, the woman stole the two hundred taels and fled under cover of night, vanishing without a trace. When the mother tried to sue again, Wang paid another twenty taels to hush the matter.

paragraphs.zh: 按：此妇是大棍之妻，查得房八止此老母，故遣妇假与为妻，激其与富店殴争，然后加力打死，则房母必告，必可得银，然后拐银而逃。是断送人一命，而彼得厚利也。世之奸险至此，人可痴心而犯其机阱乎！
paragraphs.en: Note: This woman was the wife of a veteran con man. They had discovered that Fang Ba had only this old mother, so they sent the woman to pretend to be his wife, provoked him into a brawl with a rich shop, then beat him to death with added force. The mother would surely sue, and they would surely get silver; then they would make off with the silver and flee. Thus, they sacrificed a man's life to gain a fat profit. When the world's treachery has come to this, can anyone still be simple-hearted enough to walk into such traps?

stories.title_en: A Woman Marries a Street-Sweeper and Costs Him His Life

paragraphs.zh: 福建春元洪子选在京将纳妾，媒数引看，多未称意。适有崔命妇者，年近三十，犹绰约如处子。以为夫除服，入寺建醮。二棍套定，一为媒先引洪春元到寺亲看。洪见其容貌秀雅，言动庄重，大是快意。媒曰：“既称意，须与其大伯言之，此妇是伯主婚。”径引春元到其家，先袖钱五十文，入付其小家僮曰：“有一春元来尊府看大厦，托讨三杯茶与吃。”再出邀春元曰：“他大伯在外即回，可入厅坐。”少顷，一棍称为伯，从外入。三人叙礼，复坐，小仆捧茶出。媒曰：“令弟妇欲改造，此福建春元欲求娶，敬问礼银若干？”伯曰：“路太远些，恐弟妇外家不允。”媒曰：“他目今受官，即叫令弟舅同到任，亦何惮远？况他世家宦族，姻眷满朝，即在京亦多人看顾，此不可错过。但老爷尚未得见令弟妇。”伯笑曰：“舍弟妇人品德行女流第一，往日亦不肯令人见。今日除服，在某寺建醮，往彼处看之易矣。”媒曰：“尊府所出，亦不须看。但问何时肯去，及礼银若何？”伯曰：“她除服了，亦不拘时去。礼银须一百以上，她首饰妆奁，亦有五六十两。”旋引媒起，密曰：“我上贺须四十两，莫与弟妇知，其身资可减些。”再复入坐，复曰：“明日若交银，可在花园馆中。家中有俗忌，不交银也。”媒曰：“须请令弟舅同见为好。”伯曰：“彼来自多称说，待娶后即通未迟。”便送媒与春元出。媒曰：“适间伯与我言，须上贺银四十两，其身资可减些。彼不欲弟妇知，欲在园交银。”
paragraphs.en: Hong Zixuan, a Fujian provincial graduate, was in the capital preparing to take a concubine. Matchmakers led him to view several women, none of whom pleased him. There happened to be a titled lady of the Cui house, nearly thirty, yet still graceful as a maiden. Having completed her mourning period for her husband, she had gone to a temple to hold rites. Two sharpers had devised their scheme: one, posing as a matchmaker, first led Graduate Hong to the temple to see her himself. Hong found her appearance refined and her speech and bearing dignified, and was greatly delighted. The matchmaker said, "Since she suits you, we must speak to her elder brother-in-law; this woman’s marriage is arranged by him." He led the graduate straight to the house, first slipping fifty cash into his sleeve, went inside, and handed them to a young page: "A graduate has come to inspect your fine residence; please ask for three cups of tea for him." He then came out again and invited the graduate: "Her elder brother-in-law is out but will return shortly. Come sit in the hall." Shortly after, a trickster, posing as the elder brother, entered from outside. The three exchanged formalities, sat down again, and the young servant brought tea. The matchmaker said, "Your younger brother’s wife wishes to remarry. This Fujian graduate seeks to marry her and respectfully asks how much betrothal silver is required." The "elder brother" replied, "The road is rather far; I fear her natal family will not agree." The matchmaker said, "He will soon take office and can have her brother accompany him to the post; why fear the distance? Besides, he comes from an official family for generations, with in-laws filling the court; even in the capital many will look after her. This opportunity must not be missed. Only his lordship has not yet seen your younger brother’s wife." The elder brother smiled: "My younger brother’s wife is first among women in character and conduct, and in the past would not let people see her. Today her mourning is over; she is holding rites at such-and-such a temple. To go there and see her is easy." The matchmaker said, "From a house like yours, there is no need to see her. Just ask when she will leave and what the betrothal silver should be." The elder brother said, "Her mourning is over; she can leave anytime. The betrothal silver must be a hundred taels or more; her jewelry and trousseau are also worth fifty or sixty taels." He then led the matchmaker aside and whispered, "My congratulatory gift must be forty taels; do not let my brother’s wife know. The bride-price can be reduced a little." He sat down again and added, "If the silver is handed over tomorrow, do it in the garden lodge. There is a household superstition; we do not accept silver in the house." The matchmaker said, "It would be better to invite her brother to meet as well." The elder brother said, "If he comes, he will talk too much. After the marriage, it will not be too late to send word." He then saw the matchmaker and the graduate out. The matchmaker said, "Just now the elder brother told me the congratulatory silver must be forty taels, and the bride-price can be reduced a little. He does not want his brother’s wife to know, and wants the silver handed over in the garden."

paragraphs.zh: 次日，媒引春元及二管家同往园馆，又去邀崔家大伯同一小仆挟天平至。媒曰：“要叫一人写礼书。”伯曰：“亡弟未在，何用婚书？”媒曰：“京城交易，不比共府作事，只记一帐，亦有凭据。”伯曰：“吾自写何如？”媒曰：“最好。”即取纸与。写到财礼处，伯曰：“六十两。”媒曰：“减些，只四十。但要安顿令弟妇有好处，不必多索银。”伯曰：“两项可都一样。”媒曰：“易说的。”写完了，媒曰：“婚书放在我手，看对银。”先对四十两作一总封，又对二十两付与伯收。伯起曰：“吾取四十两，财礼任你家中面交；不然，亦不消说。”媒曰：“再加十两。”伯亦不肯。媒顾春元曰：“何如？”春元曰：“凑起四十两在你手，到他家交与妇人。”媒曰：“婚书并银，都要在我手，一同家中，两相交付。”伯曰：“我的非今日言明，要背交，昨已议定了。若事不成，岂能赖得？”媒惟取四十两并婚书在手，同春元回店，雇人去接亲。媒以婚书付春元曰：“事已定矣，不消带去。”只同两管家，领十餘人至崔家，先入厅旁坐。媒曰：“吾叫大伯来。”脱身去矣。
paragraphs.en: The next day, the matchmaker led the graduate and two stewards to the garden lodge, then went to invite the Cui elder brother, who arrived with a young servant carrying a balance. The matchmaker said, "We should have someone write the betrothal letter." The elder brother asked, "My late brother isn't here—what use is a marriage letter?" The matchmaker replied, "Transactions in the capital differ from those in your home prefecture; even a simple account serves as proof." The elder brother offered, "Shall I write it myself?" "Best," said the matchmaker, and paper was produced. When they reached the section on betrothal silver, the elder brother said, "Sixty taels." "Reduce it," countered the matchmaker. "Just forty. Just ensure your brother's widow is well provided for; no need to demand much silver." The elder brother noted, "Both sums can be equal." "Easy enough," said the matchmaker. Once written, the matchmaker declared, "Keep the marriage letter in my hand while we weigh out the silver." First, they weighed forty taels into a single sealed packet, then weighed twenty taels and handed them to the elder brother. The elder brother rose: "I'll take the forty taels. The betrothal gift can be delivered at the house in her presence; otherwise, there's nothing to discuss." "Add another ten taels," insisted the matchmaker. The elder brother refused. The matchmaker turned to the graduate: "What do you say?" The graduate suggested, "Combine the forty taels in your hand, and deliver them to the woman at their house." The matchmaker countered, "Both the marriage letter and the silver must remain in my hand; we go together to the house and make the exchange." The elder brother argued, "This wasn't decided today; it was agreed yesterday that delivery would happen without her immediate presence. If the deal falls through, how could I keep it?" The matchmaker took only the forty taels and the marriage letter, returned to the inn with the graduate, and hired men to fetch the bride. He gave the marriage letter to the graduate, saying, "The matter is settled; no need to take it along." Then, taking only the two stewards and a dozen men, he went to the Cui house and sat by the side of the hall. "I'll call the elder brother," he said, before slipping away.

paragraphs.zh: 崔家见许多人来，出问曰：“你辈何干？”管家对曰：“来接亲。”崔家人曰：“你走错门了，接甚亲？”管家曰：“媒人引我来，怎会错？”崔家人曰：“哪位是媒？”管家曰：“媒去叫你大伯。”崔家人曰：“有甚大伯？”管家曰：“是你家交银主婚的。”崔唾其面曰：“你一伙小辈该死的！此是崔爷府中，你信何人哄，在此胡说？”管家曰：“昨同洪相公在你家吃茶，许议亲事，已在花园交银了，今反退悔。我岂怕你的，难道脱得我银去？”崔家人曰：“谁把茶你吃，谁受你银？我家哪有出嫁的人？”管家曰：“你前日在寺中建醮的娘子要嫁。”崔家人曰：“啐！那是我主母，曾受朝廷诰命，谁人娶得！我去禀巡爷，把这伙棍徒锁去！”两管家见媒人请大伯不来，心中不安，各逃回店。崔家人尾其后，查是春元洪子选强婚，即往府尹告强娶命妇事。洪春元闻告，始知被棍脱，即逃出京去。及府尹差人来提，回报已无期走矣。府尹曰：“他自然要走，怎敢对得！”遂为立案存照，以俟后提。
paragraphs.en: The Cui household saw so many people coming and asked, “What is your business?” The stewards said, “We have come to fetch a bride.” The Cui people said, “You have the wrong door. What bride?” The stewards said, “The matchmaker led us. How could we be wrong?” The Cui people said, “Which of you is the matchmaker?” The stewards said, “The matchmaker went to call your elder brother-in-law.” The Cui people said, “What elder brother-in-law?” The stewards said, “The one in your house who took the silver and gives the bride in marriage.” The Cui people spat in their faces: “You pack of lowborns, you deserve to die! This is Lord Cui’s residence. Who fooled you into talking this nonsense here?” The stewards said, “Yesterday we drank tea in your house with Master Hong, agreed on a marriage, already handed over silver in the garden, and now you go back on it. Are we afraid of you? Think you can make off with our silver?” The Cui people said, “Who gave you tea, who took your silver? Who in our house is to be married out?” The stewards said, “The lady who was having rites in the temple the other day wants to remarry.” The Cui people said, “Pah! That is our mistress, who holds an imperial patent of rank. Who can marry her! We will report to the patrol officer and have this pack of swindlers locked up!” The two stewards, seeing the matchmaker did not come back with the “elder brother,” grew uneasy and each fled to the inn. The Cui people followed, found it was Graduate Hong Zixuan forcing a marriage, and went to the prefect to charge him with forcibly marrying a titled lady. When Hong heard of the charge he knew he had been swindled, and fled the capital. When the prefect sent men to bring him in, they reported he had already gone, vanished with no known destination. The prefect said, “Of course he would run. How would he dare face it!” So the case was filed for the record, to be taken up later.

paragraphs.zh: 按：此棍巧处，在见崔家主仆皆在寺，乃哄其家小仆进茶；又云大伯欲背索上贺，在园交银，故可行其骗。洪春元既失银，又着走。又府尹信其强娶，为之立案。在外娶妾，信然难哉！作事何可不审实也？
paragraphs.en: Note: The swindler's cleverness lay in seeing that Master Cui and his servants were all at the temple; he then tricked a junior household servant into bringing tea. He also claimed the elder brother wished to settle a debt secretly with silver handed over in the garden—thus enabling the fraud. Graduate Hong lost his silver and was forced to flee on top of it. Moreover, the prefect believed the story of a forced marriage and filed the case. To take a concubine outside one's home and have it believed? Truly difficult! How can one act without verifying the facts?

stories.title_en: A Matchmaker Cons a Provincial Graduate into 'Marrying' a Titled Lady

paragraphs.zh: 广东蔡天寿者，为人慷慨仗义，年四十无子。其妻泼甚，弗容娶妾。一日，贩广锡三十餘担，往苏州府卖，与牙人萧汉卿曰：“我未得子，意欲在此娶一妾，亦有相因的否？”汉卿曰：“有银何怕无当意女子？”即领去看几个室女。汉卿曰：“我年过四十，此女皆年纪不相宜，吾不娶也。”
paragraphs.en: Cai Tianshou of Guangdong was open-handed and stood by his word. At forty he had no son, and his wife was such a shrew that she would not let him take a concubine. One day he brought more than thirty loads of Guangdong tin to Suzhou to sell, and said to the broker Xiao Hanqing, "I still have no son, and I would like to take a concubine here. Is there anyone suitable on reasonable terms?" Hanqing said, "When you have silver, why worry about finding a girl to your liking?" He led him to look at several unmarried girls, but none suited: "I am past forty; these girls are too young to be a match for my years, so I will not take them."

paragraphs.zh: 忽有荡子国延纪，家有寡母邓氏，年三十三岁，容貌端好。夫死，遗家资千金，被延纪赌荡罄空，更欠赌银二十餘两，逼取无办。乃与棍商议，诈称母为妻，欲嫁以偿债。媒传于汉卿，领天寿看之，年貌合意，议身资银四十餘两。延纪曰：“氏系过江出身，恐外家阻挡，不与嫁远。其银可封牙人手，待临行上船，我叫人送到船来，人与银两相交付。”牙人以为可。
paragraphs.en: There happened to be a wastrel named Guo Yanji. His household included a widowed mother, née Deng, thirty-three years old, of decent looks. When her husband died, he left a thousand taels; Yanji gambled it all away and still owed over twenty taels in gambling debts, pressing him with no way to pay. He plotted with a crook to pretend his mother was his wife, intending to marry her off to settle the debt. Word reached Hanqing through a matchmaker. He took Tianshou to inspect her; age and appearance suited them, and they agreed on a bride-price of a little over forty taels. Yanji said, "She comes from across the river. I fear her natal family will block it and not let her marry far. Seal the silver with the broker. When you are about to board, I will have her sent to the boat, and person and silver can be exchanged." The broker thought this would do.

paragraphs.zh: 临行，延纪自雇轿，诈称母舅家接母。上船后，始知子将己脱嫁于客，心中甚怒，只忍气问曰：“夫既以我嫁人，何必相瞒，且娶我者是谁？”天寿应曰：“是不才。”妇曰：“看君谅是个富翁，我亦无恨。但我因夫赌荡，衣资首饰悉藏母家。我同你去取，亦且令母家得知。”天寿信之，与邓氏偕往。氏入诉其子背将己嫁之事。其兄邓天明发怒曰：“哪有子敢嫁母者！是何客人敢斗胆而娶？”出将天寿乱打。邓氏救止曰：“谅客人亦不知情，只不孝延纪，胆大该死！”天明即具状告县。邹爷准状，差拘延纪，逃走不出；先拘汉卿、天寿到。邹爷审出大怒，将婚主、媒人各责二十，以天寿收监，着汉卿讨延纪。数月，终不能拿，累被拿限拷打。天寿投分上释监，邹爷竟不许。人教天寿曰：“贼要贼拿，赌钱要赌钱人拿。何不许银与赌棍人拿？”不数日，贼指延纪所在，差人拿到。邹爷审出延纪以子嫁母与远客作妾，责四十板，拟重典，身资银追入官；汉卿、天寿各拟杖惩；其母取氏，着兄邓天明领归供养，任自择嫁，批照付之。
paragraphs.en: When it was time to leave, Yanji hired a sedan himself and fabricated a story that his mother-in-law's family was coming to fetch her. Only after boarding the boat did she discover her son had married her off to a traveling merchant. She was furious but swallowed her anger and asked, "Since my husband has sold me to another, why hide it? And who is taking me?" Tianshou replied, "This unworthy man." The woman said, "You appear to be a wealthy man; I bear no grudge. However, because my husband gambled away our funds, all my clothes and jewelry are stored at my mother's house. Come with me to retrieve them and inform my mother's household." Tianshou believed her and went along with Deng. Upon entering, she told her brother how her son had secretly married her off. Her elder brother, Deng Tianming, erupted in anger: "How dare a son marry off his mother! What guest has the audacity to take her?" He rushed out and beat Tianshou severely. Deng intervened, saying, "I suppose the guest knew nothing. It is only the unfilial Yanji who deserves death for such daring!" Tianming then filed a complaint with the county magistrate. Magistrate Zou accepted the case, sent runners to summon Yanji, but Yanji fled and refused to appear. Instead, Hanqing and Tianshou were brought in first. After hearing the facts, Magistrate Zou was enraged, ordering twenty strokes each for the groom and the matchmaker, imprisoning Tianshou, and commanding Hanqing to produce Yanji. For months, they failed to catch him; Hanqing was repeatedly summoned under deadline and beaten. Tianshou sought release through connections, but Magistrate Zou refused. Someone advised Tianshou: "It takes a thief to catch a thief, a gambler to catch a gambler. Why not offer silver and have gambling crooks seize him?" Within days, the thieves identified Yanji's location, and the runners captured him. Magistrate Zou found that Yanji, a son, had sold his mother to a distant traveler as a concubine, sentenced him to forty strokes, proposed a heavy penalty, and confiscated the bride-price silver. Hanqing and Tianshou were each sentenced to corporal punishment as a warning. The mother, née Deng, was placed under her brother Deng Tianming's care for support, free to remarry at will, and a written order was issued accordingly.

paragraphs.zh: 按：为嗣娶妾，礼律不禁，特当娶于附近小户。若出外省，慕色而娶，多酿后患。若此类者，可为炯戒矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: Taking a concubine for the sake of an heir is not forbidden by ritual or law. Only, one should take her from a nearby small household. If you go to another province and marry out of lust for looks, you often brew later trouble. Cases of this kind may serve as a stark warning.

stories.title_en: Taking a Concubine in Another Province Triggers a Lawsuit Disaster

paragraphs.zh: 徐州人陈彩，家资巨富，机智深密，有莽、操之奸。年三十岁，妻妾俱无子。邻舍潘，常借彩银，出外为商。彩往家，见其妻游氏美貌绝伦，遂起不良心。邀同本往瓜州买绵花，发广州等处卖。货收完，二人同归。路经西关渡，此幽僻之处，往来者稀。上渡，以篙撑船。彩暗忖：“此机可乘。”从后将一推落江。奔起水面，彩再以篙指落深渊。浸死之后，彩故叫渔翁捞其尸，以火焚之，裹骨归家。
paragraphs.en: Chen Cai of Xuzhou was enormously rich, deep and close in his schemes, possessing the cunning of Wang Mang and Cao Cao. At thirty, neither his wife nor concubines had borne him a son. A neighbor named Pan often borrowed silver from Cai to go out trading. While visiting the Pan household, Chen saw that Pan’s wife, surnamed You, was unmatched in beauty, and an evil thought arose in him. He invited Pan to invest together, buying cotton at Guazhou to sell in Guangzhou and elsewhere. Once the goods were sold, they traveled home together. Their route passed the West Gate ferry, a secluded spot with little traffic. Upon boarding, a pole was used to push the boat. Chen secretly thought, "This chance can be seized." From behind, he shoved Pan into the river. When Pan broke the surface, Chen again used the pole to push him down into the depths. After Pan drowned, Chen deliberately summoned fishermen to retrieve the body, had it burned, wrapped the bones, and headed home.

paragraphs.zh: 彩穿白衣，见父母先大哭，而后报凶情。家大小都恸，乃细问身死因由。彩曰：“因过西关渡，上渡撑船，与篙并入水中。水深急，力不能起，遂致浸死。我雇人捞尸，焚骨而归。”言毕，潘家又哭。彩用将所卖帐薄并财本一一算明，交还之父母。满家反怀其德，哪知彩之设计谋死也。
paragraphs.en: Dressed in white mourning clothes, Cai went to see Pan's parents, wept loudly first, and then reported the tragic news. The entire household wailed and asked in detail how he had died. Cai said, "While crossing at the West Gate ferry, he boarded the boat and took the pole to push off, and plunged into the water along with the pole. The water was deep and swift, and he lacked the strength to come back up, so he drowned. I hired men to recover his body, cremated his bones, and brought them home." When he finished speaking, the Pan household wept again. Cai then accounted clearly for the sales ledger and all the capital, item by item, and returned them to the parents. The whole family felt grateful for his kindness—how could they know that Cai himself had plotted the murder?

paragraphs.zh: 至半年后，父潘玉年老，有二幼孙不能抚养，欲以媳招人入赘，代理家事，与彩商议。彩曰：“入赘事久远，必得得当人方可；不然，家被他破害，后悔何及？依彩愚见，小心支持守节，勿嫁人为尚。”彩言虽如此，而中藏机械甚深。后有议入赘者，玉亦与彩议，彩皆设机破之。因先贿游氏之外家。
paragraphs.en: Half a year later, Pan Yu, now old and unable to support his two young grandsons, proposed taking a man into the family as a live-in son-in-law to manage the household, and discussed this with Cai. Cai replied, "A live-in marriage is a long-term affair; one must secure the right man. Otherwise, the house will be ruined, and regret will come too late. In my humble opinion, it is best to carefully maintain the household and uphold widowhood rather than remarrying." Cai spoke thus, but his true design ran much deeper. Whenever anyone was proposed as a live-in son-in-law, Yu would consult Cai, who always found a way to thwart the match. First, however, he bribed You Shi’s natal family.

paragraphs.zh: 布谋已定，自言于玉曰：“吾与令郎至知，本无自赘之理。但事有经权，试与尊叔自筹之。”玉曰：“尊见何如？”彩曰：“吾欲以叔产业悉付我理，请叔族亲议立文书，递年几多供应尊叔夫妇食用，几多供应祭坟纳役，餘者悉付叔存之，以备二孙婚娶；令媳与我为次室。况我拙荆颇贤，必无妒恚之患。后倘得产男女，必不亏她。是令媳得所归，而公家亦有所付托矣。”媳曰：“古云‘宁作贫人妻，莫作富人妾。’我夫与他为友，我嫁他为妾，似不好观瞻。请公公再详。”玉曰：“难得此人家富忠厚，况又代我理家。我不劳而坐享衣食，餘剩者又存与孙婚娶。文字有我族人为证，何等安妥，不必再疑。”海军家大小皆以为然，游氏父母亦同声曰“可”，游氏只得听命。
paragraphs.en: When the plot was set, he said to Yu, "I am very close to your son; there is no reason I should move in myself. But sometimes one must weigh principle against expediency. Try discussing this with your uncle." Yu asked, "What is your view?" Cai replied, "I propose that you hand over all your property to me to manage. Please have your clan relatives draw up a document specifying how much each year will supply you and your wife for food and daily needs, how much for ancestral graves and labor service, and the rest kept for you to provide for the two grandsons' marriages. Let your daughter-in-law become my secondary wife. My own humble wife is virtuous; there will surely be no jealousy. Later, if we have children, I will not neglect her. Thus, your daughter-in-law will have a secure place, and the family will have someone to rely on." The daughter-in-law said, "It is said, 'Better to be a poor man's wife than a rich man's concubine.' My husband was his friend; if I marry him as a concubine, it will look bad. Please, Father-in-law, consider again." Yu said, "It is rare to find a household so wealthy and honest, and he will manage our affairs besides. I can sit back and enjoy food and clothing without labor; the remainder is saved for the grandsons' marriages. The agreement is witnessed by my clansmen. How secure that is! No need to doubt further." The entire Pan household agreed; You Shi's parents also unanimously said, "Agreed." You Shi had no choice but to obey.

paragraphs.zh: 不觉嫁后二十餘载，生有二子，又养一长孙。前二子皆已娶媳，亦生二孙。彩之正室前十年已故，游氏与夫极和顺。一日，大雨如注，天井水满。忽有青蛙浸于水中，跃起庭上。彩以小竹挑入水中去，如此者数次。彩平时是谨密之人，是日天牖其衷，暗忖游氏恩情已久，谅谈前情，妻必不怨，不觉漏言曰：“你前夫亦似此青蛙。若不生计较，安得与你成夫妇？”游氏曰：“计较若何？”彩曰：“昔时见你貌无双，要得同床伴我眠。心生一计同贸易，过渡踢他落波心。你夫奔起浮水面，再将篙指落深渊。连奔连指两三次，亦如青蛙此状情。”游氏惊号，大骂曰：“你这狼子野心贼，当千刀万剐！哪有人如此狠心者！”彩被妻骂，无一语可应之。游氏哭奔于路，高声叫曰：“我前夫被这贼谋死，谋我为妾！我必经官告论，为前夫报仇！”左邻右舍皆卒听惊骇。彩叫二子强抬游氏入家，皆跪下苦劝曰：“看家中大小之面，勿说此话。”游氏指骂二子曰：“你父奸谋子岂昌，无端造恶忒强梁。险邪暗害同曹贼，天牖其衷自说扬。呈官告论清奸孽，斩他首级振纲常。我夫虽然归黄土，九泉之下也心凉。”
paragraphs.en: Unawares, over twenty years had passed since the marriage; she had borne two sons and raised an eldest grandson. Both older sons had married and also produced two grandsons. Cai's principal wife had died ten years prior, yet You Shi and her husband lived in perfect harmony. One day, rain poured down until the courtyard flooded. Suddenly, a frog soaked in the water leaped onto the hall. Cai used a small bamboo stick to poke it back into the water, repeating this several times. Ordinarily a man of few words, that day Heaven revealed his inner thoughts. He thought: "You Shi has been affectionate for so long; if I mention the past, she surely won't resent me." Unintentionally, he let slip: 'Your former husband was just like this frog. If I hadn't hatched a scheme, how could I have become your husband?' You Shi asked, "What scheme?" Cai replied, "Back then, seeing your unmatched beauty, I wanted you in my bed. I devised a plan under the guise of trade. At the river crossing, I kicked him into the waves. Your husband broke the surface, so I used my pole to push him back into the deep abyss. Twice or thrice he rose, and I pushed him down—just like this frog." You Shi cried out in shock and cursed loudly: "You wolf-hearted thief! You deserve a thousand cuts! Who is so vicious!" Cursed by his wife, Cai had no answer. You Shi ran weeping into the road, shouting, "This thief murdered my former husband and plotted to make me his concubine! I will go to the officials to avenge my husband!" Neighbors on both sides heard and were shocked. Cai ordered his two sons to forcibly drag You Shi inside; they all knelt and pleaded, "Think of the honor of our entire household; do not say such things." You Shi pointed and cursed her sons: 'Your father's treacherous plot—how can sons flourish? He did evil without cause, far too violent. He harmed his trading partner with dark, crooked treachery; Heaven revealed his heart, and he boasted of it himself. I will take it to the officials to clear this wicked crime, cut off his head to restore moral order. Though my husband has returned to yellow earth, under the Nine Springs his heart will find peace.'

paragraphs.zh: 长子潘槐、次子潘杨闻游母出，路扬陈彩谋杀其父之事，与潘族众来问其详。游氏见二子并小叔，恸哭甚而言曰：“当你父在日，出外为商，尝问这贼借本。他见我先时有貌，即起歹意。邀你父出外贸易，归西关渡，踢你父于江中。奔起水面，复以篙指落深渊。如此者数次，因此浸死。”众等曰：“何以知之？”游氏曰：“适间大雨，天井水溢，有一青蛙被浸，跃起庭上。贼以竹打，抽下数次，蛙因打困浸死。天不容奸，他见此蛙，因自道其故，所以知之。儿可去告，我来作证。”槐、杨闻言，捶胸号天，大哭曰：“这仇不共戴天，扯来打死他！”直入内堂，将陈彩揪打。彩家理亏，自然不敢对敌。彩怒曰：“我纵谋人，罪有明条，岂该你打！”游氏曰：“他罪不容诛，若未经官，错手打死，则仇未报反成人命。”方闹嚷间，潘家族众倏集百餘人，中有无藉者欲掠其家。游氏曰：“物是我的。贼犯法当死，非他所有。我不出证其罪，汝众何得掠我财物？”
paragraphs.en: The eldest son, Pan Huai, and the second, Pan Yang, heard their mother You going about spreading news that Chen Cai had murdered their father, and came with the Pan clan to ask for details. You Shi, seeing her two sons and her husband’s younger brother, wept bitterly and said: “When your father was alive and went out trading, he often borrowed capital from this thief. He saw that I was handsome then, and an evil thought arose. He invited your father out to trade; returning at the West Gate ferry, he kicked your father into the river. When he broke the surface, he used the pole again to push him down into the deep. Several times like this, and so he drowned.” They asked, “How do you know?” You Shi said: “Just now in the heavy rain the courtyard overflowed. A frog was soaked and leaped onto the hall. The thief beat it with bamboo and poked it down several times; the frog, worn out by the beating, drowned. Heaven will not tolerate treachery. He saw this frog and confessed his own guilt; that is how I know. You sons can go and charge him; I will come as witness.” Huai and Yang heard this, beat their breasts, cried to heaven, and wept: “This feud cannot share the same sky. Drag him here and beat him to death!” They went straight into the inner hall, seized Chen Cai, and beat him. Cai’s household, being in the wrong, naturally dared not fight back. Cai said in anger: “Even if I plotted against a man, the law has a clear article. How dare you beat me?” You Shi said: “His crime is so great that death is insufficient. If we have not gone through the officials and kill him by a wrong blow, then the feud is not avenged and we have made a homicide case instead.” In the midst of the uproar, more than a hundred of the Pan clan gathered; among them some ne’er-do-wells wanted to loot the house. You Shi said: “The goods are mine. The thief has broken the law and should die; they are not his. If I do not come forward to prove his crime, how may you lot plunder my property?”

paragraphs.zh: 游氏与二子抱牌急告本县。魏爷准其状，差拿陈彩到官，无半语推辞，一一招认。魏爷打彩三十板，立拟典刑，即申上司讫。游氏并二子槐、杨各讨保，候解两院。是日，县看者何止数百人，皆曰：“此妇原在潘家，处中户；今处于陈，万金巨富，驱奴使婢，先作妾而今作正室；况年已久，生子及孙。徇情者初谈及此，未免哽咽喉干，吞声忍气而罢。今径呈之公庭，必令偿前夫命，真可谓女流中节侠，行出乎流俗者也！”
paragraphs.en: You Shi and her two sons clutched the petition and rushed to the county magistrate to report the crime. Magistrate Wei accepted their complaint, ordered Chen Cai brought to court. Without a word of denial, he confessed to everything. Magistrate Wei beat Cai thirty strokes, immediately sentenced him to death, and reported the case to the superior authorities. You Shi and her two sons, Huai and Yang, each posted bail to await transfer to the provincial courts. That day, hundreds gathered at the county office to watch. They all said: "This woman was originally in the Pan household, living in a respectable station; now she is with Chen, a man worth ten thousand taels of gold, commanding slaves and maids, first a concubine and now the principal wife. Years have passed, and she has borne sons and grandsons. A sentimental person, upon first hearing of this, would likely choke up, swallow their voice, and let it drop. But she went straight to the public court, demanding the life for her former husband. She can truly be called a woman of honor among her sex, acting beyond the common run!"

paragraphs.zh: 两院倒案已毕，陈彩正典刑已定。彩托禁子叫游氏并二子来狱中嘱咐。游氏不肯去见，只叫二子往见之。彩嘱二子传命曰：“我偿潘之命已定，她之怨已酬，而结怨之恩已报矣，何惜见我一面？我有后事欲以付托。”游氏曰：“我与他恩谊绝矣，有何颜再见他？”二子入狱中回话，彩大怒曰：“我在狱受尽苦楚，不日处决。她在家享受富贵，是他潘家物乎，陈家物乎？”言毕，二子以父言传于母。游氏曰：“我在你父家二十餘载，恩非不深，但不知他机谋甚巧。今已泄出前情，则你父实我仇人，义当绝之。你二人是我毛里天性，安忍割舍？你父不说富贵是他家的，我意已欲还潘家；今既如此说，我还意已决。当你母已死，勿复念也。”二子曰：“母亲为前夫报仇，正合大义，我父不得生怨。须念我兄弟年幼，方赖母亲教育，万勿往他家也。”游氏不听，召集陈门亲族，将家业并首饰等项交割明白，空身而还潘家，甘处淡泊，人皆服其高义，羡潘之有妻，仇终得报；叹子彩之奸谋，祸反及身也。
paragraphs.en: The two courts had finished reviewing the case; Chen Cai’s capital sentence was fixed. Cai asked a jailer to summon You Shi and their two sons to the prison to give his final instructions. You Shi refused to go see him; she only sent her two sons. Cai charged them to pass word: “I am to pay Pan’s life; that is settled. Her grievance is paid, and the debt of that old wrong has been repaid. Why begrudge seeing me once? I have final arrangements I wish to entrust.” You Shi said, “All kindness and duty between us are cut. What face do I have to see him again?” The two sons went into the jail and answered. Cai said in a great rage, “I suffer every misery in jail and will be executed any day. She enjoys wealth at home—is it the Pan house’s goods, or the Chen house’s?” When he had finished, the two sons passed their father’s words to their mother. You Shi said, “I was in your father’s house for over twenty years; the kindness was not shallow. I only did not know how clever his schemes were. Now that the past has come out, your father is in truth my enemy, and by right I must cut him off. You two are of my flesh and blood; how could I bear to give you up? Your father need not say the wealth is his house’s; I already meant to go back to the Pan house. Now that he has spoken so, my mind to return is fixed. Take your mother as already dead; think of me no more.” The two sons said, “Mother avenging her former husband is exactly great duty; our father has no call to resent it. Only think that we brothers are young and still depend on Mother’s teaching. By all means do not go to that other house.” You Shi would not listen. She gathered the Chen clan, handed over the estate, jewelry, and everything else clearly, and went back empty-handed to the Pan house, content to live simply. People all admired her high sense of duty, envied Pan for having such a wife, so that the feud was at last repaid, and sighed that Cai’s treacherous plot had brought the disaster back on himself.

stories.title_en: A Frog Exposes a Murderous Marriage Plot

paragraphs.zh: 宗化人羽崇，家资殷富，性最好淫，常以银穀生放于乡下。乡人唯早午晚在家食饭，午前后都往耕田，并无男子在家。崇偏于半午前往人家取帐，遇单居妇女，千方挑之，多与通好。
paragraphs.en: Yu Chong of Zonghua was a man of ample means and lecherous by nature. He often lent silver and grain at interest in the countryside. Villagers were home only for their morning, noon, and evening meals; before and after midday they were all out plowing the fields, leaving no men at home. Chong made a point of going to collect debts just before noon. When he found a woman alone, he tried every way to seduce her, and he often got her into bed.

paragraphs.zh: 人有问之者曰：“凡妇人与初相见，面生情疏，茫不相识，怎好开口便通野话？倘怒骂起来，后何以登其门？”崇曰：“凡撩妇人，临机应变，因事乘机。或以言挑，或以利诱，或以势压，或以恳求，何止一端，全在察其心情而投中之。或无可入机者，试与之讲梦，说我昨夜梦一所在去，宛似你家一般，某物在此，某物在此。又梦与你相交，一夜快活，醒来乃是一梦。今日到此，全与梦中相同。如此且笑且说，讲了一遍，看她言貌或喜或怒，或不睬，或应对，或疑猜，便可以言投入。彼若发骂，我只说梦；彼若不拒，我便可取事矣。“我尝往一所在取帐。男子另一处造纸，两妯娌对焙纸。其伯姆半宿妇人，其婶子极是少美，我欲挑之。若半声推拒，隔焙便闻，何以动手？我生一计，包银一钱，作一块，密密轻轻与说曰：‘我欲挑你伯姆，把此一钱银送你；再一包五分，託你代送与伯姆，替我说个方便’。妇人接四包银，把自己包开看过，见银作一块，心中有些喜意，答曰：‘你爱她你自与她说，自然是替，我不好替说。’我便曰：‘若爱只是爱你，但恐你不肯，故託你通伯姆。’罢不应，我便搂之，默然应承。只隔焙幹事，那边全不知。若不如此，反生计较。彼恐伯姆知之，怎肯默然应允？惟先说挑伯姆，彼心道：‘那边可干事，我这边密密幹，亦何妨？’故不劳而成也。”
paragraphs.en: Someone asked him: "When you first meet a woman, you are strangers, with no feeling between you. How can you open your mouth with indecent talk? If she flies into a rage and scolds you, how will you ever enter her door again?" Chong said: "Seducing a woman depends on reading the moment and using whatever the situation offers. You may bait her with words, tempt her with profit, press her with rank, or plead—there is more than one way. The whole art is to watch her mood and hit it. If there is no opening, try telling her a dream: say that last night you dreamed you went to a place that looked just like her house, this thing here, that thing there; and you dreamed you were with her all night, then woke and found it was a dream; and today you arrive, and it is exactly as in the dream. Tell it with a smile. Watch whether her face is pleased or angry, whether she ignores you, answers, or grows suspicious—then you know how to speak. If she scolds, I say it was only a dream. If she does not refuse, I can proceed. I once went to collect a debt. The men were making paper elsewhere; two co-sisters-in-law were drying paper facing each other. The elder brother's wife was an older woman; the younger brother's wife was very young and pretty. I wanted to seduce the younger one. If she made even half a sound of refusal, it would be heard across the drying rack—how could I act? I thought of a plan. I wrapped a single lump of silver worth one qian and said quietly: 'I want to seduce your sister-in-law. I'll give you this one qian; here is another packet of five fen—please pass it to her and intercede for me.' The woman took four packets of silver, opened her own packet, saw the silver in a lump, and was somewhat pleased. She answered: 'If you like her, tell her yourself. Of course I'll help, but I shouldn't be the one to speak.' I said: 'If I like anyone, I like you. I only feared you would refuse, so I asked you to speak to your sister-in-law.' She did not answer. I embraced her, and she silently consented. We did it with only the drying rack between us; the other side never knew. If I had not done it this way, she would have thought twice. She would have feared her sister-in-law would know, and would never have silently agreed. Only by first saying I wanted the sister-in-law would she think: 'If that side can do it, I can do it quietly here too—what's the harm?' So it was done without effort."
