paragraphs.zh: 有方外道士，利得其金也，私臆懸度，謂「古方云『土以土補，木以木補，人以人補』，意必食人可補人也。」妄去獻方云：「烹童男膾肝脯肉，食其精髓，則精液充滿，陽物復生，可姦婦生子矣。」閩高閹信之，先售以百金，候服有驗，再來領萬金。由是，命牙爪往窮鄉僻邑，買貧民幼童，詐云「高衙欲養為子，日後富貴無窮。」貧民信之，多賣以博眼前重利，且希望後日富貴。後先買者，難以稽數。但鬻子之家，有託人往​​查己子者，並無聲息；即衙中走僕，亦不知內之養子若何也。原來買之幼童，盡養以錦衣美食。廚子能烹調一童以進食，賞銀十兩，深禁其秘密。每殺一童，廚子提刀追趕，眾童各涕泣奔呼，候其走熱氣揚，則執其肥者烹之。
paragraphs.en: A wandering Daoist, greedy for that gold, made a wild guess of his own: “The old formulas say earth is mended with earth, wood is mended with wood, man is mended with man—so eating human flesh must mend a man.” He went recklessly and offered up a recipe: “Boil a young boy, mince the liver, dry the flesh, and eat the essence and marrow. Then the vital fluid will be replenished, the organ will grow back, and you can lie with women and father sons.” The eunuch Gao of Fujian believed him. He paid a hundred taels up front; if the dose proved effective, the man could return for ten thousand taels. From then on he sent his henchmen into poor villages and remote counties to buy young boys from destitute families, lying that “the Gao household wants to raise them as sons, and later they will have wealth and honor without end.” The poor believed it, and many sold their sons for the heavy profit in hand, hoping besides for riches to come. How many were bought in all is impossible to reckon. But some of the families who had sold sons sent people to ask after their boys—and there was never any word. Even the servants who ran errands in the yamen had no idea how the adopted sons inside were faring. In fact, the purchased boys were all kept in brocade and fed the finest food. Any cook who could prepare a boy for the table was rewarded with ten taels, and the secret was guarded under the strictest ban. Each time a boy was to be killed, the cook chased the children with a knife while they ran weeping and screaming; when they had run themselves hot and their blood was up, he seized a fat one and cooked him.

paragraphs.zh: 內有一童十二歲，跪廚子涕泣哀告，叩頭求救。廚子亦淚曰：「吾怎能救你，吾亦不奈何墮此也。」有頃，外人傳某鄉官相拜。廚子曰：「憑你命，吾放你出去，外有鄉官相拜，你扯其衣死哀求救；肯帶你去，則你可生，我代你死罷。你可傳知外人，切勿將子賣入太監府也。」此幼童直奔至鄉官前，哀告：「廚子要殺我！」太監即令查拿廚子斬首，———彼恨其縱出此童也，笑顏諭幼童入後。幼童死扯鄉官衣求救。鄉官疑有緣故，為之帶出。幼童歷敘內中殺諸童之由，鄉官不勝嗟嘆。思起本未得諸童買來之由，又無廚子證據，亦不敢留養此童，遣其出外別投生。此童後流丐於建郡等處。人問其太監府之事，多能言其中之富貴，皆非人世所有也。自後方知太監之食人，始不肯以子賣之。近年，高閹以罪去。其鬻子之父母，累十百候於途，並不見一幼子與姦閹生去者，無不墮淚，痛其子之必遭烹也。
paragraphs.en: Among the boys was one of twelve who knelt before the cook, weeping and pleading, knocking his head on the ground and begging for his life. The cook wept too: “How could I save you? I fell into this against my own will as well.” Presently word came from outside that a certain retired official had come to pay a call. The cook said: “I will leave it to your fate: I am letting you out. A retired official is calling—grab his sleeve and wail for your life. If he will take you away, you may live, and I will die in your place. And tell the people outside: never sell a son into a eunuch’s house.” The boy ran straight to the official and cried out, “The cook is going to kill me!” The eunuch at once ordered the cook seized and beheaded—he hated him for letting the boy slip out—and with a smiling face commanded the boy to return inside. The boy clung desperately to the official’s sleeve, begging to be saved. The official suspected there was more behind it and took the boy out with him. The boy recounted in full how the children inside were being slaughtered, and the official sighed without end. But reflecting that he had never learned how the boys had been bought in the first place, and that with the cook dead there was no witness, he dared not keep the boy himself; he sent him out to find some other way to live. The boy later drifted as a beggar around Jian Prefecture and thereabouts. When people asked him about the eunuch’s household, he could tell them much of the wealth and splendor within—things this world has never seen. Only then did people learn that the eunuch ate human flesh, and only then did they refuse to sell their sons. In recent years Eunuch Gao was removed for his crimes. The parents who had sold their sons waited along the road in scores and hundreds, and not one saw a young son come out alive with that vile eunuch. There was none who did not shed tears, grieving that his boy must surely have been cooked.

paragraphs.zh: 按：貧民賣子，極為至愚。若不能養，何不若鳳陽府父子俱丐，猶可骨肉相保。必不得已，唯可賣之富戶為僕。固不可供太監之啖，亦不可賣入庵寺為行童侍者，其賤尤在乞丐下也。國家置閹尹，以供掃除傳命耳。至使握利權，享用已極，更思生陽物淫婦人，為不可必得之事。雖食人而可為汝欲扶已朽之軀，曾不惜人渾全之命乎？是可忍也，孰不可忍也！孟子曰：「善戰者服上刑」，猶為強兵而殺人也；此為何事而視人命如草菅乎？王法若明，當不令此閹得生還矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: For poor people to sell their sons is folly of the deepest kind. If you cannot raise them, why not do as they do in Fengyang Prefecture, where father and son beg together? At least flesh and blood stay together. If there is truly no other way, sell them only to a rich household as servants. You must never feed them to a eunuch’s appetite, nor sell them into convents and temples as boy servants and attendants—that degradation is lower than beggary itself. The state keeps eunuchs to sweep the palace and carry messages, nothing more. To let them grasp the power of profit, glut themselves on every luxury, and then attempt to restore their virility so they can debauch women—a thing they cannot possibly have! Even if eating human flesh could feed your lust and prop up your rotting carcass, have you no pity for another person’s whole and unbroken life? If this can be endured, what cannot be endured? Mencius said, “Those skilled in war should suffer the heaviest punishment”—and that was for killing to make an army strong. What cause is this, that human lives should be treated as weeds? If the law of the land were truly enforced, this eunuch would never have been allowed to return alive.

stories.title_en: A Eunuch Cooks Men and Eats Their Essence

paragraphs.zh: 凡学道出巡，各处棍徒云集追随，专体探富家子有谋钻刺者，多方献门路，以图蛊骗。或此路不售，后一帮又生一端以投，年年有堕其术者。但受骗之家羞以告人，故后次人又蹈之。
paragraphs.en: Whenever the Provincial Education Commissioner goes on tour, crooks from every quarter gather and follow him, hunting for rich men’s sons who want to buy influence. They offer openings of every kind, hoping to cheat them. If one pitch does not take, another gang comes along with a different angle; every year some fall for it. But the families who are cheated are too ashamed to tell anyone, so the next people walk into the same trap.

paragraphs.zh: 有一学道，考选至公，不纳分上。忽一棍自言能通于道者，人不之信。棍曰：“此道爷自开私门，最不喜人央分上前途。唯对手干者，百发百中，但人不敢耳。如真肯干者，但要现钱，彼当面接之，可稳保成就。”赵甲问曰：“从何处献之？”棍曰：“候退堂后，先用手本开具某县某人银若干，求取进学。彼肯面允，便进上银；如不允，银在我手，彼奈我何？”赵甲曰：“我要在旁亲看。”棍曰：“自然与你亲看。学道的二门，其缝阔一寸，从外窥之，直见堂上，任你看之。”赵甲曰：“若道肯亲手接银，吾敢投之。”即写手本，以手帕包银二百两作一封。
paragraphs.en: There was an education commissioner, scrupulously fair in his examinations, who took no private requests. Suddenly a con man claimed he could channel directly to the commissioner; no one believed him. The con man said, “This commissioner has opened a private door himself. He hates it when people send introductions through intermediaries. Only those who deal with him face-to-face succeed every time—people just don’t dare. If you truly mean to do it, all you need is ready money; he’ll take it in person, and success is as good as guaranteed.” Zhao Jia asked, “Where do we present it?” The con man said, “Wait until he leaves the hall. First use a petition listing such-and-such county, so-and-so, so many taels of silver, asking to be admitted to the school. If he agrees in person, then hand over the silver; if he doesn’t, the silver remains in my hands—what can he do to me?” Zhao Jia said, “I want to stand beside you and watch for myself.” The con man said, “Of course you’ll watch for yourself. The second gate of the education commissioner’s office has a crack an inch wide; peeking from outside you can see straight into the hall—watch as you wish.” Zhao Jia said, “If the commissioner will take the silver with his own hands, I’ll dare to go in.” He wrote a petition and wrapped two hundred taels in a handkerchief as one packet.

paragraphs.zh: 下午出堂，往道前候之。棍曰：“要二包过门银。”甲付与之。将退堂之际，棍以银与手本挨入堂去，嘱甲曰：“才封门时，即要在门缝来看。”及道退堂后，甲于二门缝中看，见道仍旧纱帽圆领而出。棍先以手本高递上，一门子接进。道展看了，笼入袖中去。棍又高擎一封银上，道顾门子，门子接上银。道一看即转身，门子随后捧银包而入。棍趋至二门，隔门谓甲曰：“好了，好了，事已妥矣！你见否？”甲应曰：“我亲见了，果是自接。”棍曰：“今夜不能出，我你须在门内外宿矣。”甲曰：“但得事妥，不吃晚饭亦好。”
paragraphs.en: That afternoon they went out and waited in front of the commissioner's office. The con man said, "I need two packets of silver to get through the gate." Jia paid him. As the session was about to end, the con man took the silver and the petition and slipped into the hall, telling Jia, "The moment they seal the gate, come look through the crack." After the commissioner left the hall, Jia looked through the crack in the second gate and saw a man still in gauze cap and round-collared robe come out. The con man first held the petition high; a yamen attendant took it in. The commissioner opened it, looked it over, and tucked it into his sleeve. The con man then held a packet of silver high; the commissioner glanced at the attendant; the attendant took up the silver. The commissioner glanced at it and turned; the attendant followed him in, carrying the silver packet. The con man hurried to the second gate and said through the door, "It's done, it's done! Did you see?" Jia said, "I saw it myself; he did take it with his own hands." The con man said, "I can't go out tonight; you and I will have to sleep on either side of the gate." Jia said, "If the business is settled, going without supper is fine."

paragraphs.zh: 次日开早门，棍与甲方同出，即到甲店拜贺。甲大设席待之。棍曰：“高取后须厚谢我。”甲曰：“加一谢是定规，不加亦不减矣。”此为信棍之戒。
paragraphs.en: The next morning, when the early gate opened, the con man and Jia went out together and visited Jia’s shop to celebrate his success. Jia hosted a lavish feast. The con man said, "Once you secure your winnings, you must reward me generously." Jia replied, "Adding an extra thank-you gift is the fixed rule; I won’t add anything beyond that, nor will I subtract anything." Let this serve as a warning against trusting crooks.

paragraphs.zh: 后揭晓日，本生无名。棍查不见踪，方知前受银之道，乃此棍先与宿衙人套定，盖妆假道也。
paragraphs.en: On the day the results were announced, the victim's name was nowhere to be found. The swindler had vanished. Only then did they realize that the way the silver had been taken earlier was because this swindler had first colluded with the night-duty yamen men to stage a fake official.

paragraphs.zh: 二门望入堂上，虽可亲见，终是路遥，哪见得真？故落此棍骗而不知。若真道自接银，何必衣冠出？何必堂上递手本？又何必堂上交银？独不可私递手本乎？况堂上有宿衙人役，岂私受银之地？此村富不识官体，故以目见为稳，不知与你目见，正所以骗你也。
paragraphs.en: Looking from the second gate into the hall, though you can see it yourself, the distance is still great—how can you see clearly? So they fell for this swindle without realizing it. If an official were truly accepting silver personally, why come out in full dress? Why present a petition in the hall? Why hand over silver in the hall? Couldn't the petition be passed privately? Besides, the hall has staff on duty—is that a place to accept silver in secret? This rustic rich man did not understand official protocol, so he took seeing with his own eyes as proof; he did not realize that letting you see with your own eyes was exactly how they cheated you.

stories.title_en: A Swindle: Presenting Fake Silver to the Education Commissioner

paragraphs.zh: 富人钱一，欲为子买进学。歇家孙丙，有意骗之，与之言曰：“此中李乡官，原与学道同僚，二人极相得。今若说一名进学，此断可得。吾试与商议之。”钱一曰：“可。”孙丙往匠铺，见两挂箱一样，用钱三钱买其一，又以银二分定后只，嘱曰：“我停会引人来买，更出三钱，不可别换。”又买两把一样的锁。后以挂箱与锁付李乡官家人曰：“你可秤定二百两石头，装在挂箱内，外加锁之，放在你家主房内。少顷，我领人央你老爷说进学，以二百两好银与你封。你把放银的箱收入，换放石的箱出来，然后将这银与我均分。”李家人许曰：“可。”
paragraphs.en: Rich man Qian Yi wanted to buy his son a place in the school. Innkeeper Sun Bing intended to cheat him and said, "There is a retired official named Li here who was once a colleague of the education commissioner; the two are very close. If we speak up for one candidate, we can certainly secure admission. Let me try discussing it with him." Qian Yi said, "All right." Sun Bing went to a craftsman's shop, saw two identical chests, bought one for three qian, and paid a deposit of two fen to reserve the second, telling them, "In a moment I'll bring someone to buy it; he will pay another three qian—do not swap it for a different one." He also bought two identical locks. Then he gave a chest and lock to Official Li's servant: "Weigh out two hundred taels of stones, put them in the chest, lock it from the outside, and place it in your master's room. Shortly I will bring someone asking your master to speak for school admission, bringing two hundred taels of good silver for you to seal. You take in the chest with the silver, swap it for the chest with the stones, then split this silver with me." Li's servant agreed: "All right."

paragraphs.zh: 孙丙领李家人来，对钱一说：“我面见李老爷了，他道此事容易，只把现银对于他家人看过锁住，送到他家加封条，仍以银箱付还我，以锁匙付他收。待有名进学之后，将原银谢他，不得开箱再换。”钱一曰：“在你家借一挂箱来用。”孙丙曰：“新锁有，挂箱可往街买之。”领钱一家人，以银三钱，往铺买到。钱一将银二百两同李家人、孙丙三面对定，收入挂箱中，外加锁定。
paragraphs.en: Sun Bing brought Li’s servant and told Qian Yi: “I met Lord Li in person. He said this is easy: have the ready silver shown to his servant, checked and locked, sent to his house to be sealed, then return the silver chest to me while giving him the key to keep. Once he passes the examination and enters the academy, the original silver will serve as his thanks; the chest must not be opened or swapped.” Qian Yi said, “I’ll borrow a chest from your place.” Sun Bing replied, “I have a new lock; you can buy the chest at a shop.” He led one of Qian’s men, paid three qian, and bought it. With Li’s servant and Sun Bing watching, Qian Yi verified two hundred taels of silver, placed them in the chest, and locked it securely.

paragraphs.zh: 孙丙负银，同钱一到李乡官家，求加封条。李乡官推病，在厅左房内坐。李家人持箱入门边曰：“银已看对阴白，只讨一封条。”李乡官曰：“既看明白，还他自收，来接封条。”李家人仍以银箱出，再领出一封条，对三面封讫。钱一解锁匙，付李家人收。孙丙复负银箱归，交与钱一自收藏，皆谓事极妥矣。
paragraphs.en: Sun Bing carried the silver chest with Qian Yi to Official Li’s house, requesting a sealing strip. Official Li feigned illness and sat in a room to the left of the hall. Li’s servant held the chest at the doorway: "The silver has been verified against the mark; we only need one sealing strip." Official Li replied, "Since it’s been checked clearly, give it back for him to keep, and come fetch the sealing strip." The servant took the chest out again, then brought out a sealing strip and sealed all three sides before them. Qian Yi handed over the key to Li’s servant. Sun Bing carried the silver chest back and gave it to Qian Yi to store away; everyone thought the matter perfectly secure.

paragraphs.zh: 及揭晓，钱一子无名。孙丙曰：“事不成，银现在，可速收拾归，免得李家人来索轿价。”钱一既失望，怏怏而归。及到半路，叫匠人开锁启视，则皆石头矣。惊异复回，大闹歇家曰：“你何通同骗我？”孙丙曰：“我与你当面干事，何处是骗你？若三面共开挂箱，犹怪得李家；今去半日，私自开箱，我那知中间是银是石？”钱一明知是孙、李合骗，只事无凭证，谅是难取，但辱骂歇家一场而归。此为信乡官之戒。
paragraphs.en: When the results were posted, Qian Yi's son had no name on the list. Sun Bing said, "It didn't work; the silver is still here. Pack up and head home quickly, lest Li's people come asking for sedan-chair fees." Qian Yi, disappointed, headed home dejected. Halfway there he called a carpenter to open the lock and look: all stones. Shocked, he went back and made a scene at the inn: "How did you collude to cheat me?" Sun Bing said, "I did the business with you face to face; where was the cheat? If the three of us had opened the chest together, you could still blame the Li household; now after half a day's travel you opened the chest in private—how would I know whether inside was silver or stone?" Qian Yi knew perfectly well that Sun and Li had cheated him together, but there was no proof; he figured the silver would be hard to recover, so he only cursed the innkeeper roundly and headed home. Take this as a lesson: do not trust retired officials.

paragraphs.zh: 按：两挂箱共样，本是难辨。但加封条，只须在外封之，何必持入内禀乃请封条乎？向令当时若告，追究卖挂箱之家，问两箱何以一样，或能证出孙丙先买其一，后领人买一。或遇明官，便可从中勘出换包之骗矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: Two chests of identical pattern are naturally hard to distinguish. Yet applying a seal only requires doing so on the outside; why carry them inside to report and then request the seal? Had the victim reported it to the magistrate at the time, investigating the shop that sold the chests and asking why two were alike might have revealed that Sun Bing first bought one, then arranged for another to be purchased. With a clear-sighted official, the package-swap swindle could have been exposed from this.

stories.title_en: The Swindler's Seal: A Trick in a Retired Official's Private Quarters

paragraphs.zh: 建宁府郝天广，世家巨富，有几所庄，多系白米。时建宁无价，其智家罗五闻省城米价高腾，邀主人带二仆，以米十馀船装往省粜。时宗主王爷发牌考延、建二府，各有告示，将考儒童。米才上船，有一客人带二仆，来搭船往省。船中暇坐，问其何干。答曰：“王爷家来投书者。”后又谈及可夤缘之事，天广有长子出考，言甚合意；只宗主前考甚公，并无私窦，未敢深信其事。
paragraphs.en: Hao Tianguang of Jianning Prefecture came from an old wealthy family with several estates, mostly stocked with white rice. At the time, rice prices in Jianning were low; his steward Luo Wu heard that prices in the provincial capital were soaring and invited his master, along with two servants, to load ten-odd boats of rice to sell there. Just then, the Prince had issued orders to examine students from both Yanping and Jianning prefectures, with proclamations announcing the civil service exams for young scholars. As the rice was just being loaded, a guest accompanied by two servants arrived to book passage to the capital. Seated at leisure on the boat, they asked what his business was. He replied, "I have come from the Prince's household to deliver a letter." Later, the conversation turned to securing favors through connections. Tianguang had his eldest son taking the exam; the talk suited him well. However, since the Prince had conducted the previous examinations very fairly, with no backdoor channels, he did not quite dare to believe it.

paragraphs.zh: 至省中，棍辞别去，曰：“王爷有公子在学，必共看卷。试与谈尊府事，倘许诺，我再出回你诺；若不出，则事不谐耳，再亦无信。”天广曰：“是也。”密遣一仆，踪迹棍所去处，果入学道衙去。数日后出来曰：“事谐矣。可将银对定，以我皮箱藏之，外加封条，银仍与你自收掌。后有名进学，即以皮箱银交出与我。”天广思“银虽对定，仍是我藏，有何不可？”即依言对讫，不知此棍有甚法。银明是天广自投自锁，棍只加封票一条而去，再约曰：“今夜间公子或可潜出，我与之同看过，事即美矣。”连候数夜不来，天广以皮箱开看，其内尽是砖石，前银已被赚去矣。此为封银防换之戒。
paragraphs.en: At the provincial capital, the crook took his leave: "The Prince has a young master in the school; they are sure to look at papers together. I'll try talking about your honorable house; if he agrees, I'll come out and bring you the yes; if I don't come out, the matter isn't on, and there will be no further word." Tianguang said, "Right." He secretly sent a servant to track where the crook went; indeed he went into the Prince's yamen. After several days he came out: "It's arranged. Weigh out the silver, hide it in my leather case, add a sealing strip outside; the silver stays in your own keeping. After the name is on the list for school, you hand the leather case of silver over to me." Tianguang thought, "Though the silver is checked, I still keep it—what's wrong with that?" He followed the instructions and weighed it out, not knowing what method this crook had. The silver was clearly put in and locked by Tianguang himself; the crook only added one sealing ticket and left, and further agreed: "Tonight the young master may slip out; I'll look it over with him, and the matter will be fine." They waited several nights; he did not come. Tianguang opened the leather case: all bricks and stones; the silver had been cheated away. Let this be a warning: when sealing silver, guard against a swap.

paragraphs.zh: 按：买进学、买帮补，甚至买举人，此事处处有之，岁岁有之，而建宁一府，叠遭骗害为甚。盖建郡民富财多，性浮轻轻故也。虽累受骗，而继起营买者未已，此光棍途中常以逢考建宁为一桩好生意也。特其封银法，至今人看不破。明以银与之同封，复还我收，及棍去后开之，则皆砖石矣；或以为有一遁银法。如此神矣哉，上智难防也！唯明鉴乎此，勿信为上。若急欲买进，可勿封银，须以榜上有名为定。若只信其漏报，虽至三四次见金榜矣，亦未可以银付之，方可防其脱也。
paragraphs.en: Note: Buying a school place, buying a stipend, even buying the juren degree—this happens everywhere, every year, and Jianning Prefecture has been cheated over and over, worse than anywhere else. The people of Jian commandery are rich with much wealth, and their nature is light and flighty. Though they have been cheated again and again, those who follow up to buy still do not stop; so sharps on the road often treat the Jianning exams as a lucrative business. The method of sealing silver, especially, people still cannot see through to this day. Clearly, you seal the silver together, it is given back for you to keep, and after the crook leaves, you open it—all bricks and stones. Some think there is a method of making silver vanish. How miraculous—even the wisest can hardly guard against it! Only see this clearly; not believing is best. If you urgently want to buy entry, don't seal silver; take a name on the posted list as the settlement. If you only believe his leaked reports, even if you see the golden list three or four times, you still must not hand over silver; only then can you guard against being cheated out of it.

stories.title_en: Sealed Silver Swapped for Bricks

paragraphs.zh: 骗局多端，唯仕进一途，竟奔者多，故遭骗者众。棍尝有言，唯虚名可骗实利，唯虚声可赚实物。盖仕进之人，求名之心胜，虽掷重利不暇顾惜，遂入棍术中而不及察。
paragraphs.en: Swindles take many forms; yet in the path of official advancement, so many rush headlong that the number of victims is vast. Swindlers often say: only an empty name can cheat one out of solid profit; only hollow reputation can earn real goods. For those seeking office, their hunger for fame is so intense that they throw down heavy sums without pausing to consider, thus falling into the swindler's trap without noticing.

paragraphs.zh: 有一巨富家子，欲营谋进学，所带管家者极为能干。往省考大续，寓一歇家中，令其求关通之路。数日内，以门路投者，更进迭来。管家者窥其行径，穷其来历，皆察其言事不相应，踪迹不分明，多与歇家有套同情弊，悉拒却之，不信其哄。后一棍妆为仆价，言语迟钝，举动村朴，自方跟一罢职乡官，与宗主有旧，来此打秋风。引管家去见乡官，果似贫薄小官样。面酌定一名进学，只谢银一百两亦肯讲，只要现银，来伊店封。管家曰：“在我店封。”乡官曰：“事宜慎密，你店内人众，传扬不便。此下有一所空房，是顾秀才的，前欲在彼借寓，以借什物不便，故迁在此。可与我小价在彼处封定，最是稳当。”管家强求乡官来所住店看封为妥。乡官曰：“汝更有疑，我只小价一人，任你多用人来同封。”管家回以“外人不可与知，只同本主去。”果只村仆一人在，把银出对定。忽有棍数人，打开门入曰：“汝辈买秀才，吾拿去出首！”将三人打倒，银尽抢去。
paragraphs.en: A wealthy family's son sought to scheme his way into the academy; the steward he brought was extremely capable. They traveled to the provincial capital for the examination and lodged at an inn, instructing the steward to find a way through. Within days, various people offering connections arrived one after another. The steward observed their conduct, traced their backgrounds, and found their words inconsistent with their actions, their tracks unclear, and many colluding with the innkeeper. He rejected them all, refusing to believe their lies. Later, a crook dressed as a servant, slow of speech and rustic in manner, claimed he followed a dismissed country official who had old ties with the patron and had come here to sponging off others. He led the steward to see the official, who indeed looked like a poor minor official. They agreed face-to-face on one name for the academy; even a hundred taels as a bribe he would discuss, provided it was ready silver, sealed at his inn. The steward said, "Seal it at my inn." The official replied, "The matter must be discreet; your inn has too many people, making it inconvenient if word spreads. Down below there is an empty house belonging to Xiucai Gu. I intended to lodge there before, but borrowing furnishings was inconvenient, so I moved here. You and my little servant can seal the deal there; that is most secure." The steward insisted the official come to their inn to witness the sealing. The official said, "If you still doubt, I have only one little servant; you may send as many people as you like to seal together." The steward replied, "Outsiders must not know; I will only go with my master." Indeed, only the rustic servant was present. They brought out the silver and checked it. Suddenly several crooks burst in: "You are buying a xiucai! We'll take you and report it!" They beat the three men down and robbed all the silver.

paragraphs.zh: 村仆爬起，做烦恼样。管家起，挈其手曰：“不须恼，此银亦不多，同在我店再封。”村仆不肯去。富子曰：“事已错矣，何可再干？”管家曰：“我自有处。”强邀村仆再来，一面令富子速收拾回家。管家雇募店中人，将自己当作儒士，与村仆对锁，送入县中，口告被脱抢之故。县官曰：“你不合买进学，与者受者各有其罪。况被棍抢银，与乡官家人何干？”管家曰：“抢银者即此棍之伙。但穷究此银出，情愿追入官；更愿大罚，与此棍同罪。”县官再差人去叫乡官，早已走了。县官曰：“此果是棍。”严刑拷打。棍仆受刑不过，愿赔一半。追完，管家又告愿全追，甘与同配驿。棍仆死不肯摊出同伙；又累受刑，无可追。乃将棍仆拟徒，管家者只拟杖发归。此为封银防抢之戒。
paragraphs.en: The rustic servant got up, putting on a distressed look. The steward rose, took his hand, and said, “Don’t worry; this silver isn’t much. Come to my inn with me, and we’ll seal it again.” The servant refused to go. The rich son said, “The matter has already gone wrong; how can we do it again?” The steward replied, “I have a way.” He forced the servant to return, while simultaneously telling the rich son to pack up and head home quickly. The steward hired men from the inn, passed himself off as a scholar, had them lock themselves together with the rustic servant, and sent them to the county yamen, where he verbally accused them of being robbed. The magistrate said, “You shouldn’t have bought into the scholar-official class; both giver and receiver are guilty. Besides, being robbed by crooks—what does that have to do with a retired official’s servant?” The steward said, “The robbers were this crook’s accomplices. Only thoroughly investigate where this silver came from; I am willing to have it recovered for the government, and I am also willing to be heavily fined, sharing the same crime as this crook.” The magistrate then sent people to summon the retired official, but he had already fled. The magistrate declared, “This is indeed a crook,” and ordered harsh torture. The servant-crook could not bear the punishment and agreed to repay half. After recovering that amount, the steward again petitioned, demanding full recovery and willing to accept joint exile to a garrison station. The servant-crook would rather die than name his accomplices; tortured repeatedly, nothing more could be recovered. Thus, the servant-crook was sentenced to penal servitude, while the steward received only beating and was released. This serves as a warning: when sealing silver, guard against robbery.

paragraphs.zh: 按：管家虽有能，终落棍所脱抢。特既抢后，即能拿棍仆同解，甘与同罪，终能追其一半，棍亦无所利。若富子自己，必不肯与棍同罪，而一抢之后，无如之何矣。或曰：管家顶认儒士，若官考之何如？曰：央分上之人，已是天才，官何须考？即考不得，亦无妨也。
paragraphs.en: Note: Although the steward was capable, he ultimately fell victim to the swindler's theft. However, after the robbery, if he were willing to arrest the swindler and accept joint liability for the crime, he could eventually recover half the money, leaving the swindler with no profit. If it had been the rich son himself, he would surely refuse to share the blame with the swindler; once robbed, there would be nothing to be done. Some ask: What if the steward claimed to be a scholar? How would the official test him? Answer: A man who secures influence through connections is already a master of the game; why would the official need to test him? Even if he failed the exam, it wouldn't matter.

stories.title_en: Sealing Silver in an Empty House, Then a Staged Robbery

paragraphs.zh: 简学宪最廉明。考大续时，有秋风客到，寓于开明僧舍。次日，有一棍带三仆来，亦与同寓。内中相拜，自称彼系县堂亲眷，亦来打秋风者。外则炫耀冠服，仆从扔卫更盛，每与（冠）盖往来寺中。尝有生儒遇之，辄误指曰：“此学道乡亲也。”又见简道亲回拜，又请酒，偕真秋风客往，而棍专外影窃其名，以欺诳人。简公是严明人，不数日，真秋风客已打发行矣，唯棍在寺。其外棍伙故四下传扬曰：“学爷乡亲在某寺。”生儒中亦甚传之，多有求取大续者，只无人可担当银。棍背套学道衙中书手、皂隶来，过付银封于其家。人既信是真秋风客，又衙门有身役人与同事，银封其家，亦复何虑？棍客动云，彼要说十名，每名要三百两。当赴场人众，各务兢趋，数日已满十人之数。共日封于各书、皂之家，明白交付，共银三千两。背地各瓜分已讫。
paragraphs.en: Education Commissioner Jian was renowned for his integrity and clear judgment. During the student renewal examinations, a favor-seeking visitor arrived and lodged in the monks' quarters at Kaiming Temple. The next day, a swindler arrived with three servants and took lodgings there as well. Inside the temple they exchanged courtesy calls, and the swindler claimed to be a relative of the county magistrate who had also come to solicit favors. Outwardly, he flaunted splendid robes and caps, with a retinue even grander than the other's, frequently coming and going through the temple under official canopies. Students who saw him often mistook him, saying, "This is the Education Commissioner's hometown relative." When they saw Commissioner Jian's real relative return a courtesy call and invite him for wine, the swindler tagged along with the genuine visitor while secretly borrowing his name on the outside to deceive people. Commissioner Jian was a strict and upright official, and within a few days the genuine favor-seeker was sent on his way, leaving only the swindler at the temple. His outside accomplices deliberately spread word everywhere: "The Education Commissioner's hometown relative is staying at such-and-such temple." The rumor circulated widely among the candidates; many who wished to buy a place in the examination were eager to pay, yet lacked a reliable person to handle the silver. Behind the scenes, the swindler colluded with clerks and runners from the Education Commissioner's yamen, having them come forward so the silver could be sealed and deposited at their homes. Since people already believed he was the genuine relative, and since official yamen staff were involved, what was there to worry about in sealing the silver at their houses? The swindler announced that he could secure ten places at three hundred taels each. With so many candidates competing eagerly, the quota of ten was filled within days. On the appointed day, the silver—three thousand taels in all—was openly checked, sealed, and deposited at the various clerks' and runners' homes; behind the scenes, the gang divided the spoils at once.

paragraphs.zh: 但思后日无名，不能回复诸人，银亦何以得去？乃雇一人，往学道出首：“见得衙门书、皂某某等，外同客棍招揽生童银若干两，封于某某等家。”简准状，即出白牌，提拿客棍风火至急，秋风棍即乘机逃去。又拿在衙书皂拶夹，皆不肯招，各打三十，革役。又差人往衙役家搜缉。凡有名与列钻刺者，闻踪迹露出，唯恐指名逮捕，各各四散，走回本县，银都弃撇，不敢来问。由是棍得安享所分之银。书皂虽革役，无赃可据，后复陆续谋入。唯一时受夹打，彼刑用在衙人役，亦仅如搬戏；而所得之多，奚止偿失也！此为信秋风客之戒。
paragraphs.en: But they thought: later, if they have no name to give, they cannot answer anyone—and how will they get the silver away? So they hired someone to go to the Education Office and report: "Clerks and runners so-and-so of the yamen, together with an outside traveling swindler, solicited so many taels from students, sealed at so-and-so’s homes." Jian accepted the complaint, issued a plain warrant to seize the traveling swindler with utmost haste; the Autumn Wind Swindler then used the chance to flee. Then they seized the yamen clerks and runners, put them to the squeezers and presses; none would confess; each was beaten thirty strokes and dismissed. They sent men to search the yamen staff’s homes. Anyone named as having bought their position, hearing their tracks were exposed, feared being named and arrested, scattered in all directions, fled back to their home counties, abandoned the silver, and dared not come ask. Thus the swindler could enjoy in peace the silver he’d split. The clerks and runners, though dismissed, had no stolen goods that could be proven; later they gradually schemed their way back in. They only suffered squeezing and beating for a time; using punishment on yamen staff is also just like putting on a play; and what they got was more than enough to repay the loss! Let this serve as a warning against trusting the Autumn Wind Swindler.

paragraphs.zh: 按：此棍称学道乡亲，而学道既已来拜，又请吃酒，则的是乡亲矣。况书、皂皆有身役人，为之翼护，人孰疑之？不知真乡亲已去，而此乃其托名者。彼衙门人唯利是图，所敛既多，何惜数十之板？况其顶头银仍在，虽革役，乌足以惩之。今人谓衙役知法，不知侮法者正是知法之人。唯蹈实地行实事，以真学问博真功名，勿萌侥幸，勿图钻刺，棍骗何从入哉？彼遭骗者，皆惰学不肖之徒，自取灾眚者也。
paragraphs.en: Note: This crook claimed to be the education commissioner’s hometown relative. Since the commissioner had already visited and invited him to drink, he truly seemed a hometown relative. Besides, clerks and runners all held official posts, shielding him—who would suspect? They didn’t know the real relative had departed, and this was merely someone borrowing his name. Those yamen men care only for profit; having collected so much, why would they hesitate to inflict a few dozen strokes? Moreover, the silver they paid to buy their posts remains intact; even if dismissed, how could that serve as punishment? People today say yamen runners know the law; they fail to realize that those who abuse the law are precisely those who know it best. Only walk on solid ground, do solid things, and win true fame through true learning. Do not sprout hopes of lucky breaks, nor plot to buy influence—how then could swindles take hold? Those who are cheated are all lazy, unworthy students who bring disaster upon themselves.

stories.title_en: Impersonating a Favor-Seeking Guest to Solicit Exam Bribes

paragraphs.zh: 有三棍合帮，共骗得银三百两，未肯遂分，更留合装骗棚，以图大骗。先遣一人过省，离会城两日之府，用银七十两买屋，内系土库，城外铺舍开一客店。又用银五十两娶一妻，买一婢，又买一家奴。更有数十两在手上，调度供家。人见其店有家着奴婢，食用丰足，多往宿其店。此府相近省城，往年文宗考科举不及，常调邻府生童到此合考，以便往返，每富家生童择店，必居于此。
paragraphs.en: Three crooks in a gang cheated out of three hundred taels together but refused to split them; instead, they pooled the silver to set up a front for a bigger swindle. First, they sent one man across the province to a prefecture two days from the capital, where he spent seventy taels to buy a house with an earthen storehouse inside and opened shop premises outside the wall as a guest inn. Another fifty taels went toward marrying a wife, buying a maid, and purchasing a male slave. They kept several tens of taels on hand for household expenses. Seeing that the inn had a family, servants, and abundant provisions, many travelers chose to stay there. This prefecture was near the provincial capital; in previous years, when the provincial examinations were held elsewhere, students from neighboring prefectures were often transferred here for joint exams to make travel easier. Consequently, wealthy students selecting an inn invariably stayed at this one.

paragraphs.zh: 壬子科六月，科期已迫，复调外两府生员来此选考。本店住建郡三个秀才，皆系巨富。一日，有客儒人品丰厚，衣冠鲜整，泊船城外，入此店来，密问店主曰：“你识科举秀才中有大家者乎？”店主曰：“我店中三位都富家，你问何干？”客儒曰：“有好事与他讲。”店主曰：“甚好事，何不对我说？”客儒曰：“你不在行，只好与秀才讲。”店主出，向三秀才曰：“此客先生问科举秀才何人最富，有好事对他说。我问他何事，又不肯言。列位试问其说何事。”三人共入叙礼，问曰：“老丈问富家，小弟等家皆万金，有何好事说？”客曰：“列位肯计较中否？”三秀才曰：“中都肯计较，兄有何门路？”客曰：“我亦不能为力，亦不识门路。但果肯计较者，各备银一千两，来此店对过封定，付还你收，自有指示的路。”三人约四日后家中取银来对，客儒辞去。三人密遣人跟随客去，见其下船，船中止一家人。归报如此，三秀才喜曰：“此必大主考的人，可信也。”店主出问：“适间说何事？”三秀才曰：“此未必然事，若事可成，自有大抬举你。”
paragraphs.en: In the sixth month of a Renzi year, with the exam deadline pressing, students from two outer prefectures were again summoned here for selection. Three xiucai from Jian commandery resided at our inn, all men of great wealth. One day, a visiting scholar, impressive in appearance and neatly dressed, moored his boat outside the city wall and entered the inn. He asked the innkeeper in secret: "Do you know among the exam xiucai any from wealthy families?" The innkeeper replied: "The three in my inn are all rich; why do you ask?" The guest said: "I have a good matter to discuss with them." The innkeeper asked: "What good matter? Why not tell me?" The guest replied: "You are not versed in this matter; I can only speak with the xiucai." The innkeeper went out and told the three: "This gentleman asked which of the exam xiucai is the richest; he has a good matter to share. When I asked what it was, he refused to say. You gentlemen should try asking him." The three went in, exchanged courtesies, and asked: "You asked about rich families; our households each possess ten thousand taels; what good matter is there?" The guest said: "Would you gentlemen be willing to negotiate the arrangement?" The three replied: "We are all willing to negotiate; what channel do you have, brother?" The guest said: "I cannot act on my own, nor do I know a channel. But if you truly wish to negotiate, each prepare one thousand taels, come to this inn, verify the silver and seal it, then hand it back for you to keep; a path will be pointed out." The three agreed to fetch the silver from home in four days to verify; the visiting scholar departed. The three secretly sent someone to follow him; they saw him board a boat where only one servant remained. They reported this; the three rejoiced: "This must be an associate of the chief examiner; he can be trusted." The innkeeper came out and asked: "What did you just discuss?" The three replied: "This is not yet certain; if the matter succeeds, we will ensure you are greatly elevated."

paragraphs.zh: 四日后，三家人都取银到。客儒应期来问，各答“银都齐备。”客曰：“今夜对明封定。”三秀才言：“银多夜间不便，明日入店主内庭去对。”客曰：“店主恐不密事，不知外客房中封更密。”三秀才曰：“明日临时相商。”客辞去。夜饭后，店主出曰：“列位与此客议封银事，客人难防。这门壁浅薄，若夜间统人来劫，可要提防。依我说，可藏入我城门内，你外间好心关防，可保安稳。”三秀才曰：“是也。”共将六皮箱银都寄入店主家内去。家主瞒过妻婢，将银尽从后门藏出，与棍伙夤夜逃去。唯嘱其妻曰：“明日三秀才问我，只说早间出去寻人，少刻即归。”
paragraphs.en: Four days later, the servants from all three households arrived with the silver. The visiting scholar came on schedule to inquire, and each of the three scholars replied, "The silver is all ready." The visitor said, "Tonight let us verify it under bright light and seal it." The three scholars said, "There is a great deal of silver, which makes nighttime inconvenient; tomorrow let us go into the innkeeper's inner courtyard to verify it." The visitor said, "The innkeeper may not keep this matter confidential; sealing it in the outer guest rooms would be more discreet." The three scholars said, "Let us discuss it when the time comes tomorrow." The visitor took his leave. After supper, the innkeeper came out and said, "You gentlemen were discussing sealing silver with that visitor—traveling strangers are hard to guard against. These doors and walls are thin; if they bring a gang to rob you in the night, you must be on your guard. In my opinion, you should store the silver inside my house within the city gate while you keep watch outside; that will be completely secure." The three scholars agreed and entrusted all six leather chests of silver to the innkeeper's house. Concealing it from his wife and maid, the innkeeper slipped all the silver out through the back door and fled late at night with the gang of crooks. Before leaving, he merely instructed his wife: "Tomorrow, if the three scholars ask for me, just tell them I went out early to look for someone and will be back shortly."

paragraphs.zh: 次日，客儒欣欣喜色来对银。秀才曰：“银付店主收藏，今早出外，少待即归。”等到午间，店主不回。客辞归船。午后又遣家人来问，又以店主未归答之。至第三日午间，问店主妇取皮箱，妇答云：“并未见甚箱。”及出溪边寻客船，亦不见矣。再问店妇取，苦执未见。任入搜之，竟不见踪。问：“店主果何去？”妇云：“前夜已出，教我如此应你。”三人正慌。
paragraphs.en: The next day, the visiting scholar arrived in high spirits to weigh and verify the silver. The scholars said, "We gave the silver to the innkeeper for safekeeping; he went out early this morning and will be back shortly." They waited until noon, but the innkeeper did not return, so the visitor went back to his boat. In the afternoon, the visitor sent his servant to ask again, and once more they answered that the innkeeper had not yet returned. At noon on the third day, the scholars asked the innkeeper's wife for the leather chests, but she replied, "I have never seen any chests." When they went out to the riverbank to look for the visitor's boat, it too had vanished. They questioned the innkeeper's wife again, and she stubbornly insisted she knew nothing of the chests. She let them search the house as they pleased, yet not a trace was found. "Where did the innkeeper really go?" they demanded. The wife replied, "He left the night before last and told me to answer you this way." The three scholars were thrown into a panic.

paragraphs.zh: 适此三棍脱得银去，已出境外。晚投宿一店，店主见其来晚，提其六箱皆重，疑是窃贼，明日将集众擒之。三棍闻其动静，次早天未明，只挑得四箱去，以二箱寄店。店主越疑是贼，出首于官。太府将银逐封开之，内封有一合同文书，称某人买举人者。太府提某生员到，不敢认。太府以甘言赚之，乃招认，即收入监。后又投分上解释，再骗去银四百两方免申道。又没入店主之屋，及官卖其妻婢，并箱内一千都追入库。彼四箱被棍挑去者，幸得落名，不受再骗。是府官亦一棍也。此为信店家一戒。
paragraphs.en: By then these three crooks, having made off with the silver, were already out of the territory. At night they lodged at an inn. The innkeeper saw they came late, hefted the six cases—all heavy—and suspected they were thieves; he planned to gather people to seize them the next day. The three heard the stir; next morning before dawn they carried off only four cases and left two at the inn. The innkeeper became even more convinced they were thieves and reported them to the officials. The prefect opened the silver packets one by one; inside one seal was a contract document stating that so-and-so was buying a juren degree. The prefect summoned that student; he dared not admit it. The prefect lured him with sweet words until he confessed, whereupon he was thrown into jail. Later, he sought connections to settle the matter but was cheated out of another four hundred taels before they would refrain from reporting it to the commissioner. They also confiscated the innkeeper’s house, sold his wife and maid by official order, and recovered the thousand taels in the cases into the treasury. The four cases the crooks carried off luckily had no names on them, so those students were not cheated again. Thus the prefectural official was also a crook. Let this serve as a warning to innkeepers.

paragraphs.zh: 按：店主有家眷，最可凭者。彼肯代藏银，孰不信之？谁知其妻妾皆买下以装棍棚者。彼骗得厚利，则弃此而去，别娶妻妾，享大富贵矣。以有眷属之店尚不可信，世路之险，一至于此！人若何不务实而可信棍以行险哉！
paragraphs.en: Note: An innkeeper with a family is the most reliable. If he agrees to store your silver, who wouldn't trust him? Yet who would guess that his wives and concubines were all purchased merely to play the part of the crook's accomplices? Once he has reaped a fat profit, he abandons them and departs, marrying new wives and concubines to enjoy great wealth. Even an innkeeper with dependents cannot be trusted—the perils of the road have reached such extremes! Why do people not stick to honest work, instead trusting crooks to gamble on dangerous paths?

stories.title_en: Silver Left with an Innkeeper, Who Steals It and Flees

categories.title_zh: 第二十一類 僧道騙

paragraphs.zh: 夏六月间，一行脚僧过于路，见小竖牧一伙牛。内有黄牝牛，大而肥。牧竖伸左脚与之舐，牝牛舐之；又与右脚与舐。僧问曰：“此牛何为舐你脚？”牧竖曰：“此牛最驯熟，吾甚爱之。我脚多汗咸，故牛爱舐。”僧知牛爱舐咸味，密此牛，系索长者家所畜的。
paragraphs.en: In the sixth month of summer, a traveling monk was passing along the road when he saw a herd-boy tending a herd of cattle. Among them was a large, fat yellow cow. The herd-boy held out his left foot for the cow to lick, and she licked it; then he offered his right foot, and she licked that too. The monk asked, "Why does this cow lick your feet?" The boy replied, "This cow is very tame, and I am very fond of her. My feet sweat a lot and taste salty, so she loves to lick them." Realizing that the cow was fond of salt, the monk quietly noted her down and learned that she belonged to the household of Elder Suo.

paragraphs.zh: 次日，僧取浓盐汁，厚涂头脸及遍身手足等处，寻到索长者家，跪门涕泣曰：“愿赐慈悲心，超度我母子。”索老曰：“我不会说法念经，怎能超度人？”僧曰：“我先母在生，不肯修斋布福。今已死七年，知冥中必受罪谴，奈家贫不能功果追荐。因慕目连救母，情愿削发从师，专求度母。前月得遇善知识，指老母在长者家投生为黄牛母，敬来求超度。”索老曰：“我栏有四头牝牛，知何牛是？”僧曰：“愿同往看。畜物更有灵性，母子相见，必有恩爱情在，自与别的不同。”索老与僧同到栏前，放出群牛。僧见大牝牛到，即揭下袖蒂帽，涕泣跪向前曰：“此是吾母也！”牝牛嗅其咸味，以舌遍舐其头脸，若怜惜状。僧愈加流涕，又自剥去衣服，牛遍舐其身，不忍去。索老看见果异，真似母之爱子，但不能言耳。问曰：“既是你前生之母，今须何以超度？”僧曰：“我若有银，当以半价买去养，奈贫僧衣钵罄空。愿长者权舍贫僧，牵往山庵，日采草煮粥喂养。待其谴罪完满，天年数终，贫僧当收埋，念经卷超度，庶来世转身为人，不堕畜生道矣。”长者怜其词情恳切，曰：“吾舍与你去。”僧叩头拜谢，牵此牛往三日路外，付出庵寄养。
paragraphs.en: The next day the monk took thick salt brine and smeared it generously over his head, face, and entire body, hands, and feet. He went to Elder Suo's house, knelt at the gate weeping, and said: "Please show compassion and deliver my mother and me." Elder Suo replied, "I cannot preach or recite sutras; how could I deliver anyone?" The monk said, "While my late mother was alive, she refused to keep vegetarian fasts or give alms. Now that she has been dead for seven years, I know she must be suffering punishment in the underworld. However, our family is poor, and I cannot afford the rites to save her. Admiring Mulian's rescue of his mother, I shaved my head and became a monk, seeking only to deliver her. Last month I met a wise teacher who told me my old mother had been reborn as a yellow cow in your household. I have come respectfully to ask that she be delivered." Elder Suo said, "I have four cows in the pen. How would one know which one it is?" The monk replied, "Please let me go with you to look. Beasts possess even more spiritual nature. When mother and child meet, there will surely be affection, unlike the others." Elder Suo went with the monk to the pen and released the cattle. When the monk saw the large cow approach, he removed his cap, knelt forward weeping, and said, "This is my mother!" The cow smelled the salt and licked his head and face all over, appearing full of pity. The monk wept even more, then taken off his clothes; the cow licked his entire body and would not leave. Elder Suo saw that it was truly strange—just like a mother's love for her child, except it could not speak. He asked, "If this is your mother from a former life, what must be done now to deliver her?" The monk said, "If I had silver, I would buy her at half price and raise her, but this poor monk's robe and bowl are empty. I beg the elder to grant her to me temporarily. I will lead her to a mountain hermitage, gather grass daily, and cook gruel to feed her. When her punishment is complete and her natural lifespan ends, I will bury her and recite sutras to deliver her, so that in the next life she may be reborn as a human and not fall into the animal path." The elder, moved by the earnestness of his words, said, "I grant her to you." The monk kowtowed in thanks, led the cow three days' journey away, and left her at a hermitage to be cared for.

paragraphs.zh: 至十月，天气寒凉，叫屠子来宰，以一半分与，卖得价银一两五钱；一半僧自留，做成干粮，收藏衲袄中各处。径到索长者厅前，结双趺而坐。长者出曰：“何僧敢升厅而坐？”僧曰：“你颇认得我么？”长者曰：“不知你是何人，怎么认得？”僧曰：“亦自然觉得面熟么？”长者曰：“并无相会，何处面熟？”僧长叹曰：“你本来灵性且尽丧，何故不识故人色相！”长者曰：“何为是故人？”僧曰：“昔佛印点醒东坡，远公唤回乐天，非苏、白二公之故人乎？你前生与我同修，因尘心未断，复来享此人福。我今特来度你，急宜丢手尘债，再去勤修，庶不废前生功行也。”长者曰：“你安能识得前生？”僧曰：“我功行高你一倍。你今且享半生福禄，我又加半生苦修，何难知三生事因？”长者曰：“你今生若何苦修？”僧曰：“从前苦修且休提，现今已辟谷三年矣。”长者始惊曰：“你能辟谷，在我家辟一月何如？”僧笑曰：“三年于是，何有一月？”长者曰：“亦服茶汤乎？”僧曰：“清茶滚水，日一瓯耳。”长者留之，扫一空室与坐，早进瓯茶，夜进瓯滚水。
paragraphs.en: When the tenth month came and the weather turned cold, the monk called a butcher to slaughter the cow, giving half the meat to the butcher, who sold it for one tael and five qian of silver; the other half the monk kept for himself, curing and drying it into provisions that he hid throughout the lining of his patched robe. Then he went straight to Elder Suo's hall and sat down cross-legged in full lotus. The elder came out and asked, "What monk dares come up into my hall and sit?" The monk said, "Do you happen to recognize me?" The elder said, "I do not know who you are—how would I recognize you?" The monk said, "Doesn't my face look naturally familiar to you?" The elder said, "We have never met; where would any familiarity come from?" The monk heaved a long sigh: "Your original spiritual nature has been completely lost—no wonder you fail to recognize an old friend's features!" The elder asked, "What do you mean, an old friend?" The monk said, "In the past, Master Foyin awakened Su Dongpo, and Master Huiyuan called back Bai Letian—were they not old friends of Su and Bai from former lives? In your previous life you cultivated the Way alongside me, but because your worldly desires were not yet severed, you were reborn here to enjoy this earthly wealth. I have come expressly to deliver you. You should quickly cast aside your worldly debts and return to diligent cultivation, so as not to waste the merit of your former life." The elder asked, "How can you know of former lives?" The monk replied, "My cultivation is twice yours. While you have been enjoying half a lifetime of worldly fortune, I have added half a lifetime of bitter ascetic practice—why would it be hard for me to know the karmic causes of three lifetimes?" The elder asked, "What bitter practice have you undertaken in this life?" The monk said, "Never mind my earlier austerities—for the past three years I have abstained completely from grain." Startled at last, the elder said, "If you can abstain from grain, what say you fast for one month here in my house?" The monk laughed: "After three years of it, what is a single month?" The elder asked, "Do you still take tea or hot water?" The monk replied, "Only a single bowl of clear tea or boiling water a day." So the elder kept him there, had an empty room swept clean for him to sit in, and sent in one bowl of tea in the morning and one bowl of boiling water at night.

paragraphs.zh: 连坐七日，再请出，答对如常。长者惊服，问曰：“我当如何修？”僧曰：“只弃家长往，自有修行善方。”长者曰：“妻寡子幼，产业付谁？此事不能。其次修何如？”僧曰：“唯有舍施，修寺奉佛，来生亦受福报。现今庐山一庵，化人独力修造。倘捐五百金，一完修之，亦一大功德也。”长者依言，遣仆同僧送五百金往，交付与住持明白，留仆住数日，送归报主。后僧分住持银二百五十两而去。其以辟谷动富翁，则私食所带之干粮耳，宁有人而真辟谷者！
paragraphs.en: He sat there for seven days, then was invited out again and answered just as before. The elder was amazed and convinced, asking, "How should I cultivate?" The monk replied, "Just abandon your household and go far away; the proper way to practice will present itself." The elder said, "My wife would be left a widow and my children are young. Who would inherit the property? This I cannot do. What is the next-best cultivation?" The monk said, "Only giving. Repair temples and serve the Buddha, and in the next life you will receive blessed rewards. Right now, a hermitage on Mount Lu is being rebuilt by a single donor. If you donate five hundred taels to complete the repair at once, that too is a great merit." The elder followed his advice, sent a servant with the monk to deliver five hundred taels, handed them over clearly to the abbot, kept the servant for several days, then sent him back to report to his master. Later, the monk took two hundred fifty taels from the donation and departed. As for moving the rich man with fasting from grain, he was privately eating the dried provisions he had brought. Who would believe anyone truly fasts from grain!

paragraphs.zh: 按：此僧脱牛，犹其小者，转卖之可也。名为生前母而宰食之，罪浮于天矣。至用为干粮而诈称辟谷，其骗亦大。虽半舍入庵，亦是好事，僧若得劝缘功。然周急赈贫，自当施于邻里，何必投入于庵？此愚人信福田利益之过也，亦未读傅奕公《高识传》矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: This monk making off with the cow was still the lesser offense; he could have resold her. To call her his mother from a past life and then slaughter and eat her—the crime towers over Heaven. Then using her as dried provisions while falsely claiming to fast from grain: that swindle too was great. Though half the offering went to the monastery, it was still a good deed, and the monk would gain the merit of soliciting donations. But relieving urgent needs and aiding the poor should be directed to neighbors; why must it be thrown into a monastery? This is the fault of fools who believe in the profits of the field of merit—and of not having read Master Fu Yi's Gaoshi zhuan.

stories.title_en: A Monk Claims a Cow Is His Mother

paragraphs.zh: 有僧自称能辟谷者，富家多召而试之。连七八日不食一粒，或间二三日，服滚汤一瓯而已。传名甚广，人争以金帛舍之。一乡官见褚县尊，偶道及此，称世间有此高僧，真仙佛再生于世出。褚公最正大，素不信僧道辈，曰：“人受此色身，哪能断绝食色？假托辟谷者，不过暗藏干粮，以哄惑愚民耳。明理君子，何可信此辈？若果能辟谷，彼将远遁深山，唯恐名落人间，何必浪游市里？受人施舍金帛，将何所用？”乡官被褚公一驳，似乎己为信邪，更欲取信其言，乃曰：“老父母不信，可召而试之，方知晚生言非妄矣。”
paragraphs.en: There was a monk who claimed he could live without grain. Rich families often summoned him to test it. For seven or eight days running he would not eat a single grain, or every two or three days he would take only one bowl of boiling water. His name spread widely, and people competed to give him gold and silk. A local official, seeing Magistrate Chu, happened to mention this, saying the world had such an eminent monk, truly an immortal or Buddha born again. Master Chu was most upright, and had never believed monks and Daoists. He said: "People receive this physical body. How can they cut off food and sex? Those who pretend to live without grain only hide dried provisions in secret, to fool the ignorant. How can a gentleman who understands principle believe this sort? If they could truly live without grain, they would flee far into the deep mountains, fearing only that their fame would reach the world. Why would they wander the markets? And if they accept gifts of gold and silk, what would they use them for?" The local official, rebuked by Master Chu, felt as if he himself had been caught believing swindlers, and wanted still more to prove his words were true. So he said: "If Your Honor does not believe, you may summon him and test him, and then you will know this junior's words are not false."

paragraphs.zh: 褚公即差人唤至，令搜其身。别无夹带，唯持二十四个弥陀珠，诛之带入。扫一净室，布床席与坐，外遣人轮番密窥。日遣人明开门一视，出仍锁门。两日内，果结双趺而坐，容貌如故。第三日开视，见脸有乏汗，求滚水饮。褚公命与之，复出锁门。密窥者来禀曰：“僧以一弥陀珠调水饮讫，容貌复好。”后每两日进滚汤一碗，密窥者辄禀云：“以珠调吃。”
paragraphs.en: Master Chu immediately had men summon him and ordered his body searched. Nothing else was hidden on him, only twenty-four Amitabha beads, which he was permitted to keep. They swept out a clean room, spread a bed and mat for him to sit upon, and stationed people outside to watch him in secret rotation. Each day, someone would open the door openly to take a look, then lock it again upon leaving. For two days, he sat in full lotus posture, his appearance unchanged. On the third day, when they opened the door to look, they saw sweat of exhaustion on his face, and he asked for boiling water to drink. Master Chu ordered it given, and after they left and locked the door, the secret watchers reported: "The monk mixed one Amitabha bead into the water, drank it, and his countenance recovered." Thereafter, every two days they sent in a bowl of boiling water, and the watchers always reported: "He mixed in a bead and swallowed it."

paragraphs.zh: 经十一日，召之出，取其弥陀珠视之，止十九枚在手耳。褚公收其珠，命收入轻监不许揽动，听彼静坐，以候发落。密嘱禁子曰。“铁容僧道人入见，两日后必问你乞食。你问其弥陀珠何以做？做来以水调之，与此珠一样，后重赏你。”
paragraphs.en: After eleven days, Master Chu summoned the monk out, took his Amitabha prayer beads, and inspected them: only nineteen beads remained in his hands. Master Chu confiscated the beads, ordered the monk placed in light detention where no one was to disturb him, and left him to sit quietly awaiting judgment. He then secretly instructed the jailer: "Do not allow any monks or Daoists to come in and see him. After two days he will surely beg you for food. When he does, ask him how those Amitabha beads are made. If you can make a batch that dissolves in water just like these beads, I will reward you handsomely afterward."

paragraphs.zh: 次日，僧即问禁子求食。禁子曰：“你教我作珠方法，便与你食。”僧曰：“此药极难得。你但与我食，出外多以银谢你，不必问此方。”禁子不与之食，三日饿倒，面青黄无人色矣。
paragraphs.en: The next day, the monk asked the jailer for food. The jailer said, "Teach me how to make the fake pearls, and I will feed you." The monk replied, "This medicine is extremely rare. Just give me food now; when I am released, I will reward you with much silver. There is no need to ask for the formula." The jailer refused him food. After three days, the monk collapsed from starvation, his face turning green and yellow, devoid of any human color.

paragraphs.zh: 褚公提出，审曰：“我早知此珠是孩儿丹矣。你供出制造方法来，免汝一死。”僧诈作将死形状，不敢应。褚公笑曰：“众看此辟谷僧，在褚爷前辟三日谷，即饿死矣。此丹妇人胎内孩子，必须谋死孕妇，剖其婴孩，以作此丹。不知你害死多少命，以造此恶业，你怎敢说出口？我岂求汝方乎？若打死你，罪还轻。”命衙前搭起一台，以十九枚珠发出，将四个调与众百姓看，以滚水调之，满碗都是膏液。有敢饮者，又香又甜，只饮两口，一日亦饱。后十五枚发与医生治补损。然后缚此僧在台上凌迟之。褚公曰：“县令为民父母，岂忍杀人？但为众冤泄恨矣。”众皆称快，而乡官后亦永不信僧道矣。
paragraphs.en: Master Chu had him brought out for questioning: "I knew from the start these beads were infant elixir. Confess the method of manufacture, and I will spare your life." The monk pretended to be dying and dared not answer. Master Chu laughed: "Look at this fasting monk! In front of me, he has gone three days without food and is about to starve. This elixir comes from a child in a woman's womb; you must plot to kill a pregnant woman and cut out the infant to make it. Who knows how many lives you have destroyed to create this evil karma? How dare you speak the formula aloud? Do I want your recipe? If I beat you to death, the crime would still be light." He ordered a platform built before the yamen, produced the nineteen beads, and mixed four for the common people to see. Mixed with boiling water, the whole bowl turned into a thick paste. Those who dared to drink found it fragrant and sweet; two mouthfuls were enough to last a day. The remaining fifteen were given to doctors to treat injuries and deficiencies. Then they bound the monk on the platform and executed him by lingchi (death by a thousand cuts). Master Chu said, "A county magistrate is the father and mother of the people; how could he bear to kill? But this is to vent the hatred of the many wronged." All cried out in satisfaction, and afterward the local gentry never again trusted monks or Daoists.

paragraphs.zh: 按：此诈辟谷者，多是藏干粮，其服孩儿丹者少。此粮非藏于身，恐人搜也。都寄于丐乞者之身，有人试之，则密以干粮付。又有服松毛竹叶者，松毛用羊蹄草同吃，竹叶用嫩蕨同吃，皆滑而可食。僧亦尝以此惑人，谓彼能服此。然从古有辟谷之说者，乃仙方，非人间所有也。曾见有遇异人授辟谷者，述之于左。
paragraphs.en: Note: Those who fake fasting from grain mostly hide dried provisions; those who take infant elixir are few. This food is not hidden on the body, for fear people will search. It is all entrusted to beggars; when someone tests them, they secretly pass the dried provisions to them. There are also those who take pine needles and bamboo leaves: pine needles eaten together with yangti herb, bamboo leaves eaten together with tender ferns, all slippery and edible. Monks have also used this to fool people, saying they can live on these. But from ancient times, the methods of living without grain that exist are immortal recipes, not things of the human world. I once heard of a man who met an extraordinary person who taught him to live without grain; I record it below.

paragraphs.zh: 武夷山有贫民结庐于岩曲，仅容床灶，垦山种茶，卖以供食。积十数年，所开茶山，岁可收鬻三四金，每日力作不息，唯大寒、暑甚、风雨，终日寂坐岩庐下，不识经典，亦不通往来。
paragraphs.en: On Mount Wuyi, a poor man built a hut in a bend of the cliffs, barely enough space for a bed and a stove. He cleared the mountain to plant tea, selling it to support himself. After ten-odd years, the tea slopes he had opened yielded three or four taels annually. Every day he labored without rest; only in severe cold, extreme heat, or wind and rain would he sit silent all day beneath his cliff hut. He knew no scriptures and had no dealings with others.

paragraphs.zh: 忽一日一道人过其庐，谓曰：“汝耕山劳苦，何不以茶山付人代耕，岁收一金，以买衣资？吾授汝辟谷方，则不须买米，不劳耕山，可安坐自足矣。”山民曰：“吾尝间修行人有辟谷方，若肯教我，愿拜师父求学。”道士曰：“你性子恬静，尽可修行。今后唯早晨煎清泉二罐，煎至半落，以两罐合煎作一罐，早午晚各饮二瓯。饮后澄心息想，以舌抵上颚，合口闭目，终日静坐。或天清神爽，爰出游，行则慢步闲观，随意所适，不拘半午，不拘片时。凡行住坐卧，只从心不拂。或山果草实可食者，遇着稍食一二不妨，但不可有意寻求。如此便可辟谷矣。记之不可轻易传人。”山民依此行之，一年果不食一黍，颜如金黄，轻健如常。同山旁居人，常不见其籴米，或过其庐，亦无锅甑。问之，答曰：“近年学得辟谷方。”居人转相传异。有拜之求方者，辄逃避不授，曰：“师嘱勿轻传泄。”次年传于远近，多有来册拜访者。或赍粮宿其居庐看守，至匝月，果唯见饮滚水，饮后静坐，寂无一为，亦无闲谈。不知者或穷问之，或与谈修养，微笑而起，出游山径，迨午晚归，复暖滚水而饮。凡人之来者不迎，去者不送，亦无半语讯问人。人问之，有可答者，随口答一二句。问其餘闲事，则摇首不应，若有厌烦之意，唯自去静坐。凡言动应酬，总是付之无心而已。第二年后，名益著。富家贵人，多备鞍轿迎者，坚逃不往。富贵人身往劝逼之，后亦遍往诸家，所到不食人一物，唯向空室静坐，若一木佛，然有言动而已。
paragraphs.en: Suddenly one day a Daoist passed his hut and said, "You toil on the mountain. Why not hand over the tea slopes to someone else to till, receive one tael a year to buy clothes, and let me teach you a method of living without grain? Then you need not buy rice or labor on the mountain; you can sit at ease and be self-sufficient." The mountain man said, "I have heard that practitioners possess methods of living without grain. If you are willing to teach me, I will bow to you as master and ask to learn." The Daoist said, "Your nature is quiet; you are well-suited for cultivation. From now on, each morning boil two jars of clear spring water until reduced by half, then combine them into one jar and boil again. Drink two bowls each time—morning, noon, and evening. After drinking, still your mind and cease your thoughts, press your tongue to the upper palate, close your mouth and eyes, and sit quietly all day. Or if the sky is clear and your spirit fresh, go out walking: stroll slowly and look about leisurely, going wherever suits you, whether for half a day or just a moment. In walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, simply follow your mind and do not resist it. If you encounter mountain fruits or plant seeds that are edible, eating one or two causes no harm, but do not seek them intentionally. In this way you can live without grain. Remember this and do not lightly pass it to others." The mountain man followed this practice. After one year he indeed ate not a single grain of millet; his face was golden-yellow, and he was light and vigorous as ever. Neighbors living nearby often did not see him buying rice; or if they passed his hut, there was no pot or steamer visible. When asked, he answered, "In recent years I have learned a method of living without grain." The neighbors spread the wonder from one to another. Those who bowed and begged for the method would always flee and refuse to teach, saying, "My teacher ordered me not to leak it lightly." The next year the news spread near and far, and many came with letters of introduction to pay respects. Some brought grain and lodged in his hut to watch for a full month: they indeed saw him only drink boiling water, then sit quietly afterward, silent, doing nothing, with no idle talk. Those who did not understand might question him hard or discuss cultivation with him; he would smile, rise, walk the mountain paths, returning at noon or evening, then warm boiling water and drink again. He neither welcomed those who came nor saw off those who left; he did not ask people a single word. If people asked him and he could answer, he would reply with one or two sentences offhand. If they asked about other idle matters, he would shake his head and say nothing, appearing annoyed, and simply go sit quietly himself. All his speech, movement, and social responses were met with an empty mind. By the second year, his fame grew even greater. Rich households and nobles often prepared saddles and sedan chairs to receive him; he firmly fled and would not go. When the rich and noble went in person to urge and pressure him, he later visited various houses. Wherever he arrived, he would not eat a single thing from them, only sit quietly in an empty room like a wooden Buddha, except that he still spoke and moved a little.

paragraphs.zh: 经二年半后，有潭阳富人礼迎之，虔奉更肃，若敬神明。时进茶果，稍为食些少。后备清茶精饭，苦劝之食，坚辞不能，不得已为食一瓯。少顷饥甚，服滚汤。又饥饿不能禁，又索食。富人欢喜，肃进之。连三日内，皆一日五食，仅能止饥。山民自惊疑，急求归山，依旧服汤静坐，不免肚饥。后只得复食，三餐如寻常人矣。
paragraphs.en: After two and a half years, a wealthy man from Tanyang welcomed him with great ceremony, treating him even more solemnly, as if he were a deity. He would occasionally serve tea and fruit, and the man ate only a little. Later, the host prepared clear tea and fine rice, earnestly pressing him to eat. The man firmly refused, claiming he could not; yet, under pressure, he was compelled to eat one bowl. Shortly after, he grew extremely hungry and drank boiling water. Hungry again and unable to endure it, he asked for food once more. The rich man was delighted and served him respectfully. For three consecutive days, he ate five times a day, barely managing to quell his hunger. The mountain man began to suspect and fear himself, urgently requesting to return to the mountain. He resumed drinking water and sitting quietly as before, but could not escape the gnawing hunger. Eventually, he had no choice but to eat again, taking three meals like an ordinary person.

paragraphs.zh: 按：山民所遇之道士，明是仙人。若辟谷三年完满，必有超度矣。惜哉为名所累，致人迎奉，致人逼食，而自毁前功。此劝食之愚。富人彼意，欲虔奉之，以分生佛之福，岂诚心奉道哉！此山民既为所误，而彼福亦安在也？且堕百劫之罪，来生必与山民结一大仇矣。观此，则辟谷乃仙方，不徒在服滚水静坐也。不然，后仍服之坐之，而何谷不能辟哉？则今之托辟谷索人钱米者，真盗贼僧道也。真辟谷者，敢令人知乎？
paragraphs.en: Note: The Daoist whom the mountain man met was clearly an immortal. Had he completed three years of fasting, he would surely have attained deliverance. Alas, he was burdened by fame, which drew people to welcome and serve him, forced him to eat, and caused him to ruin his prior achievements himself. This was the folly of urging him to eat. That rich man's intent was to serve him devoutly, hoping to share in the blessings of a living Buddha—was that truly a sincere heart devoted to the Way? The mountain man had already been misled, and where then were those blessings? He will also incur the sin of a hundred kalpas, and in his next life he is bound to become great enemies with the mountain man. From this we see that fasting is an immortal method, not merely a matter of drinking hot water and sitting still. Otherwise, if afterward he continued to drink and sit as before, why would he not still be able to fast? Thus, those today who feign fasting to demand money and rice are nothing but thief-monks and rogue Daoists. Would anyone truly practicing fasting dare let others know?

stories.title_en: Taking Infant Elixir to Fake Fasting from Grain

paragraphs.zh: 徽州人丁达，为人好善喜舍。一日，与友林泽往海澄买椒木，到临清等处发卖，货已卖讫。此处有一寺，内有名僧号无二者，年近三十餘，相貌俊雅，会讲经典，善谈因果，风动多少良家子弟，往寺参拜，常有被其劝化，削发出家者。时丁达邀林泽去谒无二。林泽曰：“你素性好善，闻此僧巧嘴善言，累诱人削发为僧。你若见之，被其哄惑，何以归见父母？”达曰：“劝在彼，从在我。我自有主，彼何能拿？”若要往拜之。见无二举动闲雅，谈及因果之事，达被打动，尽舍其财本，入寺拜无二为师，欲削发为僧。泽怒曰：“未到此处，我早言之。今果被哄惑，何以为人？”再三苦谏不听。泽自回去，达在寺修行。
paragraphs.en: Ding Da of Huizhou was a charitable and generous man. One day, he traveled with his friend Lin Ze to Haicheng to buy pepper trees and timber, then sold the goods at Linqing and other places once they were finished. In that town stood a temple housing a famous monk named Wuer, nearly thirty years old, handsome and refined, skilled in lecturing on scriptures and discussing karma. He attracted countless young men from respectable families to visit the temple, often convincing them to shave their heads and become monks. At this time, Ding Da invited Lin Ze to visit Wuer. Lin Ze said, "You are always kind-hearted. I hear this monk has a silver tongue and frequently lures people into becoming monks. If you meet him and fall for his tricks, how will you face your parents upon returning home?" Ding Da replied, "Persuasion lies with him, but choice rests with me. I have my own mind; what power does he have over me?" Insisting on visiting, he found Wuer’s manner calm and dignified. When they discussed karma, Ding Da was deeply moved. He gave away all his trading capital, entered the temple, bowed to Wuer as his master, and intended to shave his head and join the clergy. Lin Ze grew angry: "I warned you before we even arrived. Now you’ve truly been deceived. How can you still call yourself a man?" Despite repeated earnest advice, Ding Da refused to listen. Lin Ze returned alone, while Ding Da remained in the temple to devote himself to monastic life.

paragraphs.zh: 过二年后，僧无二因有董寡妇入寺烧香，容貌甚美，亦信善好念弥陀。带一使女，十七岁，国色娇媚，到寺亦参拜。无二以巧言劝诱，寡妇亦心服，即拜无二为师，欲削发为尼，暂在寺宿几夜。其丫头常往无二房送果吕，无二欲心难制，以白金十两戏之。丫头收其银，与之通情。无二又思及其嫠妇，夜潜入其房，候董氏熟睡，欲强奸之。董氏坚贞不从，喊曰：“何人无理，敢来奸盗？”言未数声，无二以手巾紧勒其颈，须臾而死。
paragraphs.en: After two years, the monk Wuer encountered Widow Dong, who came to the temple to burn incense. She was very beautiful, virtuous, and fond of reciting Amitabha. She brought along a seventeen-year-old maid, of peerless beauty and charm, who also paid respects at the temple. Wuer used clever words to persuade and lure her; the widow's heart submitted, and she immediately bowed to Wuer as her teacher, wishing to shave her head and become a nun, staying a few nights in the temple for the time being. Her maid frequently visited Wuer's room to deliver fruit and snacks. Unable to restrain his desire, Wuer offered ten taels of silver to seduce her. The maid accepted the silver and became intimate with him. Wuer then turned his thoughts to the widow. One night, he slipped into her room, waited until Mistress Dong was fast asleep, and attempted to rape her. Mistress Dong, chaste and firm, refused. She cried out, "Who is this lawless man, daring to come and rape and steal?" Before she could utter a few words, Wuer tightened a handkerchief around her neck, and within moments, she was dead.

paragraphs.zh: 次日，使女去报知董氏之子李英。及到寺，无二已先逃走矣。但无二久出名，各处人多认得。李英雇人遍处缉拿，不两日拿到送县。王爷即点民兵百餘，围绕其寺。时寺僧已四散逃命，无僧可拿。王爷再命焚其寺，将无二责了四十，问典刑之罪。
paragraphs.en: The next day, the maid went to report to Li Ying, son of Mistress Dong. By the time they arrived at the temple, Wuer had already fled. However, Wuer had long been notorious, and people everywhere were familiar with him. Li Ying hired men to hunt him down across the region; within two days, they caught him and delivered him to the county authorities. The official immediately mustered over a hundred militia members to surround the temple. At that point, the temple monks had scattered in all directions to save their lives, leaving no one to arrest. The official then ordered the temple burned, had Wuer beaten forty strokes, and sentenced him according to the standard legal code.

paragraphs.zh: 达悔财本俱丧，无颜回家。后家中已知达逃回，叫人寻觅归家，发长方敢出。此愚人信僧之明鉴也。
paragraphs.en: Da had lost both his capital and his reputation, feeling too ashamed to return home. Later, his family learned he had fled back and sent people to find him and bring him home; only after his hair had grown long did he dare venture out. This serves as a stark lesson for fools who trust monks.

paragraphs.zh: 按：寺门藏奸，僧徒即贼，此是常事，亦往往有败露者。人不目见，亦多耳闻，何犹不知戒？而妇人入寺，男子出家，真大愚也。董虽死犹幸完节；丁达虽幸逃生而财本已丧。使当时与无二并获，何分清浊？必并死狱中矣。故邪说引诱人者，无论士农工商，皆当勿信而远之可也。
paragraphs.en: Note: Temple gates conceal villains; monks are thieves. This is common, and such cases often come to light. Even if people have not seen it with their own eyes, they have surely heard of it. Why do they still fail to take warning? Women entering temples and men becoming monks—this is truly great folly. Dong, though she died, was fortunate to preserve her chastity intact; Ding Da, though fortunate to escape with his life, had already lost his capital. If at that time he had been arrested alongside Wuer, how could they have distinguished the innocent from the guilty? He would surely have died in prison with him. Therefore, those who use heretical talk to lure others—whether scholars, farmers, artisans, or merchants—should all refuse to believe them and keep their distance.

stories.title_en: Believing a Monk's Talk, He Nearly Came to Ruin

paragraphs.zh: 天元寺年久倾颓，住持僧完朗有意修之，恐工费浩大，非有大力者发愿独任，未易举手。忽一日，游方僧若冰来寺投宿，身干魁梧，面方而黑，目圆耳长，宛似本寺伽蓝形象。完朗一见心喜，夜设斋款待，甚加勤敬。次日，僧若冰曰：“宝刹非兴旺，何如此肯接待十方？”完朗曰：“兴我寺者，在尊宿一臂之力，敢大有所托。”若冰曰：“山家缘薄，怎能相助？”完朗曰：“此寺须五百金方可全修，虽化些少众缘，亦不济事。看尊相，极似我本寺伽蓝，托你择巨富家，若化其全修，待彼在允否间，约其来寺亲看，我自有方法纳之。”
paragraphs.en: Tianyuan Temple had been dilapidated for years. The abbot Wanlang intended to repair it, but feared the labor and cost would be enormous; unless a wealthy benefactor vowed to undertake it single-handedly, it would be hard to get started. One day, a wandering monk named Ruobing came to lodge at the temple. He was tall and sturdy, with a square black face, round eyes, and long ears—exactly like the image of the temple's guardian deity. Wanlang was delighted at the sight, prepared a vegetarian feast that night to receive him, and treated him with extra diligence and respect. The next day, Monk Ruobing said, "This precious monastery is not flourishing. Why then are you so willing to welcome monks from all quarters?" Wanlang replied, "The one who will revive my temple depends on your esteemed help. I dare greatly to rely on you." Ruobing said, "Our mountain household has thin karmic ties. How can I possibly help?" Wanlang said, "This temple needs five hundred taels to be fully repaired. Even collecting small amounts from many donors won't suffice. Looking at your honored appearance, you resemble our temple's guardian perfectly. I ask you to seek out a hugely rich family. If you solicit funds from them for the full repair, wait until they are wavering between yes and no, arrange for them to come to the temple to see it in person, and I will have my own method to secure them."

paragraphs.zh: 若冰会意，前去大江边，有柴商财本巨万。若冰备干粮在身，直到柴排厅中，朗讽一经，结趺而坐，高叫曰：“化缘！”柴商荆秀云命手下以钱与之。僧全不视，曰：“吾非化小可钱钞。贫僧与施主有夙缘，要化千金。”秀云作色曰：“化千金何用？”僧曰：“此去二百里，有天元寺。前创时，施主有缘在，故今生大富。近年颓坏，须五百金修理，又须五百金为香灯田，后可保长久，则施主功德远大矣。”秀云曰：“你为寺化疏，前生与此寺何缘？”僧曰：“寺本我居食之地，非有缘，得久居乎？”秀云不睬之。僧在柴排坐三日不去，手下人以饭与食，亦食；不与，亦不食。又过四日，秀云曰：“吾舍三百相助，你更去化别人。”僧曰：“有缘者不能化，无缘者何劳空说？”秀云曰：“你把疏簿来，我题三百两。”僧曰：“疏簿在寺中。三百亦不够用，不须题？你图今生享福，只施五百两。若布来世津梁，非千金不可。”秀云曰：“吾不信今生来生，你且领三百两去，好心修造。不足者，岂无别善人相助？”僧曰：“吾哪要银？你自送与住持僧。”秀云曰：“吾十日后送到寺来。”僧遂合掌，念“阿弥陀佛”一声而去。归对完朗详说其事，又约“十日后柴商且来，吾远避之。”完朗大喜，早备茶果斋品以待。
paragraphs.en: Ruobing understood. He went to the edge of the great river, where a timber merchant named Jing Xiuyun held capital worth tens of thousands. Ruobing carried dried provisions, entered the timber raft yard, loudly chanted a sutra, sat in lotus position, and called out, "Collecting alms!" The merchant ordered his men to give him money. The monk ignored it entirely, saying, "I am not collecting paltry cash. This poor monk shares a karmic bond with the donor and seeks a thousand taels." Xiuyun frowned: "What use is collecting a thousand taels?" The monk replied, "Two hundred li from here lies Tianyuan Temple. When it was first founded, you had a karmic connection there, which is why you are so wealthy in this life. Recently, it has fallen into ruin. It needs five hundred taels for repairs and another five hundred for an endowment to support incense and lamps; thereafter, it will endure, and your merit will be vast." Xiuyun asked, "You are collecting donations for the temple. What karmic connection did you have with it in a past life?" The monk said, "The temple is my place of residence and sustenance. Without a karmic bond, how could I dwell there long?" Xiuyun ignored him. The monk remained on the timber raft for three days without leaving. If the men gave him rice, he ate; if they did not, he also did not eat. After four more days, Xiuyun said, "I will give three hundred taels to help. Go collect from others instead." The monk replied, "If I cannot collect from one with a karmic bond, why waste words on those without?" Xiuyun said, "Bring the donation ledger. I will write down three hundred taels." The monk said, "The ledger is at the temple. Three hundred is insufficient anyway; no need to write it. If you seek only blessings in this life, give five hundred taels. If you wish to pave the way for the next life, nothing less than a thousand taels will suffice." Xiuyun said, "I do not believe in this life or the next. Take these three hundred taels and go; kindly proceed with the repairs. If it is not enough, surely other good people will help?" The monk said, "Why would I want the silver? You send it directly to the abbot." Xiuyun said, "I will deliver it to the temple in ten days." The monk then joined his palms, recited "Amitabha Buddha" once, and departed. He returned and recounted the matter in detail to Wanlang, adding, "In ten days the timber merchant will come; I shall stay far away." Wanlang was greatly pleased and early prepared tea, fruit, and vegetarian dishes to await them.

paragraphs.zh: 至第十日，秀云果带银同两仆来。完朗知是柴商，肃迎待茶毕，问曰：“施主高姓？”秀云曰：“姓荆。”完朗曰：“施主从哪里来？”秀云曰：“前约宝刹中化疏僧，今敬从江上来。”完朗沉吟曰：“山寺未曾化疏。”秀云曰：“十七日前，有僧在柴楼中坐七日，我许他今日来。”完朗曰：“本寺僧此半月内并无人出外者，必方僧诈托也。”即命作斋相待。秀云心疑怪：“若方僧诈托，何不前日即领银去？”只存在心，遍寺闲游。到伽蓝祠去，举头看伽蓝宛似前日僧形象。两仆亦指曰：“此伽蓝好似前日僧。”秀云看越惊异，心疑是伽蓝化为僧，以劝我修寺。即以祈曰：“前日僧若是你变的，求一圣。”即打一圣。又曰：“三百金已带来，祈保今年大利。”再一圣，又得一阳。又曰：“三百不够，若要五百，求一圣。”又得一阴。”又祝曰：“我心中已悟。若更要五百两香灯，求一圣。”果掷一圣。秀云拜谢讫，来就斋席，谓完朗曰：“须用银几何？”完朗曰：“久有意要修。前日叫匠人估计，要五百两方够，故不敢举。”秀云曰：“我前日许过三百两，今现送在此，明日更送二百两来添。若修完备，再舍五百两买置香灯田，永远奉佛。”完朗闻言大喜，合掌下拜。后依约舍完，若冰密分二百两而去。
paragraphs.en: On the tenth day, Xiuyun indeed arrived with the silver and two servants. Knowing he was the timber merchant, Abbot Wanlang received him with solemn courtesy, served tea, and asked, "What is the benefactor's honored surname?" Xiuyun replied, "Jing." Wanlang asked, "Where has the benefactor come from?" Xiuyun said, "Earlier I made an appointment with a fundraising monk from this precious monastery, so today I have respectfully come up from the river." Wanlang pondered a moment and said, "Our mountain temple has not sent anyone out to solicit donations." Xiuyun said, "Seventeen days ago, a monk sat in meditation in my timber loft for seven days, and I promised him I would come today." Wanlang said, "None of the monks of this temple have gone out during the past half month; it must have been a wandering monk falsely using our name." He at once ordered a vegetarian meal prepared to entertain him. Inwardly, Xiuyun found it strange: "If it was a wandering monk falsely using their name, why didn't he take the silver that day?" Keeping the doubt to himself, he strolled around the temple grounds. When he entered the shrine of the Temple Guardian, he looked up and saw that the statue of the guardian looked just like the monk from the other day. His two servants also pointed and said, "This Temple Guardian looks the very image of that monk!" More amazed than ever, Xiuyun suspected in his heart that the Temple Guardian himself had manifested as a monk to urge him to repair the monastery. He bowed and prayed: "If the monk of the other day was your manifestation, grant me a holy cast of the divination blocks." He cast the blocks at once and got a holy sign. He prayed again: "I have brought three hundred taels today; I pray for great profit this year." Casting again, he got a yang sign. He said, "If three hundred taels is not enough and you want five hundred, grant me a holy cast." This time he got a yin sign. He prayed once more: "Now I understand in my heart. If you want an additional five hundred taels for incense-and-lamp fields, grant me a holy cast." Sure enough, he threw a holy sign. Having bowed in thanks, Xiuyun returned to the vegetarian feast and asked Wanlang, "How much silver is needed for the repairs?" Wanlang replied, "I have long wished to repair the temple. The other day I had craftsmen estimate the cost, and they said it would take five hundred taels in all, so I dared not begin." Xiuyun said, "The other day I promised three hundred taels, which I have brought with me now, and tomorrow I will send two hundred more to make up the sum. Once the repairs are complete, I will donate another five hundred taels to purchase incense-and-lamp fields to serve the Buddha forever." Overjoyed at these words, Wanlang pressed his palms together and bowed down. Later, after Xiuyun had donated the full amount as promised, the wandering monk Ruobing secretly took two hundred taels as his share and departed.

paragraphs.zh: 按：僧貌似伽蓝，故凑成此巧，亦可谓奇。然是人作成此套，何尝真有伽蓝化身乎！故富而能舍，本是善行；若谓真佛化缘而施舍者辄有福报，此两个装骗僧，岂能福人乎？吾不信也。
paragraphs.en: Note: The monk's appearance resembled that of the temple guardian, so this trick was cleverly pieced together; one might even call it remarkable. Yet, these people concocted this scheme—where did they truly become incarnations of the guardian? Thus, being wealthy and generous is inherently a virtuous act. If one claims that a true Buddha collecting alms guarantees blessings for those who donate, could these two fraudulent monks bestow such blessings upon anyone? I do not believe it.

stories.title_en: A Monk Resembling the Temple Guardian Fakes a Fundraising Appeal

paragraphs.zh: 东阳江达涧，父遗产万金。因为本府库吏累累浸润剥削，破去家产强半；又好男风，尝畜美好小仆，陪侍出入。有日，江之梁友遇其小仆，问曰：“前日为你相公买两匹青绢都长，做长衫必有剩。”小仆曰：“裁工不善做，先做一领太长，穿不得；后一领做得恰好。”梁曰：“长的可裁短，何妨？”仆曰：“他也不要得，已藏在书房大箱中去。”———原来江多衣服，其穿后不用的，都投入此箱。梁曰：“新服何忍弃，叫把与我修短服之。”仆曰：“你要问他讨，箱中第三件便是这新服。”
paragraphs.en: Jiang Dajian of Dongyang inherited ten thousand taels from his father. However, because the prefectural treasury clerks had repeatedly infiltrated and exploited him, more than half his family fortune was squandered. He also had a fondness for male favorites, keeping handsome young servants to attend him wherever he went. One day, Liang, a friend of Jiang's, met one of these servants and asked, "The other day, two bolts of dark silk bought for your master were both extra long. Surely there must be leftovers after making a long robe?" The servant replied, "The tailor was incompetent. The first robe he made was too long to wear; the second one was just right." Liang said, "Why not cut the long one shorter? What harm is there?" The servant said, "He doesn't want it anyway; it's already been put away in the large chest in the study." In fact, Jiang owned many garments; any he no longer wore after using them were tossed into that chest. Liang said, "How can one bear to discard a new garment? Tell him to give it to me so I can alter it to fit." The servant said, "If you wish to ask him for it, the third item in the chest is that new robe."

paragraphs.zh: 适一僧在旁闻得，素知江达涧肯施舍，即诈称方僧，入江相公廨中抄化。江以两文钱施之。僧曰：“吾看满衙之中，皆有怨气，唯相公府中祥光满室，后日必有好官职，前程远大。吾将化你一件好服，以结个缘。”江曰：“我无好服。”僧曰：“你有一件穿不得的，舍与我好。”江故曰：“衣皆可穿，哪有穿不得的？”僧曰：“是一件新青绢太长的，在书房大箱中，第三件该舍与我，吾为尔消灾延寿。不然，你眼下有多少是非到。”江心异之，开大箱中看，果有两件在上，新绢服第三。便疑此僧先知，持出舍与之，问曰：“既舍此服，可免是非否？”僧曰：“我试你有善心否。今果肯施，便转灾成福矣。”
paragraphs.en: A monk nearby overheard this. Knowing Jiang Dajian was generous, he pretended to be a wandering monk and entered Master Jiang's yamen quarters to solicit donations. Jiang gave him two cash. The monk said, "I see an air of grievance throughout the entire yamen, yet only in your residence does auspicious light fill the rooms. You will surely secure a good official post with a bright future ahead. Let me beg for a fine robe from you to establish a karmic bond." Jiang replied, "I have no fine robes." The monk said, "You have one you cannot wear. Give it to me; that would be excellent." Jiang feigned ignorance, saying, "All my clothes can be worn. How could there be one I cannot wear?"
