The monk insisted, "It is a new dark-silk robe, too long, kept in the large chest in the study. The third item should be given to me. I will dispel your disasters and extend your life. Otherwise, immediate calamity awaits you." Jiang found this strange, opened the chest, and indeed found two items on top, with the new silk robe as the third. Suspecting the monk had foresight, he took it out and gave it to him, asking, "Having given this robe, can I be spared the trouble?" The monk replied, "I was merely testing whether you possess a kind heart. Since you are now willing to give, disaster has already turned into fortune."

paragraphs.zh: 按：今僧皆庸人，何能前知？其称已往事者，多得于传闻；说未来事者，皆涉于矫诬。观此僧欺江相公之事，则今之称善知识者，皆此类也。江相公之易欺如此，家安得不败？世之信僧引诱者，可以此为鉴。
paragraphs.en: Note: Monks today are all ordinary men. How can they know the future? When they speak of past events, they mostly get them from hearsay; when they speak of future events, they are all false claims. Looking at how this monk cheated Master Jiang, those today who call themselves spiritual guides are all of this type. Master Jiang was so easy to cheat—how could the household not fail? Those in the world who believe monks' lures may take this as a warning.

stories.title_en: Faking Foresight to Cheat a Man Out of a Silk Robe

categories.title_zh: 第二十二類 煉丹騙

paragraphs.zh: 古有炼丹之说，点铁成金，盖仙方，非人世有也。世所传炼丹之术，用好纹银三两，杂诸铅、汞辰、朱砂药物在炉同炼，每次须炼四十九日。至四十日后，须两人轮番守炉，昼夜不得暂时离守。丹成，可得九两，内除三两银本，要三两买药物，每次只出三两。一年可炼四次，共可得十二两，仅足供两人食用。故真得此方者，亦不屑为。其炼出丹银，亦可经煎，每次渐渐亏少，复归于无。但此银第二次不可为银母，若再炼，须另以纹银为母。此相传真方，费心费工，甚不易为。若云游方士，托炼丹为名以行骗者，用砒霜、雄黄诸物，炒好银为灰砂，假称曰“丹头”；然后将此与好银同煎，仍煎成银，彼便道“丹药可点成银”，此个个是弄假行骗之套子。
paragraphs.en: Since ancient times there has been talk of refining elixirs—of pointing at iron to turn it into gold. That is an art of immortals, not something found in the human world. The elixir-refining method handed down in the world uses three taels of fine silver, mixed with lead, mercury, cinnabar, and other ingredients, all refined together in a furnace. Each round must be fired for forty-nine days. After the fortieth day, two men must take turns watching the furnace; day and night they may not leave it for a moment. When the elixir is done, you get nine taels. Out of that, subtract the three taels of silver capital, and three more taels go to buying ingredients, so each round yields only three taels of profit. You can refine four times a year, making twelve taels in all, barely enough to feed two men. So even someone who truly possesses this formula would not deign to practice it. The elixir silver it produces can stand up to remelting, but each time it shrinks a little, until it dwindles back to nothing. And this silver cannot serve as mother silver a second time; to refine again, you must take fresh fine silver as the mother. This is the genuine formula as it has been handed down: it costs care and labor and is very hard to carry out. As for wandering alchemists who use elixir refining as a pretext for swindling: they use arsenic, realgar, and such substances to cook good silver down to ash and grit, and falsely call it "elixir seed." Then they melt this together with good silver, and it melts back into silver, whereupon they say, "The elixir can transmute into silver." Every one of these is a put-up job, a fraud and a swindle.

paragraphs.zh: 有一道士，自称能炼丹者。先以银灰明煎出些与人看，人多疑信相半。一富人独信之，请至家炼。道士曰：“炼丹乃仙术，家中多秽浊，恐不能成。可于僻地开坑一丈四尺深，下仅可容一床一炉，在此处烧炼四十九日。一百两银母，可炼出三百两矣。”富人依言，于后门凿一坑，广八尺，深一丈四尺。道士入坑去，命用银十两买铅、汞辰、朱砂等来，先炼丹头，三日已讫。富人付银百两与炼，日吊下三餐饭与食，道人又命讨一手握的坚实圆木七只，每只三尺五寸长，作符；用大棕索一条，交横缚柴符上，日以大斧摧打柴符。富人每日往坑上看。至三十餘日，柴符渐渐打下，只有一尺在上，心料银将成矣。道士知一月之久，防守者必懈，夜以索一头系裹银药，一头系在腰，将七只长符，每二尺打一符于上，扳援而升，将银吊起，夤夜逃去。次早送饭，下无人接。以烛照之，不见道士矣。梯下看之，银都窃去，方知彼蹈符而上，明白被其窃骗也。
paragraphs.en: There was a Daoist priest who claimed he could refine elixirs. First, he took some silver filings and openly smelted a small amount to show people; most were half doubtful, half convinced. One rich man alone believed him and invited him home to refine. The Daoist said, "Refining elixirs is an immortal art. A house is full of foulness and impurity; I fear it cannot succeed there. You should dig a pit in a secluded spot, fourteen feet deep, the bottom just big enough to hold a bed and a furnace, and do the firing there for forty-nine days. A hundred taels of mother silver can be refined into three hundred taels." The rich man did as he said and dug a pit by the back gate, eight feet across and fourteen feet deep. The Daoist went down into the pit, had him spend ten taels of silver buying lead, mercury, cinnabar, and the rest, and first refined the elixir seed, which was finished in three days. The rich man handed over a hundred taels of silver for refining, and each day lowered three meals down to him. The Daoist also told him to find seven solid round logs, each thick as a hand's grip and three and a half feet long, to serve as talismans. He took a thick coir rope, bound it crosswise around the wooden talismans, and every day had them hammered with a great axe. The rich man went to look down at the pit every day. After thirty-some days, the wooden talismans had been driven down little by little until only a foot remained above ground, and he reckoned the silver was nearly ready. The Daoist knew that after a full month the watchers would surely relax their guard. That night he tied one end of the rope around the wrapped silver and ingredients and the other end around his own waist; then he took the seven long talisman stakes, drove them into the pit wall one every two feet, climbed up by hauling on them, pulled the silver up after him, and fled in the dead of night. The next morning, when the meal was sent down, no one below took it. They shone a candle down: the Daoist was gone. They lowered a ladder and went down to look: the silver had all been stolen. Only then did they realize he had climbed out by way of the stakes; plainly, they had been robbed and swindled.

paragraphs.zh: 按：深坑煅炼，使人不疑其逃。然用符用索，已早为出坑之计。其使人不疑处，即其脱身处也。后人鉴此，尚以炼丹为可信否？
paragraphs.en: Note: Deep-pit calcination made people suspect no escape. Yet the talismans and ropes were already his plan to leave the pit. The very thing that kept them from suspecting was his way out. Let later generations take warning from this: can elixir refining still be trusted?

stories.title_en: Refining Elixir in a Deep Pit, with Long Talismans Placed

paragraphs.zh: 方士以炼丹脱剥，受骗者历来无算，故明人皆能灼见其伪，拒绝不信。有一邴道士，术极高，拐一脚，明言已得真传炼丹术，不肯轻易为人炼。其法以丹头与人，任其以铜铅同煎，皆成银。彼自用则不须炼，但随手取出，都是银。或见人疾苦者，在手掌一捻，即取银与之；或衣袖中随来，亦是银。多肯施舍与贫人，由是，人称为“半仙”。有用银器皿设盛席待之者，食毕，令取一米桶置席上，以手取银器，件件收入桶中。及看，则空桶无一物，明言我收去不还矣。人以善言求取，则云：“已在你家内原藏器之所。”视之，果在。若恶言强取，则终不见。此谓得五鬼搬运之法。如此累显奇术，皆足骇动人。
paragraphs.en: Alchemists use elixir refining to fleece people. Those cheated have been beyond counting through the ages, so clear-eyed people can all see through the fraud and refuse to believe it. There was a certain Daoist named Bing, a master of the art, lame in one leg, who said openly that he had received the true transmission of elixir refining and would not lightly perform it for anyone. His method was to give people elixir seed and let them melt it with copper or lead: it all turned to silver. When he wanted silver himself, he did not need to refine at all; whatever he drew from his hand was silver. If he saw someone in hardship, a twist of his palm would produce silver to give them; or it would come out of his sleeve, and that too was silver. He was generous in giving to the poor, and so people called him the "Half Immortal." Once a host set out silver vessels and a lavish feast to entertain him. When the meal was over, Bing had a rice bucket brought and set on the table, picked up the silver vessels piece by piece, and dropped them into the bucket. When they looked, it was an empty bucket with nothing in it. He said openly, "I have taken them away, and I am not giving them back." If they asked for them politely, he would say, "They are already back in your house, in the place where the vessels were kept." They looked, and there they were. If they demanded them rudely, the vessels were never seen again. This was called having mastered the Five Ghosts' art of transport. Marvels like this, displayed again and again, were enough to astound everyone.

paragraphs.zh: 有富人尧鲁信之，延至于家，朝夕参拜，敬礼备至，愿学其术。道士安然受拜，未肯遂传之。每日坐享其敬，饮醉而睡，睡醒而游，全不以其敬礼为意。但有甚术，凡拜之者便倾心悦服，与共席饮酒，使称颂其道。尧鲁一家老幼婢仆，皆尊敬之。唯鲁妻辛氏始终不信，累劝夫宜绝此邪人。后邴道士知之，以银二钱与其家小仆，曰：“你主母梳头时，可取她梳下头发一根与我。”小仆早晨取与之。道士得此发即作法，至半上午，辛氏中心只爱与道士通，谓婢曰：“今日我心异也。”至午益甚，又曰：“今日心中大异。”至半下午，心不能自禁，明谓侍婢曰：“吾往日极恶邴道士，今日何爱他好？你看我脸上何如？”婢曰：“你似欲睡模样。”至晚饭后，辛氏思与道士云雨之意极切，只恨一家人在旁耳。又强制住，密谓婢曰：“你今须紧跟我，或入道士房去，你须打我两掌，批我面皮，切不可忘。”及上床睡后，夫已睡着，辛氏披上衣，裸下体，开门径奔道士房去。道士正在作法催符。婢急跟出，呼曰：“此道士房，不可去！”亦不应。道士语婢曰：“你外去。”以手扯辛氏。婢近前批主母两颊，亦不管；又在面上打两掌，曰：“你未穿衣。”辛氏方醒，曰：“我是梦中来，何故真身在此？喜得你唤醒也。”手携婢曰：“快和我进去，好羞人也！”入房蹴夫醒，详言其情及得婢唤醒之事。夫曰：“哪有此理？你素恶他，故装此情捏之，岂有心既欲去，又肯叫婢挽之？这假话我不信。”次日，不得已述于夫兄言之。兄命弟逐去道士，亦不听；乃往县告之。县提去打二十，又会寄棒，打亦不痛，乃以收监。道士明是空身入监，随手取出都是银。以银贿禁子，令买酒肉入监食。禁子更加奉承，思求其方。后又解府解道，各官都加责，以无甚证据，不肯置之死。后竟托分上，放出逃去，不知所往。尧鲁一家长幼，后相继疾故，盖受其术所蛊也。唯辛氏贞正，寿考无恙，总理家政，以抚幼孙之长，至九十餘岁而卒。
paragraphs.en: There was a rich man named Yao Lu who believed in him. He invited Bing into his home, bowed to him morning and night, honored him with every courtesy, and begged to learn his art. The Daoist calmly accepted the bows but refused to transmit the art. Every day he sat back enjoying the worship, drank himself drunk and slept, woke and wandered about, taking the family's reverence entirely for granted. But he possessed some power: whoever bowed to him would pour out their heart in devotion, drink with him at the same table, and sing the praises of his Way. Yao Lu's whole household, old and young, maids and menservants, all revered him. Only Lu's wife, Mistress Xin, never believed from first to last, and she urged her husband time and again to cut off this wicked man. Later the Daoist Bing learned of this. He gave two qian of silver to a young servant of the house and said, "When your mistress combs her hair, take one of the hairs that comes out in the comb and bring it to me." The boy brought him one that morning. Once the Daoist had the hair, he performed the ritual immediately. By mid-morning, Mistress Xin's heart was set on intimacy with the Daoist. She said to her maid, "My heart feels strange today." By noon it was worse, and she said again, "My heart feels very strange today." By mid-afternoon she could no longer hold herself back and said openly to her waiting-maid, "I used to hate that Daoist Bing bitterly; why do I adore him today? Look at my face. How does it look?" The maid said, "You look as if you want to sleep." After the evening meal, Xin's longing to sleep with the Daoist grew desperate; her only vexation was that the whole family was around. She forced the urge down and privately told the maid, "Tonight you must stay close to me. If I go into the Daoist's room, you must slap me twice across the face, hard. Whatever you do, don't forget." After they had gone to bed and her husband was asleep, Xin threw on an upper garment, left her lower body bare, opened the door, and ran straight for the Daoist's room. The Daoist was just then working his spell, urging on the talisman. The maid hurried after her, crying, "That is the Daoist's room; you must not go!" There was no answer. The Daoist told the maid, "Get outside," and pulled Xin in by the hand. The maid stepped up and slapped her mistress on both cheeks; Xin paid no heed. She struck her face twice more and said, "You have no clothes on." Only then did Xin wake. "I came here in a dream; why is my real body here? Thank heaven you woke me." She took the maid's hand and said, "Quick, come back in with me. How shameful!" In her room she kicked her husband awake and told him the whole story, including how the maid had woken her. Her husband said, "How could such a thing be? You have always hated him; you staged this scene to frame him. If your heart really wanted to go, why would you have told the maid to pull you back? I don't believe this lie." The next day, having no other choice, she told the whole thing to her husband's elder brother. The elder brother ordered his younger brother to drive the Daoist out; Yao Lu would not listen. So the brother went to the county and lodged a charge. The county had the Daoist brought in and given twenty strokes, then put him to the rod, but the beating did not hurt him, so they threw him in jail. The Daoist had plainly entered the jail with nothing on him, yet whatever he produced from his hand was silver. He bribed the jailers with silver and had them buy wine and meat to bring into the jail. The jailers grew still more fawning, hoping to get his formula out of him. Later he was sent up to the prefecture and then to the circuit; at each level the officials had him beaten, but as there was no solid evidence, they would not put him to death. In the end he called in favors, was released, and fled, no one knew where. Yao Lu's whole family, old and young, afterward fell ill and died one after another; they had been poisoned by his sorcery. Only Mistress Xin, chaste and upright, lived on unharmed to a great age. She ran the household, raised the young grandsons to manhood, and died past ninety.

paragraphs.zh: 按：妖术之暗中，如妖狐之投媚，必心邪而后能惑。苟心正者，虽入群妖之中，妖不能害。故傅奕不信死人之咒，而胡僧自死；仲淹下信杀子之鬼，而鬼自不来。辛氏心正，虽妖人灵法，能深疑于心，蚤嘱于婢，终不受其邪淫之毒。然则法虽巧，终不及人心之正也。后遇妖人者，其牢把心而勿睬之，彼邪亦安施哉？
paragraphs.en: Note: Sorcery strikes from the dark the way a fox-spirit offers its charms: the heart must be crooked first, and only then can it be beguiled. If the heart is upright, one may walk into a crowd of demons and they cannot do any harm. Thus Fu Yi refused to believe a curse could kill a man, and the foreign monk dropped dead himself; Fan Zhongyan refused to believe a ghost could kill his son, and the ghost never came. Lady Xin's heart was upright. Though the sorcerer's potent arts were uncanny, she harbored deep suspicion in her heart and warned her maid early on, so in the end she escaped the poison of his wicked lust. However clever the sorcery, it is no match for an upright human heart. Should you ever meet a sorcerer, hold fast to your heart and pay him no heed—what can his evil tricks do then?

stories.title_en: Believing in Elixir Refining Brings Ruin on a Whole Family

paragraphs.zh: 古潭一后生丁宇弘，机关伶俐，识尽世间情伪，人不能欺。偶遇一方士，自称能炼丹。宇弘早知其伪也，欲乘此以骗方士，故诈为不知之状而琐琐问之。方士曰：“丹是仙术，古来传于善人，专以济救贫穷者。先须采药炼成丹头，后用银一钱，与丹头同煎，可得三钱；一两可得三两。”宇弘曰：“更多可炼否？”方士曰：“只要有丹头，虽一百一千皆可炼。”宇弘先用银一钱与炼。方士加丹头三分，即煎出银三钱。宇弘喜，更以一两与煎，又得银三两。宇弘益喜，请方士到家，殷勤相待。及银已费尽，又求再炼添用，陆续炼出银三十餘两。惟以好言承奉之，愿学其术，终不多出银与炼，反将方士丹头之本骗来矣。
paragraphs.en: In Gutan there was a young man named Ding Yuhong, sharp and quick-witted, who knew all the falseness of the world; no one could deceive him. He chanced to meet an alchemist who claimed he could refine elixirs. Yuhong knew at once that it was a fraud, and decided to use the occasion to swindle the alchemist instead. So he feigned ignorance and pestered the man with tedious questions. The alchemist said, "The elixir is an immortal art, handed down since ancient times to good men, meant specially to relieve the poor. First you must gather ingredients and refine them into elixir seed. Then take one qian of silver, melt it together with the seed, and you get three qian; one tael yields three taels." Yuhong asked, "Can you refine more than that?" The alchemist said, "As long as there is elixir seed, even a hundred taels or a thousand can be refined." Yuhong first gave him one qian of silver to refine. The alchemist added three fen of elixir seed, and out came three qian of silver. Yuhong was delighted, gave him a tael to melt, and again got three taels of silver. More delighted still, he invited the alchemist home and waited on him attentively. Whenever the silver was spent, he asked to refine more for spending money, and batch after batch they melted out thirty-odd taels of silver. He simply plied the man with fine words and said he wished to learn the art, but he never put up much silver of his own for the refining, so in the end it was the alchemist's own elixir-seed capital that got swindled away.

paragraphs.zh: 方士思家中不奈他何，故说：“吾丹头已用尽。可多带银本，出外采药，再在外大炼。”宇弘明知其引外行骗，只自思“我用心提防，彼何以骗？”更欲尽骗其身心丹头之银，乃带银五十两，与俱出外，不肯取出费用。方士叫其取银买物，宇弘曰：“丹以换银，今已成之银，何必轻用？可取丹来炼银作路费，我银留买药。”方士尽将己丹头三两，宇弘用银十两，共炼成三十两，彼此各分一半。又远行两日，寝食严防。方士无计可脱，乃背地买砒霜在身，晚又买一鲜鱼入店。宇弘往煮熟，装作两碗，方士往捧一碗在席，放毒于内。又再捧一碗，故打忿嚏，将口馋溅入鱼上。方士曰：“这碗亵渎了，我吃。”及至半夜，宇弘腹疼。延至明晓，方士往医家求止疼药，煎服愈甚。至午，宇弘发散唇裂，腹痛难当，心疑是方士投毒，哀求之曰：“吾止有银五十五两，你能救我命，尽半与你。”时弘已不能起床矣。方士取其银置己包袱内，近床以药与之曰：“吾游方人，将攒他人银。你好奸狡，反骗去我银五十两。今止多得你五两，吾自行善心，以此药与你，凭你命当生死何如。”遂负行李逃去。宇弘急命店主以药煎。有认得者曰：“此解砒霜药也。”连服几次，疼稍止。再求近店人医之，三日始得痊愈，银已全被方士夺去矣，只沿路乞食而归。
paragraphs.en: The alchemist saw that he could do nothing to him at home, so he said: "My elixir powder is all used up. You should bring more silver capital; we will go out to gather ingredients and refine it on the road." Yuhong knew perfectly well the man was luring him out to swindle him, but he thought to himself, "If I keep my guard up, how can he swindle me?" What was more, he wanted to cheat the man out of every bit of elixir powder he still carried. So he took fifty taels of silver and set out with him, refusing to produce it for expenses. When the alchemist told him to take out silver to buy things, Yuhong said, "The elixir is for turning into silver. Now that we have finished silver, why spend it lightly? Bring out the powder and refine silver for travel expenses; my silver stays for buying ingredients." The alchemist put in all three taels of elixir powder he had left, and Yuhong ten taels of silver; together they refined it into thirty taels, and each took half. They traveled two more days, and Yuhong kept strict guard even over sleep and meals. The alchemist had no scheme by which to get away with him, so he secretly bought arsenic and kept it on his person. That evening he also bought a fresh fish and brought it into the inn. Yuhong went and boiled the fish and portioned it into two bowls. The alchemist carried one bowl to the table and put the poison in it. Then, carrying the other bowl, he deliberately let loose a violent sneeze and spattered saliva onto the fish. The alchemist said, "This bowl is defiled; I will eat it." By midnight Yuhong's belly began to hurt. The pain dragged on until dawn. The alchemist went to a doctor for a pain-relieving medicine, but once it was decocted and swallowed, the pain grew worse. By noon Yuhong's hair fell out and his lips cracked; the belly pain was unendurable. Suspecting that the alchemist had poisoned him, he begged him: "I have only fifty-five taels of silver. If you can save my life, I will give you half of everything." By then Yuhong could no longer get out of bed. The alchemist took his silver and stowed it in his own pack, then came to the bedside, gave him a medicine, and said, "I am a man of the road; I make my living hoarding others' silver. You are a cunning one; you swindled fifty taels out of me. Now I have gained only five taels extra from you. Out of the goodness of my heart I will give you this medicine; whether you live or die is up to your fate." Then he shouldered his baggage and fled. Yuhong hurriedly had the innkeeper decoct the medicine. Someone who recognized it said, "This is an antidote for arsenic." After several doses in a row, the pain gradually eased. He then found a doctor near the inn to treat him, and after three days he finally recovered. The silver had all been taken by the alchemist, and he could only beg for food along the road as he made his way home.

paragraphs.zh: 按：知防炼丹，莫如宇弘。虽百计不能骗，反骗方士银本几尽，可谓巧极矣。然终被其投毒，银尽还讫，又多去五两，且几乎丧命。幸而得生，沿路乞食，亦劳且辱矣。方士炼丹，其可信哉？
paragraphs.en: Note: No one knew better than Yuhong how to guard against elixir tricks. A hundred schemes could not swindle him; on the contrary, he swindled the alchemist out of nearly all his capital. You could call him clever in the extreme. Yet in the end the man poisoned him: all the silver went back, five taels more besides, and he nearly lost his life. Lucky to survive, he had to beg his way home along the road, toil and humiliation enough. Can anyone really trust an alchemist's elixir?

stories.title_en: When the Elixir Swindle Is Hard to Pull Off: Poison in the Mix

categories.title_zh: 第二十三類 法術騙

paragraphs.zh: 僧術中有以法咒水密咒某人，心欲何事，後令人自取照之，各隨其心之所欲，自現其形。有米春元者，富過百萬，田連兩府，年逾五十，不思會試，唯安享豪華以為樂。妖僧聞其富，欲騙其厚利也，挾咒水之術，往叩其門，自言能望氣，每見此宅紫氣上沖，有鸞鳳之彩。此百代王侯之兆，當有立翊運之功、分河山之帶礪者。米春元未信。僧曰：「吾傳有秘術，以符咒水能知此生榮枯結果。人但齋戒三日，虔心來照，則今生是何成就，自現於水中。」米乃留此僧，令家下人各齋戒。
paragraphs.en: Among the arts of monks there is one that works by chanting spells over water. The monk secretly casts the spell on a man, and whatever that man longs for in his heart, when he is then told to look into the water himself, his own image appears in it accordingly. There was a man named Mi Chunyuan, worth over a million, whose fields stretched across two prefectures. He was past fifty and no longer thought of sitting the metropolitan examination; his only pleasure was living in ease and luxury. A sorcerer-monk heard of his wealth and schemed to cheat him out of a rich profit. Wielding the water-charming art, he went and knocked at Mi's gate, claiming that he could read the aura of a place: every time he passed this residence, he said, he saw purple vapors rising into the sky, shot through with the colors of the phoenix and the luan. This was an omen of kings and marquises for a hundred generations; someone here was destined to perform great service in upholding the dynasty's fortune and to receive a fief under an everlasting oath of enfeoffment. Mi Chunyuan did not believe him. The monk said, "I hold a secret transmitted art: with talismans and enchanted water one can learn the rise and fall of this life and how it will end. A man need only fast for three days and come to look with a devout heart, and whatever he is meant to achieve in this life will appear of itself in the water." Mi then took the monk in and ordered everyone in the household to fast.

paragraphs.zh: 至第三日，注大缸水於庭。僧密語咒水，令諸人自照。米照見戴丫天冠，穿蟒袍。幼子照之，亦同。長次二子，只紗帽圓領而已。米正室照，亦妃冠鳳袍。兩長婦照，唯珠冠翟服。米大異之，僅秘於心。
paragraphs.en: On the third day, they filled a great vat with water in the courtyard. The monk muttered spells over the water in secret and had each person look into it in turn. Mi looked and saw himself wearing a Y-shaped celestial crown and a python robe. His youngest son saw the same. The two elder sons saw only gauze caps and round-collared robes. Mi's principal wife saw a consort's crown and a phoenix robe. The two elder daughters-in-law saw only pearl crowns and pheasant-plumed gowns. Mi was astonished but kept it locked in his heart.

paragraphs.zh: 後與流寓枝鄉官宴會，談及時事，枝曰：「今併後匹敵，金注支庶。禍之萌，必始宮闈。異日不為文皇之蹀血，或為沂王府之反召。此魯嫠所深卹者。」米曰：「往者逆未萌而折，宸豪已發而摧。國家如天之福，風雨何搖於牖戶也？」枝曰：「不然。文靜以監豎倡唐，姚衍以胖僧興國。若輔之得人，成敗安可料也？」米曰：「縱中土有故，水國偏在海隅，必無憂亂離也。」枝曰：「亦難保。讖云『某地出天子，江南作戰場』，正可慮也。」米曰：「使宸豪復興於今，成敗當何如？」枝曰：「今承平馳兵，更甚於昔。向令宸豪不久淹南康，某都不詐應反戈，安至以銅鐘灰也？」米聞言心喜。
paragraphs.en: Later, at a banquet with a certain Zhi, a former official residing there, the talk turned to current affairs. Zhi said, "As things stand, the rivals are evenly matched, and the stakes rest on the cadet line. The first sprout of calamity will surely arise within the palace. One day, there will be either a bloodbath like Emperor Chengzu's seizure of the throne, or a call to revolt from a princely house like the Prince of Yi's. This is precisely what the widow of Lu deeply feared." Mi said, "In the past, rebellion was crushed before it could take root, and Chenhao was destroyed as soon as he rose. The dynasty enjoys Heaven's favor—how could wind and rain shake its doors?" Zhi replied, "Not so. Liu Wenjing, a minor official, set the Tang uprising in motion; Yao Guangxiao, a monk, helped raise an emperor's house. Once a cause finds capable men to back it, who can predict success or failure?" Mi said, "Even if the central plains fall into turmoil, our watery region lies far off in a corner by the sea; surely we need not fear chaos here." Zhi said, "That too is hard to guarantee. A prophecy says, 'A Son of Heaven shall emerge from a certain place, and Jiangnan shall become a battlefield.' That is precisely what we must fear." Mi asked, "If Chenhao were to rise again today, how would it end?" Zhi said, "The realm has been at peace so long that the troops have grown slack—even worse than in those days. Had Chenhao not lingered so long at Nankang, and had a certain garrison not feigned allegiance only to turn their spears against him, how would his grand enterprise have gone up in smoke?" Upon hearing this, Mi felt secretly delighted.

paragraphs.zh: 又有一僧，能降神附童者，言往來禍福，如聲應響。米請降之密禱，以欲圖不軌事。神降曰：「金鍾興，玉氣旺，清福扶王帝業強。洪流掃蕩人安泰，裂土移宮鎮遠方。」米猶未決休咎，再求明報。降童喝曰：「此何事而敢絮叨也！」米不敢問，而未解神意。既而漁人於深淵得巨鐘，金色燁然。米以為瑞也，召枝某及二僧決謀逆，欲俟五月某日五更早，大小官俱出城送萬壽表，乃閉四門，伏兵城外，悉殲之。
paragraphs.en: There was another monk who could call down a spirit to possess a boy, and it spoke of coming fortunes and misfortunes like an echo answering a sound. Mi asked him to call the spirit down, and prayed in secret about his plan to commit treason. The spirit descended and said: "The golden bell rises, the jade aura waxes; pure fortune upholds the king, the imperial enterprise grows strong. A mighty flood sweeps the land clean and the people rest in peace; carve up the soil, move the palace, and hold the far frontier." Mi still could not tell whether this boded good or ill, and begged for a plainer answer. The possessed boy shouted, "What manner of thing is this, that you dare babble on about it!" Mi dared not ask again, and still did not grasp the spirit's meaning. Soon afterward a fisherman hauled a huge bell out of a deep pool, gleaming gold. Mi took it as an auspicious sign. He summoned Zhi and the two monks to settle their plans for revolt: they would wait for a certain day in the fifth month, at dawn, when officials high and low would all leave the city to send off the emperor's birthday memorial; then they would shut the four gates, station troops in ambush outside the walls, and slaughter them to a man.

paragraphs.zh: 至四更，兵卒供執事者早起，見城內伏兵處燈火異常，急報軍官調兵捕之。城中擾亂，又遣兵守城。見江中船無數，皆早炊飯。城上兵疑是助亂者，大呼曰：「某人謀逆，被捕獲斬首矣！」外伏者見內無號砲，城上有備，又聞呼喊聲，送表官皆不出城，知事必敗露，河邊數十號船，乘微明時各各逃散。後官以亂者作造謀反劫庫問，捕獲數十餘人，皆斬首。而首逆者，反以不知情為辭，只擬流三千里而死於道。
paragraphs.en: At the fourth watch, the soldiers on duty rose early and noticed unusual lights and fires at the places where the ambush troops were hidden inside the city. They rushed a report to the officers, who called out troops to make arrests. The city fell into commotion, and more soldiers were sent to man the walls. From the walls they saw countless boats on the river, all cooking an early meal. Suspecting they had come to aid the revolt, the soldiers on the wall shouted, "So-and-so plotted treason—he has been caught and beheaded!" The men in ambush outside saw no signal cannon from within, saw that the walls were manned, and heard the shouting; the officials escorting the memorial never came out of the city. Knowing the plot must have been exposed, the several dozen boats along the river scattered and fled in the first faint light. Later the authorities treated the rioters as having plotted rebellion and an attempt to rob the treasury; several dozen men were captured, and all were beheaded. But the ringleader pleaded that he had known nothing of it; he was sentenced only to exile three thousand li, and died on the road.

paragraphs.zh: 按：米春元年老巨富，已無心向功名，更何心圖王侯？止以咒水妖僧啟其端，降神妖僧決其志，又以枝某失職，怏怏釀成大逆。二僧已就誅，而枝某幸脫於網。天何緩討凶人哉？猶幸聖朝清明，小丑旋殄，固太平之洪福，亦此地民風素良善忠順，不當受此叛逆者之荼毒也。然信僧惑邪之禍亦酷矣。後人其深鑑之，其深戒之。
paragraphs.en: Note: In the first year of the Mingchun era, an old and enormously rich man had no thought left for rank and fame—still less any ambition to make himself a king or a marquis. It was only the water-charming sorcerer-monk who opened the door, the spirit-calling sorcerer-monk who steeled his resolve, and Zhi, out of office and nursing his resentment, who brewed it into high treason. The two monks were executed, but Zhi had the luck to slip through the net. Why is Heaven so slow to punish the wicked? Fortunately the reign is enlightened, and the petty traitors were quickly wiped out. That was the great good fortune of a peaceful age—and it was also because the people of this region have always been decent, loyal, and law-abiding, and did not deserve to be poisoned by such rebels. Yet the ruin that comes from trusting monks and being seduced by heresy is cruel enough. Let those who come after take this deeply as a mirror, and deeply as a warning.

stories.title_en: A Monk Uses a Mirror Trick to Plot Rebellion

paragraphs.zh: 老狐晝伏岩洞，夜出尋食草木之實。有偶於草木中吸得天地氤氳之情者，便有靈變，能幻化為美婦，以迷誘人，採人之陽精，以益其靈通。法師捕得而烹之。和尚如求得狐心，焙而乾之，熏以好香，於深山中構一草廬，以狐心奉祀於中，日誦諸般懺文經卷超度之，夜則群妖眾怪嗥者、呼者、悲者、泣者、叫者、嘯者、能為人言或蠻語者，千怪萬狀，於草廬外哀弔，極其淒涼。要極大膽之人，方敢中處。弔過七日，亦漸漸稀少。晝夜常誦經作法，備果食供奉。積至四十九日，然後焚了草廬，把狐心領回，香火祀之。如明日欲往見某人，先夜以錦囊盛狐心，置於心上，夜必夢婦人領之，先見其人：次日往拜其人，已夢中相會。後有所干求，人必以為異而多從之。此僧家騙化之一術也。
paragraphs.en: Old foxes hide in rocky caves by day and come out at night to feed on the fruits of grasses and trees. If one happens to breathe in the generative essence of heaven and earth among the plants, it gains spiritual powers: it can transform into a beautiful woman to bewitch and seduce men, draining their yang essence to increase its own magic. When a ritual master catches such a fox and cooks it, a monk who manages to obtain the fox's heart roasts it dry, fumes it with fine incense, builds a thatched hut deep in the mountains, and enshrines the heart inside. By day he chants every kind of penitential text and sutra to deliver its soul; by night, hordes of demons and monsters—howling, calling, moaning, weeping, shrieking, whistling, some speaking human words, some barbarian tongues, in a thousand uncanny shapes—come to mourn outside the hut, a scene of utter desolation. It takes a man of extraordinary nerve to dare stay inside. After seven days of mourning, the visitors gradually thin out. Day and night he keeps chanting sutras and performing rites, laying out fruit and food as offerings. When forty-nine days have passed, he burns the hut down, takes the fox heart home, and keeps it on an altar with incense. If he means to call on someone the next day, the night before he puts the fox heart in a brocade pouch and lays it over his own heart. That night he is sure to dream of a woman who leads him to meet the man. The next day, when he goes to pay his respects, the man has already met him in a dream. Afterward, whatever he asks for, people find it uncanny and usually grant it. This is one of the tricks monks use to swindle and convert others.

paragraphs.zh: 有富家羊老，生二子娶二媳矣。蓄積盈餘，極是慳吝，分文不肯施捨。忽夜夢兩高僧來化緣，次日果有兩僧到，容貌儼如夢中所會者，稱言：「你取財太急，人多怨氣。吾與你有夙緣，特來為你懺悔。」羊老信之，問：「懺悔當如何？」僧曰：「你合家當齋戒三日，再買果餅麵食及三牲豬羊肉，半葷半素，吾為你作法請將，誦經供佛，將生前罪過解釋，再祈後增福祿，便家門請吉，死後免墮矣。」羊老依言，齋戒買辦。
paragraphs.en: There was a rich man named Old Yang, who had two sons and two daughters-in-law. His savings were ample, yet he was a terrible miser, unwilling to give away even a single cash coin in charity. One night he suddenly dreamed that two eminent monks came begging for alms. The next day, two monks arrived exactly as they had appeared in his dream. They said, "You have been too grasping in gathering wealth, and much resentment has built up against you. We share a bond with you from a former life and have come especially to perform repentance on your behalf." Old Yang believed them and asked, "How should the repentance be done?" The monks replied, "Your whole household must fast for three days. Then buy fruit, cakes, pastries, and the three sacrificial meats—pork and mutton—half meat and half vegetarian. We will perform rites for you, summon spirit generals, chant sutras, and make offerings to the Buddha to absolve your lifetime sins. Then we will pray for increased fortune and emolument hereafter, so that your household enjoys good luck and after death you escape falling into perdition." Old Yang did as they said, fasting and buying the provisions.

paragraphs.zh: 至第三日，又有兩僧到，又留相助誦經。至晚，來一僧念咒燒符，降遣羊老自跳自喊，取利劍在手，指其妻、子曰：「此鬼也。」悉手刃之。又追殺二媳。媳求僧解勸。僧指羊老喝曰：「坐！」羊老遂提劍咬牙，昏昏而坐，不醒人事。四僧入，輪姦二婦訖，以索縛之。搜其家財幣，捆作四擔，夤夜逃去。
paragraphs.en: On the third day two more monks arrived, and they too were kept on to help chant the sutras. That evening one monk chanted spells and burned talismans, and set Old Yang jumping and shouting under a spell. Yang snatched up a sharp sword, pointed at his wife and sons, and cried, "These are demons!"—and cut them all down with his own hand. Then he chased after the two daughters-in-law to kill them. The women begged the monks to restrain him. A monk pointed at Old Yang and barked, "Sit!" Sword in hand and teeth clenched, Yang sank into a dazed stupor, dead to the world. The four monks went in, raped the two women one after another, and bound them with ropes. They ransacked the house for money and valuables, tied the loot into four carrying loads, and fled in the dead of night.

paragraphs.zh: 次日，有人入其家者，見羊老被髮伏劍，睜眼語，急出呼眾入看。親眾群擁而入，羊老只說要殺鬼。眾向前奪去其劍，呼其名曰：「你何故如此？」羊老漸漸復蘇。人又問之，才知應曰：「吾夢見鬼多，正在此殺鬼，得你們叫我醒也。」及入後室，妻與子皆被殺。羊老大哭曰：「此我記得，殺三鬼在此，又趕殺二鬼婆，被僧攔開。」及入房，二婦皆捆在床，乃呼鄰婦來解之。各稱被僧所姦，金銀財帛皆收拾去矣。一家痛恨無窮，一邊收殮三尸，一邊遣人四路趕僧，皆趕上兩日路，並不見踪而還。
paragraphs.en: The next day, someone entered the house and found Old Yang with his hair loose, crouched over a sword, eyes open and muttering. He rushed out and called for others to come look. Relatives and neighbors poured in. Old Yang kept saying he had to kill demons. They stepped forward, wrested the sword away, and called him by name: "What has happened to you?" Little by little, Old Yang came around. When they questioned him again, he finally answered: "I dreamed there were many demons here, and I was killing them—until you called me awake." When they went into the back rooms, his wife and children had all been killed. Old Yang wailed, "That much I remember: I killed three demons here, then chased two demon-women to kill them too, but the monks held me off." When they went into the inner room, both women were tied up on the beds. They called in neighbor women to free them. Each said she had been raped by the monks, and that all the gold, silver, and valuables had been gathered up and carried off. The household's grief and hatred knew no end. While they laid out the three corpses for burial, they also sent men chasing the monks on every road; the pursuers traveled two days' distance, saw no trace of them, and returned.

paragraphs.zh: 按：羊老素慳吝，則為富不仁之事有矣。乃僧悚以怨氣，便信其說，而留以作福懺悔，則心先自疚故也。僧欲行術劫財，而先形於夢，此亦得狐心引夢之術而用之。彼夢謂高僧而反為劫僧，不信晝所為而信夜所夢，亦惑矣；不行善於平昔，而求懺悔於修齋，亦愚矣。今人多殘忍不仁，貪暴不義，而欲飯僧供佛，追修懺悔，何異羊老之覆哉！甚矣！惡不可為，而僧不可信也。鑑此當為之凜凜。
paragraphs.en: Note: Old Yang was naturally stingy, so he had indeed committed acts of heartlessness befitting a rich man. Yet when the monks frightened him with talk of resentment, he believed their words and kept them on to perform blessings and repentance—because his conscience was already guilty. The monks intended to use magic to rob him, revealing themselves first in a dream; this was the fox-heart art of inducing dreams put to use. He dreamed they were eminent monks, yet they turned out to be robber monks. To disbelieve what happens by daylight but believe what is dreamed at night is delusion; to do no good in ordinary times yet seek repentance through fasting is folly. Nowadays many people are cruel and heartless, greedy and unjust, yet hope to feed monks and make offerings to the Buddha, buying repentance after the fact. How are they any different from Old Yang in his ruin? It is beyond measure: evil must not be done, and monks are not to be trusted. Let this example make you shudder.

stories.title_en: Sorcerers Send a Dream, Then Plunder the House

paragraphs.zh: 往年，京城中有幼童出外，嘗被人拐帶而去，尋之又無踪。後累累有之。人多見一僧，摩幼童之臉，則幼童隨之而行。既而尋，已失之。故京城盛傳謂之「摩臉賊」。時在京僧釋人多，未察其孰是也。
paragraphs.en: Some years ago, young boys in the capital who went out were sometimes kidnapped and carried off, with searches turning up no trace. Later it happened again and again. Many people had seen a monk stroke a boy's face, whereupon the boy would follow him away; when they went looking soon after, the boy was already gone. Thus the capital buzzed with talk of a "cheek-rubbing rogue." At that time there were many monks in the capital, and no one could tell which one it was.

paragraphs.zh: 忽宓富人，止生一子，出外不返，四下跟尋甚急，各處出賞帖曰：「有收留得者，賞銀二十兩；報信者賞銀一十兩。」四出掛帖出賞，終莫得下落。
paragraphs.en: A wealthy man surnamed Mi had only one son who went out and never returned. The family searched frantically in every direction and posted reward notices everywhere: "Twenty taels of silver to anyone sheltering him; ten taels for information." They put up notices and offered rewards all around, but never learned his whereabouts.

paragraphs.zh: 住宓家小屋人班八，以淘街為生。一日，懶去掏街，往城外晦真庵閒遊，轉入後室，四旁周覽。忽破水障中一小士露頭來。班八認是宓家人，忙呼之曰：「家中四處尋你，何故在此？」宓子曰：「僧閉禁我在此，你快來救我！」班八看房門已鎖，恐一人難帶此子出，謂之曰：「你小心暫在此，我報你令尊知，即來取你矣。」飛跑而歸，報宓老曰：「令郎受禁在晦真庵中，速去救之。」宓老即招五十餘人，前後到庵。班八引至庵後房中，打開門，認出宓子，又搜出十數童輩，即令眾人捆住僧小山並同庵三人，都縛來狀送到官。
paragraphs.en: A man named Ban Ba, who lived in a small house on the Mi property, made his living scavenging the streets. One day, too lazy to go scavenging, he wandered out to Huizhen Hermitage outside the city for a stroll, turned into the rear quarters, and poked around on every side. Suddenly a small boy's head showed through a broken slatted screen. Ban Ba recognized him as the Mi family's son and called out at once, "Your family is searching everywhere for you—what are you doing here?" The Mi boy said, "The monk has me locked up in here. Come rescue me, quick!" Ban Ba saw that the door was locked. Afraid he could not get the boy out alone, he told him, "Stay put and keep quiet for now. I will report to your father and come straight back for you." He ran home at full speed and told Old Mi, "Your son is being held in Huizhen Hermitage. Go rescue him at once." Old Mi immediately rounded up fifty-odd men, who converged on the hermitage from front and back. Ban Ba led them to the back room, broke the door open, and picked out the Mi boy; a search turned up a dozen more boys. He had the men bind the monk Xiaoshan and the three others of the hermitage, and they were all trussed up and delivered to the authorities with a formal complaint.

paragraphs.zh: 官先審問眾童曰：「汝等如何被引入庵？」眾童曰：「和尚以手摩我眼睛，便見兩邊背後都是猛虎毒蛇，將來咬人傷人，唯面前一條路清淨好行，我輩只向前走，便到此庵，被和尚幽閉住。」又問曰：「和尚留汝等在庵幹何事？」眾童曰：「可恨這禿子，不拘日夜，將我等做苦春，極是疼痛。若不從，便將大杖撻打。眾人怕他，只得從他所為。」又問曰：「先拐來的後必長大，都放在何處去？」眾童曰：「有病者有長大者，和尚說放他回去，未知後都回家否。」官再審僧小山曰：「你拐來眾童後，病的長的都放哪裡去？」僧不敢應。再問同庵三人，都云：「毒死埋訖。」官聞言大怒，將小山打四十，同庵者各打二十，曰：「此罪不容於死。」令鎖出衙門外，許失童之家君聚手毆，打得身無完膚，有割其陽塞於僧口者，半日而死。人莫不恨其淫而快其死。後將其庵焚之，拐帶之禍遂息。
paragraphs.en: All the children they had kidnapped along the way were set free to go back—as for those kidnapped in previous years whose marrow had already been drained, or who had fallen ill or grown too old, the monk claimed he had let them return home, though no one knew whether they ever made it back alive. Only then did people realize that the spell ran through his sleeve: brushing a child's face was how he cast the charm, and having the child carry the turtle was how he bound the spell in place.

paragraphs.zh: 按：好男風者，禽瀆之行。此僧必有春意之方，非拐諸幼童，無以快其欲。又習得妖法，摩其眼睛則昏花見怪，故可誘引童男。其罪浮於天矣。積惡貫盈，眾戮其身，言之羞口舌，書之污簡牘，人誰不切齒之！世有負男子之軀者，其可襲此僧之惡行哉！
paragraphs.en: Note: A taste for boys is the conduct of beasts. This monk must have had some aphrodisiac formula; without kidnapping young boys he had no way to glut his lust. He had also learned a sorcerer's art: a rub over their eyes made their sight blur and showed them terrors, so he could lure the boys away. His crimes rose higher than the sky. When his measure of evil was full, the crowd did the killing. To speak of it shames the tongue; to write of it soils the page. Who would not gnash his teeth at it? Any man with a male body—how could he follow in this monk's evil ways?

stories.title_en: The Face-Rubbing Swindler Who Abducts Young Children

categories.title_zh: 第二十四類 引嫖騙
categories.title_en: Category 24 · Luring Men into the Brothels

paragraphs.zh: 富人左東溪，止生一子少山，常帶千金財本，往南京買賣。既而入院毛月華，一年不歸。東溪問於人，知子以嫖故，因貪歡忘返，累以信促之歸。初猶回音，推託以帳未取完，後信往亦不答。東溪聞其財本已費過半矣，心中甚怒。欲自往尋之，又思空行費盤纏，乃帶三百金貨物，僱僕施來祿同往京尋子。
paragraphs.en: The rich man Zuo Dongxi had only one son, Shaoshan, who would regularly take a thousand taels of trading capital to Nanjing to do business. Then he entered the brothel of Mao Yuehua and stayed away for a whole year. Dongxi asked around and learned that his son had taken to the brothels and grown so greedy for pleasure that he forgot to return home, prompting him to send letter after letter pressing him to come back. At first Shaoshan still wrote back, putting him off with talk of accounts not yet collected; later he stopped answering at all. When Dongxi heard that more than half the capital had already been spent, he was furious. He wanted to go after the boy himself, but reckoned that making the trip empty-handed would waste travel money, so he took three hundred taels' worth of goods, hired a servant named Shi Lailu, and went with him to Nanjing to find his son.

paragraphs.zh: 人貨到京，早有人報知少山云：「爾父帶貨來賣，兼欲尋汝。」少山聞言甚悶，急呼其媽毛惜卿謀之曰：「家父特來催我歸，爾計能陷他亦嫖，則我在此可久；不然，今須與你別矣。」惜卿曰：「你但深藏其間，忽與相見，我自有理會。」即遣人邀前院荀榮媽來，託他巧為牢籠。榮媽許諾而去。
paragraphs.en: When the man and his goods reached Nanjing, someone had already reported to Shaoshan: "Your father has brought goods to sell, and he means to find you as well." Dismayed at the news, Shaoshan quickly called in the brothel madam, Mao Xiqing, to scheme with her: "My father has come expressly to press me to return home. If you have a plan to trap him into whoring too, then I can stay here for good; otherwise, I must part from you today." Xiqing said, "Just hide yourself deep inside and do not let him see you; I will take care of everything." She immediately sent someone to invite Madam Xun Rong from the front courtyard and asked her to lay a clever snare for him. Madam Rong agreed and left.

paragraphs.zh: 東溪問在京客夥，知子在毛惜卿家嫖其女月華，徑尋惜卿家來，欲呼子歸。惜卿出而款待甚恭。東溪曰：「小頑少山在你家，我到京十餘日矣，可叫他出來見我。」惜卿悚敬曰：「相公即少山令尊乎？妾幸披雲睹日也。令郎前在寒舍兩三個月，今月餘前送別久矣。」即喚女月華出見，指曰：「此爾翁也。」命下拜。東溪不禮之。又命設席。東溪曰：「吾為不肖子而來，豈索汝酒食乎？速叫兒與我歸，亦不消你假意相留。」月華曰：「果是前月已去，云欲收帳回家。若果在此，何敢相瞞？」東溪不信，定要究子下落。惜卿曰：「茅舍隻數間，任相公遍搜之。豈能藏得？」月華領東溪入內，四下覓之，無踪。東溪大怒曰：「牙人說在此，如何藏開，說這鬼話？若吾兒不見，是你家謀死，必當官告你，著你尋覓！」月華驚曰：「從來院中那有謀人者？相公勿輕易怪人。」東溪詬罵而出。
paragraphs.en: Inquiring among fellow merchants in Nanjing, Dongxi learned that his son was whoring at Mao Xiqing's house with her girl Yuehua, so he went straight to Xiqing's establishment to call his son back. Xiqing came out and received him with the utmost deference. Dongxi said, "My wayward boy Shaoshan is in your house. I have been in Nanjing for over ten days now—call him out to see me at once." With respectful alarm, Xiqing replied, "So Your Honor is Young Master Shaoshan's venerable father! How fortunate I am to part the clouds and behold the sun! Your worthy son did visit my humble house some time ago, and knowing that a young man away from home ought not squander his wealth, I earnestly urged him to head back. Half a month ago he set out with several guests for Suzhou and Hangzhou to buy goods, saying he would return home directly from there. Please sit a while and take a cup of tea, Your Honor; I would not dare detain you further." Still suspicious, Dongxi glared with rage and shouted, "Every fellow merchant in town says he is right here in your house! How dare you try to fool me with wine and food? Call my son out at once to return home with me, and spare me your false show of respect!" Fixing him with a solemn look, Xiqing said, "Even in a humble house like ours, we value honesty and good faith. Why don't you search inside, Your Honor? Why let outsiders' gossip make you wrong an innocent household?" She led Dongxi through every room inside and out; finding no trace of his son, he cursed his way out the door.

paragraphs.zh: 行過院前，窗內一女將盆水傾出，淋東溪一身，冠服盡濕。時怒未散，問「此是誰人家？」僕來祿曰：「此一行都是樂戶人家。」東溪即入其門指罵。荀榮媽出，驚惶問故，知是女荀慶雲誤傾水淋著，即喚出，棒打無數。慶雲哀求勸救，東溪亦不睬。榮媽曰：「你好將新服換與相公，向前叩頭求赦，留在此陪人禮，免後日生禍。」
paragraphs.en: As he passed the front of the next house, a girl inside flung out a basin of water that drenched Dongxi from head to foot, soaking his hat and robes. His anger had not yet cooled. "Whose house is this?" he asked. His servant Lailu said, "This whole row is licensed pleasure houses." Dongxi marched straight in the gate, pointing and cursing. Mama Xun Rong came out in alarm and asked what had happened; learning that her girl Xun Qingyun had carelessly thrown the water on him, she called the girl out at once and beat her unmercifully. Qingyun begged for mercy and pleaded for someone to rescue her, but Dongxi paid no heed. Mama Rong said, "You had better bring a fresh set of clothes for the master to change into, then go to him, kowtow, and beg his pardon—and keep him here to make proper amends, so this does not bring trouble on us later."

paragraphs.zh: 慶雲叩頭訖，引入內房，取一套新衣與更，跪曰：「我等人家，最怕得罪於人。萬望海度涵容，恕妾罪過。」東溪曰：「我原不怪你，只衣濕難行。我今換去，明日即送還矣。」拂衣便起。慶雲挽曰：「更有杯酒陪禮。若便去，媽又怪責我矣。」東溪曰：「何消酒？」時筵已排列，慶雲曲意陪奉，東溪亦放懷樂飲。至晚欲去，慶雲懇留曰：「今半載空房，若不宿而去，真對面不相逢也。你宿則媽歡喜，謂我善留客。此豈費房錢乎？」又飲到二更而睡。東溪思房錢終是還之，且假意不動，以試何如。慶雲偎抱撫摩之曰：「君作柳下惠，坐懷不亂耶？是入寶山空手回也。且暮夜無知，誰知爾貞節男者？」東溪笑而從之。
paragraphs.en: When Qingyun had finished kowtowing, she led him into an inner room, brought a new set of clothes for him to change into, and knelt, saying, "People in houses like ours live in dread of giving offense. I beg you to be generous and forgive my fault." Dongxi said, "I never blamed you to begin with—wet clothes are just hard to walk in. I will change now and send these back tomorrow." He shook out his sleeves and made to rise. Qingyun held him back: "There is still a cup of wine to make amends. If you leave right away, Mama will scold me again." Dongxi said, "What need is there for wine?" But by then the feast was already laid out. Qingyun waited on him with every art of pleasing, and Dongxi let himself go and drank merrily. Toward evening he wanted to leave. Qingyun begged him earnestly to stay: "This room has stood empty for half a year. If you go without staying the night, it is as though we met face to face and never met at all. If you stay, Mama will be pleased and say I know how to keep a guest. And it will not even cost you room money." They drank on until the second watch, then went to bed. Dongxi reckoned he would pay for the room in the end anyway, so for the moment he feigned indifference and lay still, to see what would happen. Qingyun nestled into his arms and stroked him, saying, "Are you playing Liuxia Hui, sitting with a woman in your lap and staying unmoved? That is walking into a mountain of treasure and coming back empty-handed. Besides, in the dark of night no one is watching—who would ever know what a chaste man you were?" Dongxi smiled and gave in.

paragraphs.zh: 次日近午方起。才梳洗罷，酒席已備，慢慢勸飲，彈唱以奉之。靠晚，又欲歸。慶雲留曰：「肯宿媽媽甚喜。若一宵而別，真是萍水之逢，落花有意，流水無心也。妾縱奉侍不周，君何不做甘雨，濟我半載旱人？」東溪又為留一夜。第三日，堅要歸，求還舊服。慶雲曰：「已遣人送往貴寓矣。」東溪曰：「承賜身上服，明日送還。」慶雲曰：「只恐不中服，何不收作表記？」又取出一箱玩物，欲擇一件相贈。東溪見箱中皆珠玉寶玩，僅取一牙扇墜。慶雲曰：「此不敢奉，此銀的敬奉。」東溪曰：「只領你意耳，何必送銀物？」慶雲曰：「此牙的是禮部公子所贈，旁刻有號。凡孤老所賜，唯銀得用。若簪甸諸玩物，須存留之。後日有會，問及即在，方表不忘之意，故不敢轉贈於人。此銀扇墜，乃預打造，以回答人者，旁鑄有妾名，故願相贈也。」東溪受之而歸。
paragraphs.en: The next day he did not rise until nearly noon. Barely finished washing and combing when the wine feast was ready; they plied him slowly with drink and sang and played for him. Toward evening he again wanted to go back. Qingyun kept him: "If you are willing to stay, Mama will be so pleased. To part after a single night would be a mere chance meeting on the road—the fallen flowers have feelings, but the flowing stream has no heart. Even if my service has been wanting, why will you not be a generous rain and relieve a woman who has suffered a half-year drought?" So Dongxi stayed another night. On the third day he insisted on going back and asked for his old clothes. Qingyun said, "I have already sent someone to deliver them to your lodgings." Dongxi said, "These clothes you gave me, I will return tomorrow." Qingyun said, "I only fear they do not suit you. Why not keep them as a keepsake?" She also brought out a box of trinkets, meaning to choose one as a gift for him. Dongxi saw that the box was full of pearls, jades, and precious curios, and took only an ivory fan pendant. Qingyun said, "That one I dare not give you—but this silver one I offer with respect." Dongxi said, "I am grateful for the thought alone; why give me something of silver?" Qingyun said, "The ivory one was a gift from the son of a Ministry of Rites official, with his mark carved on the side. Of all the gifts our benefactors give us, only silver may be spent. Hairpins, jade ornaments, and such trinkets must be kept. If the giver visits later and asks after it, it has to be here to show we have not forgotten him—so I dare not pass it on to anyone else. This silver fan pendant was made in advance for giving in return, with my name cast on the side, so I would like you to have it." Dongxi accepted it and went back.

paragraphs.zh: 明日，謂來祿曰：「看妓家極難做，只誤傾一盆水，費盡小心承奉人，唯恐不當人意，我豈可過吃她物？我宿兩晚，又吃四席酒，以銀四兩與之；受一銀扇墜，以金銀玉三枝簪答之，並這身衣服，你送去還他，我不再去。」原來前兩夜來祿亦得婢桂英伴宿，兩人情意綢繆，更相捨不得。臨行囑咐曰：「主人若再來嫖，又得再會。」故來祿只願得主肯嫖，力勸曰：「前日空手去，也這般相敬；今日有銀有簪送她，她不留宿，豈不留酒乎？再吃她何妨？」東溪信之，再與僕往，以銀與簪送之。
paragraphs.en: The next day he said to Lailu, 'It strikes me how hard a courtesan's house has to work. Over one carelessly spilled basin of water, they exerted such great care in attending to me, afraid only of displeasing me. How could I go on consuming her substance? I stayed two nights and ate four feasts of wine—give her four taels of silver. I accepted a silver fan pendant—answer it with three hairpins, of gold, silver, and jade. Take these clothes I am wearing back too. You deliver them; I am not going again.' As it happened, on the two previous nights Lailu had been given the maid Guiying to share his bed, and the two had grown tenderly attached and could hardly bear to part. As he left she had charged him, "If your master comes whoring again, we can meet again." So Lailu's one wish was for his master to keep whoring, and he urged him hard: "The other day you went empty-handed, and they still treated you with such respect. Today you have silver and hairpins to give her—even if she does not keep you the night, will she not keep you for wine? What harm in one more meal at her place?" Dongxi believed him and went again with the servant to present the silver and the hairpins.

paragraphs.zh: 慶雲得了，喜色滿面，持入誇與媽曰：「左相公送我銀四兩、簪三根。非妾趨奉得歡喜，豈送許多禮乎？」荀媽亦大喜，出叩謝曰：「本不當受厚禮，既蒙賜，還在寒舍消耍幾日。」東溪假辭要回，慶雲挽入內房，酒席已備。東溪曰：「又煩宴我，後何以報？」慶雲曰：「前日止是陪禮，今日所賜銀，已准後帳。」東溪曰：「前銀還前，我若嫖，須從今日算起。」由是日夜流連，忘其時月。來祿亦得再與桂英會，二人喜不自勝，侍奉加殷勤，使喚加聽命。主僕皆樂而忘歸矣。
paragraphs.en: Qingyun took the gifts, her face alight with joy, and carried them in to boast to Mama: "Mr. Zuo sent me four taels of silver and three hairpins. If I had not pleased him with my attentions, would he send so many gifts?" Mama Xun was delighted and came out to kowtow her thanks: "We really should not accept such generous gifts, but since you honor us with them, do stay and amuse yourself at our humble house a few more days." Dongxi made a show of insisting on going back; Qingyun drew him into the inner room, where the feast was already laid. Dongxi said, "Troubling you to feast me again—how shall I repay it later?" Qingyun said, "Last time was only an apology. The silver you gave today already counts toward the bill to come." Dongxi said, "That silver settles what went before. If I am to whore, the reckoning starts from today." From then on he lingered day and night and lost track of the months. Lailu, too, was reunited with Guiying; the two were beside themselves with joy, waited on their betters with redoubled zeal, and jumped to obey every order. Master and servant alike were having too good a time to think of going home.

paragraphs.zh: 東溪時或謂僕曰：「當要知止，銀費去多矣。」來祿便誘曰：「人有金帛，正要追歡買笑。相公掌如許大家，才得此幾月快心，縱此銀用盡，家中何患無吃著？不及趁此未老時行樂，人生寧有百年，何必作守銀虜也？」東溪心本迷戀，又累被來祿勸誘，並不知回頭。不覺半年餘，三百金幾盡。桂英時向來祿索衣服簪珥，來祿轉於主，主曰：「亦未知我用多少，須與荀媽算之，然後留盤纏回去。」及算過，已用過三百餘兩，盡貨物還之，尚未夠，盤纏全無辦。來祿曰：「小主本多，可去借些。」東溪曰：「不好開口。你去婉轉言之。」少山知父本嫖盡，撫掌大笑，令月華設席請父。及慶雲來餞行，然後東溪與子默默同歸。只謂緣遇使然，不知為計所陷。
paragraphs.en: From time to time Dongxi would say to his servant, "A man should know when to stop. I have spent a great deal of silver." Lailu would urge him on: "When a man has gold and silk, that is exactly when he should chase pleasure and buy smiles. You run such a great household, master, and only now have you had a few months of real enjoyment. Even if this silver runs out, what worry is there of food or clothing at home? Why not take your pleasure while you are not yet old? Does a life last a hundred years? Why be a slave to guarding silver?" Dongxi's heart was already besotted, and with Lailu urging him on again and again, he never thought of turning back. Before he knew it, more than half a year had passed and the three hundred taels were nearly gone. Guiying kept asking Lailu for clothes and hairpins, and Lailu passed the requests on to his master. The master said, "I do not even know how much I have spent. I must settle accounts with Mama Xun, and then keep back travel money for the trip home." When the reckoning was done, he had spent more than three hundred taels; even handing over all his goods did not cover it, and there was no travel money to be had at all. Lailu said, "The young master has plenty of capital. You could borrow some from him." Dongxi said, "I cannot bring myself to ask. You go and speak to him delicately." Shaoshan, learning that his father's capital had been squandered on pleasure to the last, clapped his hands and roared with laughter, and had Yuehua lay a feast for his father. Qingyun came too, to see him off. Then Dongxi and his son made the journey home together in silence. He put it all down to fate, and never knew he had been caught in a scheme.

paragraphs.zh: 按：尤物移人，麗色傾城，自昔慨之。安有入蠖中而皓然不滓者？東溪非為而來，直欲尋子而歸。其深知妓之迷人與嫖之破家深矣，乃入其中而掘泥揚波，更甚於子。不邇聲色、不溺情慾者既幾人哉！孔（子）曰：「吾未見好德如好色者也。」則賢之易色者信難矣。故院中語曰：「不怕深來不乖，只怕深乖不來。」則唯勿蹈其地者，可超然樊籠外矣。不然，未有不受其羈迷者。
paragraphs.en: Note: That a rare beauty can bewitch a man and a lovely face topple a city has been lamented since ancient times. Who ever stepped into the mire and came out white and unstained? Dongxi did not go there for pleasure; he only meant to find his son and bring him home. He knew full well how courtesans bewitch men and how whoring ruins a family—yet once inside, he churned the mud and rode the waves even deeper than his son. How few are the men who keep their distance from song and beauty and do not drown in desire! Confucius said, "I have never seen a man who loves virtue the way he loves beauty." One who is worthy enough to turn his love from beauty is truly rare. Hence the saying in the quarter: "They never fear that a steady customer will not be tamed; they only fear that the truly wary man will not come." Only the man who never sets foot on that ground can stand free beyond the cage. Otherwise none escapes its bonds and its spell.

stories.title_en: A Father Goes Looking for His Son and Falls into Prostitution Himself
